Ibn ʿAṭiyya mentioned from him that he recited "min khaṭa'ihim," with a fatha on the ṭāʾ and a kasra on the yāʾ. The kasra on the yāʾ should be understood as a hamza that was softened to an intermediate sound (bayn bayn, a sound between hamza and the vowel it resembles), so it resembled a yāʾ, because the standard way of softening it is this.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how did He call them liars, when they only guaranteed something which God knew they could not fulfill? And whoever guarantees something he cannot fulfill is not called a liar, neither when he guaranteed it nor when he failed, because in both states he does not fall under the category of liars, who are those who report about a thing not as it is? I say: God likened their state, since He knew that what they guaranteed had no way for them to fulfill it, so their guarantee in His sight was like the guarantee of liars, whose report about the subject of the report is not as it is. It is also possible that He meant: they are liars, because they said that while their hearts were contrary to it, like the liars who affirm a thing while there is disagreement in their hearts about it. End of quote.

It was mentioned earlier from Ibn ʿAṭiyya that "wa-l-naḥmil" is a statement (khabar), meaning a command, but its meaning is a report. These two commands take the place of a condition and its consequence, since the meaning is: if you follow our way, and sin reaches you in that according to what you claim, then we will bear your sins. If the meaning is this, then it becomes a report about a consequence that does not correspond, and it would be a lie.

﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens﴾: the burdens of their own selves from their disbelief and their sins, ﴿and burdens along with their burdens﴾: that is, other burdens, which are the burdens of those whom they misled, so they became the cause of their disbelief. He did not specify who will bear His burdens, so it is possible for the burdens of the wronged to be included in the burden being carried by the wrongdoer, as came in the hadith: "He will retaliate against the wrongdoer on behalf of the wronged by giving to the wronged from the good deeds of the wrongdoer. If the wrongdoer has no good deed left, then something is taken from the bad deeds of the wronged and cast upon him." In Sahih Muslim there is something with the meaning: Whoever calls to misguidance, and is followed in it and acted upon after him, then upon him is the burden of everyone who acted upon it among those who followed him, and that does not diminish their burdens in any way.

﴿And they will surely be questioned on the Day of Resurrection﴾: that is, a questioning of rebuke and reproach.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 29, verses 1–13 (part 1 of 3):

Surat al-'Ankabut has sixty-nine verses and is Meccan.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

[p. 138] ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾ ﴿Do people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and that they will not be tested?﴾ ﴿We certainly tested those before them, and God will surely know those who are truthful, and He will surely know the liars.﴾ ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they will outrun Us? Evil is what they judge.﴾ ﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting with God, then the term of God is surely coming, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And whoever strives, he strives only for himself. Indeed God is Free of need from the worlds.﴾ ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely remove their evil deeds from them and We will surely reward them with the best of what they used to do.﴾ ﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents. But if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them. To Me is your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely admit them among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in God," but when he is harmed for the sake of God, he considers the trial of people like the punishment of God. And if victory comes from your Lord, they will surely say, "Indeed we were with you." Is not God most knowing of what is in the breasts of the worlds?﴾ ﴿And God will surely know those who believe, and He will surely know the hypocrites.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "Follow our way, and we will bear your sins." But they will not bear anything of their sins. Indeed they are liars.﴾ ﴿And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens, and they will surely be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about what they used to fabricate.﴾

This surah is Meccan; this was said by Jabir, 'Ikrimah and al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said it is Madinan. Yahya ibn Salam said it is Meccan except from its beginning up to ﴿and He will surely know the hypocrites﴾. Its opening verses were revealed concerning some Muslims in Mecca who disliked fighting when it was enjoined in Medina; this was said by al-Suddi. Or they were revealed concerning 'Ammar and his like, of those who were tortured for God; this was said by Ibn 'Umar. Or concerning Muslims whom the disbelievers of Quraysh used to harm; this was said by Mujahid, and this is close to what came before. Or concerning Mihja', the freed slave of 'Umar, who was killed at Badr, and his parents and wife grieved over him, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said about him: "Mihja' is the master of the martyrs, and he is the first to be called to the gate of Paradise." Or concerning 'Ayyash, the brother of Abu Jahl, who betrayed and apostatized.

The word "al-nas" (people) has been explained as referring to the one concerning whom the verse was revealed. Al-Hasan said: "al-nas" here means the hypocrites, that is, that they would be left merely for their saying, "We believe."

The verb ﴿ḥasiba﴾ (to think, suppose) requires two objects. Al-Hawfi, Ibn 'Atiyyah and Abu al-Baqa' said: "an" and what follows it, with its complement, takes the place of the two objects. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ﴿an yaqūlū﴾ be a substitute (badal) for ﴿an yutrakū﴾. And "an yakūnū" is in the position of the accusative after the removal of the preposition, and they estimated it as "bi-an yaqūlū" (by their saying) and "li-an yaqūlū" (because they say). Ibn 'Atiyyah and Abu al-Baqa' said: when the preposition "bi" is assumed, it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the meaning with "bi" and with "li" differs. With "bi," it is like your saying: "I left Zayd in his condition." With "li," it means "for the sake of," that is: they supposed that their faith was the cause for leaving them alone. The explanation of the meaning, as the grammarians explain it, is their supposition that the leaving was for the sake of their uttering faith with the tongue.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "Where is the statement that indicates the content which the supposing requires?" I say: it is in His saying ﴿that they will be left to say, "We believe," and that they will not be tested﴾. Its estimate is: they supposed that their being left, while not being tested, was for their saying "We believe." So the leaving (al-tark) is the first of the two objects of ﴿ḥasiba﴾, and their saying "We believe" is the predicate; and as for "not being tested," it is a complement of the leaving, because it is of the leaving which has the meaning of making (al-taṣyīr), like his saying:

"So I left him as prey for the beasts, tearing him."

Do you not see that before bringing the supposing, you could say: "I left them untested because of their saying, 'We believe'," on the estimate of something established and settled before the lam? If you say: "that they say" is the cause of their being left untested, how can it validly occur as the predicate of a subject? I say: just as you say, "His going out was for fear of harm, and his striking him was for discipline." Here "discipline" and "fear" in your saying, "I went out for fear of harm and struck him as discipline," are two causes. And you also say: "I supposed his going out for fear of harm, and I thought his striking him for discipline," so you make them two objects just as you made them subject and predicate. End of quotation. This is a statement which contains confusion.

He first mentioned that the estimate "untested" is a complement [p. 140], meaning that it is a circumstantial clause, because he derived it from His saying ﴿and they are not tested﴾, and this is a circumstantial clause. Then he mentioned ﴿that they will be left﴾ here as the leaving which is of the making type, and this is not valid, because the second object of the making verb cannot be "for their saying": the estimate would become "that they will become for their saying, ﴿and they are not tested﴾," and this statement is not valid. As for the verse of poetry he gave as an example, it is valid, and "jazar al-sibā'" (prey of the beasts) can be the second object of "taraka" with the meaning of "ṣayyara" (made), unlike what was estimated in the verse.

As for his estimate of their leaving "untested because of their saying 'We believe'," on the estimate of something established and settled before the lam, it is not valid: since their leaving has the meaning of making them, "untested" would be a circumstantial clause, because a subject and predicate cannot be formed from their leaving in the sense of making them and their saying, since the leaving in the sense of making needs a second object; because "untested," in his view, is a circumstantial clause, not a second object.

As for his saying: "If you say, 'that they say,' to the end," it requires some understanding. That is because his saying "that they say" is the cause of their leaving; this is not so, because if it were a cause of it, it would be dependent, as it depends on the verb. But it is the cause of the omitted predicate, which is established or existing, and the predicate is other than the subject. If "for their saying" were a cause of the leaving, it would be part of its completion, and then it would need its predicate. As for his saying, "just as you say, 'His going out was for fear of harm'," then "for fear" is not a cause of the going out, but of the omitted predicate, which is established or existing.

﴿And they are not tested﴾. Al-Sha'bi said: the trial here is what the believers were charged with of migration, from which they were not left exempt. Al-Kalbi said: it is like His saying ﴿or He will confuse you into factions﴾ [al-An'am: 65]. Mujahid said: they are tested in their souls and their wealth.

﴿Those who were before them﴾: the believers, the followers of the prophets, who suffered from the trials by which a believer was split in two with a saw, and was combed with iron combs, and did not turn back from his religion.

﴿God will surely know﴾ through testing ﴿those who are truthful﴾ in their faith, ﴿and He will surely know the liars﴾. In it, "'ilm" is of the transitive type which takes one object in each of the two places. It is impossible for knowledge to newly arise in God, exalted is He. So the meaning is: His knowledge will be related to it as existing, just as it was related to it when it did not exist. The meaning is: the truthful will be distinguished from the liars among them. Or the knowledge is used to express the recompense, that is: He will make apparent the truthful and will punish the liar. The meaning of "they were truthful in their faith" is that their saying and belief agree with their deeds, and "the liars" is the opposite of that. 'Ali and Ja'far ibn Muhammad read ﴿fa-la-yu'lamanna﴾, the causative form of the verb "'alima" (to know), which takes one object by the transitive prefix hamza; the second object is omitted, that is: their ranks in the Hereafter, of reward and punishment; or the first object is omitted, that is: "He will make the people know those who are truthful," that is, He will publicize these in good and those in evil, and this will be in this world and the Hereafter; or it is from "'alāma" (to mark), which takes one object, that is: He will mark them with a sign suited to them, like His saying (ﷺ): "Whoever keeps a secret, God will clothe him in its mantle." Al-Zuhri read the first as the reading of the majority, and the second as the reading of 'Ali.

﴿Or do they think﴾: Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "am" is a counterpart (mu'āddilah) to the alif in His saying ﴿Do they think?﴾, and as if He, glorified and majestic, established both groups: He established the believers in their supposition that they will not be tested, and He established the disbelievers who commit evil deeds in harming the believers and other things, in their supposition that they will outrun the vengeance of God and make Him unable. End of quotation. But "am" here is not a counterpart to the alif in "ḥasiba," as was mentioned, because in that case it would be connected (muttaṣilah), and it has two conditions. One: a question particle (hamzat al-istifhām) must come before it, and this condition is present here. The second: a single noun must come after it, or something that has the status of a single noun. Example of a single noun: "Is Zayd standing, or 'Amr?" Example of something with the status of a single noun: "Did Zayd stand or sit?" Its answer is the specification of one of the two things, if the equivalence is between two things; or among things, if it is between more than two. Here after "am" there is a clause, and the answer cannot be one of the two things; rather "am" here is disjunctive (munqaṭi'ah), with the meaning of "bal" (rather), which is used for transition, meaning a shift from one matter to another, not for cancellation. The interrogative particle and the questioning here serve reproach, rebuke and denial, so they do not require an answer, because it means: how did this supposing occur?

﴿Those who commit evil deeds﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: he means al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Jahl, al-Aswad, al-'As ibn Hisham, Shayba, 'Utba, al-Walid ibn 'Utba, 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'it, Handhala ibn Abi Sufyan, al-'As ibn Wa'il, and their likes among the notables of Quraysh. End of quotation [p. 141]. Even if the verse was revealed because of a particular cause, it includes all who commit evil deeds, whether disbeliever or Muslim. Mujahid said: ﴿that they will outrun us﴾ means: that they will make us unable, so we will not be able to take vengeance. It was also said: that they will hasten the decree that is determined, and it was said: that they will flee from us and escape by themselves. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿that they will outrun us﴾ means that they will escape us; that is, the recompense will certainly reach them, while they did not hope to escape, nor did they entertain it in their minds; but because of their heedlessness, their little reflection on the outcome, and their persistence in sins, they are like one who anticipates it and hopes for it. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿and you will not be able to frustrate Him on earth﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 22], and ﴿Let not those who disbelieved think that they have outrun; indeed they will not frustrate Him﴾ [al-Anfal: 59]. If you ask: where are the two objects of "ḥasiba"? I say: the clause of "an," containing a predicate and a subject, takes the place of the two objects, like their saying: ﴿Or did you suppose that you would enter Paradise?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214]. It is also permissible that "ḥasiba" be taken to mean "qaddara" (estimated), and "am" be disjunctive. The meaning of the transition in it is that this first supposing is that one estimates he will not be tested for his faith, and this one thinks he will not be repaid for his evil deeds. End of quotation.

As for his saying: "they did not hope to escape," up to his saying "and hope for it," it is not as he mentioned. Rather, they believe that there is no resurrection and no recompense; especially the secret matter about which Ibn 'Abbas explicitly stated. What al-Zamakhshari mentioned is based on the belief of one who knows that God will repay him, but who hopes for God's pardon. As for his saying: "the clause of 'an' contains," up to the end of it, it should have been estimated in His saying ﴿that they will be left﴾, so that would take the place of the two objects; but he did not estimate what cannot validly be estimated. As for his saying: "It is also permissible that 'ḥasiba' be taken to mean 'qaddara'," then it is determined that "an" and what follows it are in the position of one object. Transitivization (al-tadmīn, i.e., the implicit borrowing of meaning) is not a regular analogical rule, and one does not resort to it except when there is a need for it, and there is no need for it here.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on surah 29, verses 1–13 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Evil is what they judge.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya said, in substance: "ما" (ma) is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul) and "يَحْكُمُونَ" (yahkumun) is its relative clause (silah). Or it is a specifier (tamyiz) in the sense of "شيء" (thing), and "يَحْكُمُونَ" is a descriptive clause. The object of the blame (al-makhsus bil-dhamm) is omitted, so the sense is: "that is, their judgment." End of quote. Whether "ما" is a relative pronoun in the nominative after "ساء" (sa'a), or an accusative specifier, is a known disagreement in grammar. Ibn Kaysan said: "ما" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), so the sense is "evil is their judgment." On this view the specifier is omitted, meaning: "evil in judgment is their judgment." Here "ساء" (sa'a) has the sense of "بئس" (bi'sa, "evil"). The rule for "بئس" when followed by "ما" and a verb was already discussed in full in al-Baqarah, in the words of God: ﴿Evil is that for which they sold themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:90]. The verb is in the present tense, "يَحْكُمُونَ" (yahkumun). It is said this signals that their judgment is blameworthy both now and in the future. It is also said that the present tense is used in place of the past for the sake of the verse-ending (fasilah), as a license of usage.

The apparent meaning is that "يَرْجُو" (yarju, "hopes") retains its ordinary sense. "لِقَاءَ اللَّهِ" (liqa'a Allah, "meeting God") means reaching the final outcome of the matter: death, resurrection and recompense. His case is compared to a servant who returns to his master from a long journey, and the master has learned what he did in his absence. If he did good, he is received with kindness, and if he did evil, he is met with the opposite of kindness.

﴿Surely the term of God is coming﴾: this means the term God has appointed and set for it, not the Self (of God) itself, which is inevitable. So let him hasten to do what fulfils his hope. Abu 'Ubayda said: "يَرْجُو" (yarju) means "يَخَافُ" (yakhafu, "fears"). The apodosis (jawab) of the conditional is evidently omitted, meaning: ﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting of God﴾ should hasten to good works that realise his hope, for what God has appointed of the meeting with His recompense is coming.

The apparent meaning of ﴿And whoever strives﴾ is: whoever strives against his own self by patience in acts of obedience, the fruit of his striving, which is the reward prepared for him, belongs only to him, not to God. God is free of need of him and of all the worlds. He imposed these duties only as a kindness to them.

﴿We shall surely remove from them their misdeeds﴾: this includes one who was an unbeliever and then believed and did good, for God drops the punishment for what he did before faith of unbelief and disobedience. It also includes one who grew up as a believer doing righteous deeds but who erred in some of his acts; God expiates that from him, and his misdeeds are overwhelmed by his good deeds.

﴿And We shall recompense them with the best of what﴾: that is, the best recompense for their deeds. Ibn 'Atiyya said: there is an omitted noun (mudaf) here, and the sense is: "the reward of the best of what they used to do." End of quote. This reading is not acceptable, because it implies that they are recompensed only for their best deeds, and nothing is said of the reward for their lesser good deeds, whereas they are recompensed for both the best and the good. The only way out is to remove "أَحْسَن" (ahsan) from its usual sense of comparative and take it to mean "حَسَن" (hasan, "good"), which is permissible. As for the reading given before, its sense is that they are recompensed with the best recompense for the deed. Since their deed merits a good deed being repaid with its like, they are given the best of its recompense, which is that it is multiplied tenfold.

These verses contain a stirring and spur to those who held back from the emigration (hijrah), to hasten to make up for what they neglected of it. They also praise the believers who hastened to emigrate, and honour their rank.

﴿And We enjoined upon man﴾: In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi it is related that it was revealed about Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, whose mother swore that she would neither eat nor drink until she died, or until he disbelieved. It was also said to be about 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a, who embraced Islam and emigrated with 'Umar. His mother loved him intensely and swore a similar oath. Abu Jahl and his brother al-Harith tricked him, and when he went out with them from Medina to see his mother, they bound him in chains. Each of them flogged him a hundred lashes, and they brought him back to his mother. She said: "He will remain in punishment until he disbelieves in Muhammad." This is in a long narration mentioned in the biographies (siyar).

﴿And We enjoined upon man concerning his parents﴾: that is, We commanded him to care for them and to show consideration toward them. The word "حُسْنًا" (husnan, "goodly") is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), described by the verbal noun of "وَصَّيْنَا" (wassayna, "We enjoined"), meaning: an enjoining of goodness, that is, enjoining that is good. Or it is in the accusative for emphasis (mubalaghah), meaning: it is in itself goodness.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: it may be in the accusative as an object (maf'ul), and this carries an encouragement that it be general in its meanings, as you say: "وَصَّيْتُكَ خَيْرًا" (wassaytuka khayran, "I enjoined you to good") and "أَوْصَيْتُكَ شَرًّا" (awsaytuka sharran, "I enjoined you to evil"), and by this he expresses the totality of what I said to him. It is better to do this without a preposition. The preposition in ﴿concerning his parents﴾ has the meaning: "We enjoined man concerning goodness towards his parents." A similar example is the verse of the poet:

"I marvelled at Dahma'a when she complains about us,
and at Abu Dahma'a when he enjoins us."

End of quote. The same is the saying of al-Hutay'a, enjoining his daughter Barra:

"I have enjoined upon Barra, a free-hearted one,
good concerning the dog, and evil concerning the mother-in-law."

On this reading the original is "بِخَيْرٍ" (bikhayr, "with good"), which is the second object. The "ba'" (ب) in ﴿bi-walidayhi﴾ and in "بِالْحَمَاةِ" (bil-hamah) and "بِالْكَلْبِ" (bil-kalb) is adverbial of place (zarfiyyah), meaning "in", that is: We enjoined man, in the matter of his parents, with good.

Ibn 'Atiyya also said: it is possible that the second object in ﴿bi-walidayhi﴾ is the second object, and "حُسْنًا" (husnan) is in the accusative by an implied verb whose sense is: "he should behave with goodness," and it is in the accusative like a verbal noun. In al-Tahrir it is said: "حُسْنًا" (husnan) is in the accusative according to the Basrans by repetition, meaning "We enjoined him goodness." It is also said to be in the accusative by detachment from the preposition, the sense being: "We enjoined goodness," meaning that it is accusative when the preposition is removed. The people of Kufa said: "We enjoined man that he do goodness," so a verb is supposed for it. End of quote. In this view there is an omission of "أن" (an, "that") and its clause while the operand is retained, which is not permissible according to the Basrans.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "We enjoined him to show kindness to his parents, or to bestow goodness upon his parents," that is, an act that is good, and something that is in itself good because of its surpassing goodness, as in His words: ﴿And speak to people goodly﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:83]. End of quote. This reading involves the governing of an omitted verbal noun while retaining its operand, which is not permissible according to the Basrans.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: "حُسْنًا" (husnan) may be taken as in the saying "زَيْدًا" (Zaydan), with an implied "اضْرِبْ" (idrib, "strike"), when you see him ready to be struck. You govern it by an implied first of the two, or "افْعَلْ بِهِمَا" (if' bihima, "do to both of them"), because the enjoining of the two is indicative of it, and what follows corresponds to it. It is as if he had said: "We said: Do good to both of them." End of quote.

'Isa and al-Jahdari read "حَسَنًا" (hasanan) with two fatHas. The majority read it with a damma on the ha' and sukun on the sin, and the two are like "البُخْل" (al-bukhl) and "البَخَل" (al-bakhal, both meaning "miserliness"). Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: its accusative is by a verb other than the earlier enjoining, because the enjoining has already taken its two objects together, unrestricted and in a prepositional phrase. So "حُسْن" (husn) here is an adjective set in place of the noun it describes, meaning "a matter that is good". End of quote. That is, "أَمْرًا حَسَنًا" (amran hasanan, "a good matter"), with "أمرًا" omitted and "حُسْن" put in its place. His saying "unrestricted" (mutlaqan) refers to the human being, and there is looseness in this, for it is rather an object (maf'ul bih). The unrestricted object is the verbal noun, because it is an object that is not restricted, in terms of its explanation, by a preposition, unlike the other objects. For you say: object of the verb (maf'ul bih), object of place (maf'ul fihi), object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ahu), object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). In the codex of Ubayy it reads: "إحسانًا" (ihsanan, "kindness").

﴿And if they strive with you﴾: that is, and We said: if they strive with you ﴿to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge﴾, that is, of its divinity. The negation of knowledge here means the negation of the object of knowledge: that is, to associate with Him something that cannot be a god and is not fit to be one. ﴿Then do not obey them﴾ in what they strive with you about, which is association. ﴿To Me is your return﴾ includes the enjoiner, the enjoined, the striver and the one striven against. ﴿Then I will inform you﴾, that is, I will recompense you ﴿of what you used to do﴾, whether of righteousness, or disobedience, or obedience, or rebellion.

God repeated what He has prepared for the believers, their entry ﴿among the righteous﴾, to stir souls to attain their ranks. The meaning of ﴿among the righteous﴾ is among their number. The rank of righteousness is noble. God reported it of Abraham, and Solomon asked for it, peace be upon them both. God also said that He would place those who obey God and His Messenger together with them. It is possible that the sense is: "in the reward of the righteous," which is Paradise.

When God had mentioned what He prepared for the sincere believers, He mentioned the condition of the hypocrites, people who believed with their tongues. When the unbelievers harmed them, they made that harm, which is the trial of people, a deterrent from faith, just as God's punishment deters believers from unbelief. That these verses were revealed about hypocrites is the view of Ibn Zayd. Al-Zajjaj said: they became anxious as one becomes anxious at God's punishment. This is the sense of the saying of Mujahid and al-Dahhak. Qatada said: it concerns those who emigrated, whom the polytheists returned to Mecca. It was also said: it concerns believers whom the polytheists took out to Badr, and they apostatised. These are the ones of whom God said: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:97].

﴿And if there comes a victory from your Lord﴾: that is, for the believers, ﴿they will surely say﴾, that is, the speakers will say: "We were harmed for God's sake," ﴿We are with you﴾, that is, following you in your religion, or fighting with you, supporting you, sharing with you in the spoils you obtain. This sworn clause exposes their deception, for if their faith were sound they would have endured the harm of the unbelievers. Even if these were about those who emigrated, they would have scheming in their affairs and would have faced every peril in their emigration.

It was read "لَيَقُولَنَّ" (layaqulanna) with a fatha on the lam. This was mentioned by Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi and al-Zamakhshari. "أَعْلَمَ" (a'lam) is a superlative (ism tafdil) meaning "more knowing of themselves," that is, of what is in their breasts. "بِمَا فِي صُدُورِهِمْ" (bima fi sudurihim, "of what is in their breasts") means: of what their breasts conceal of faith and hypocrisy. This is a question whose meaning is affirmation: God has already known what the hearts hide of good and evil.

﴿And God will surely know the hypocrites﴾ evidently means that what precedes this sentence concerns the hypocrites, as Ibn Zayd said. His knowledge of the believer is a promise to him of reward, and of the hypocrite a threat of punishment. Having mentioned the condition of believers and hypocrites, He mentioned the speech of the unbelievers, both their words and their belief. They were the leaders of Quraysh. Mujahid said: they used to say to those among them who believed: "We will not be raised, nor will you. If there is any sin upon you, it is upon us." It was also said that the speaker of this was Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and Umayya ibn Khalaf, who said to 'Umar: "If remaining in the religion of the fathers is a sin, then we will bear it on your behalf." It was also said that the speaker was al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: His words ﴿And let us bear﴾ inform that they will bear their sins, in the manner of a comparison with transfer. But they expressed it in the form of a command, because the command is more binding and stronger in confirmation in the soul of the hearer than a mere conditional statement. Of this kind is the saying of the poet:

"I said: call, and I will call, for more resonant
is the voice when two callers call."

End of quote.

Because it is a statement (khabar), their lying in it is apt. Al-Zamakhshari said: They told them to follow their way, which is their path that they were upon in their religion, and they told themselves to carry their sins, so the command was placed upon the command, and they meant: so that these two commands may be combined in their realization, that they follow our way and that we carry your sins. The meaning is that carrying the burden is made conditional upon following, and this is the statement of the chieftains of Quraysh, who used to say to those among them who believed: "We will not be resurrected, nor will you. If that should happen, then we will bear your sin on your behalf." End of quote.

His saying "fa-in 'asā" (then if perhaps) is a non-Arabic construction, not an Arabic one, because the conditional particle "in" does not enter upon "'asā," since it is a rigid verb (fi'l jāmid, a verb that does not inflect). Conditional particles do not enter upon a rigid verb. Also, "'asā" is not followed by "kāna," and he used "'asā" without a subject or predicate, and he did not use it as a complete verb.

Al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā, and Nūḥ al-Qāriʾ recited "wa-linaḥmil" with a kasra on the lam of the imperative (lām al-amr). It is also transmitted from ʿAlī, and it is the dialect of al-Ḥasan regarding the lam of the imperative. The word "al-ḥaml" (carrying) here is figurative: he likened bearing the consequences that result from sin to carrying a load on the back, and the sins to the thing carried. Mujāhid said: "naḥmil" here is from ḥimāla (surety, taking responsibility for another), not from ḥaml (carrying).

The majority reading is ﴿min khaṭāyāhum﴾ (from their sins). Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind, as mentioned by Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī, recited "min khaṭī'atihim" in the singular, and he said: its meaning is the category (jins), and what indicates this is that it is described by a plural pronoun. Ibn Khālawayh and Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī mentioned that this Dāwūd recited "min khaṭī'ātihim," using the sound plural of khaṭī'a with alif and ta'. Ibn ʿAṭiyya mentioned from him that he recited "min khaṭa'ihim," with a fatha on the ṭāʾ and a kasra on the yāʾ. The kasra on the yāʾ should be understood as a hamza that was softened to an intermediate sound (bayn bayn, a sound between hamza and the vowel it resembles), so it resembled a yāʾ, because the standard way of softening it is this.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how did He call them liars, when they only guaranteed something which God knew they could not fulfill? And whoever guarantees something he cannot fulfill is not called a liar, neither when he guaranteed it nor when he failed, because in both states he does not fall under the category of liars, who are those who report about a thing not as it is? I say: God likened their state, since He knew that what they guaranteed had no way for them to fulfill it, so their guarantee in His sight was like the guarantee of liars, whose report about the subject of the report is not as it is. It is also possible that He meant: they are liars, because they said that while their hearts were contrary to it, like the liars who affirm a thing while there is disagreement in their hearts about it. End of quote.

It was mentioned earlier from Ibn ʿAṭiyya that "wa-l-naḥmil" is a statement (khabar), meaning a command, but its meaning is a report. These two commands take the place of a condition and its consequence, since the meaning is: if you follow our way, and sin reaches you in that according to what you claim, then we will bear your sins. If the meaning is this, then it becomes a report about a consequence that does not correspond, and it would be a lie.

﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens﴾: the burdens of their own selves from their disbelief and their sins, ﴿and burdens along with their burdens﴾: that is, other burdens, which are the burdens of those whom they misled, so they became the cause of their disbelief. He did not specify who will bear His burdens, so it is possible for the burdens of the wronged to be included in the burden being carried by the wrongdoer, as came in the hadith: "He will retaliate against the wrongdoer on behalf of the wronged by giving to the wronged from the good deeds of the wrongdoer. If the wrongdoer has no good deed left, then something is taken from the bad deeds of the wronged and cast upon him." In Sahih Muslim there is something with the meaning: Whoever calls to misguidance, and is followed in it and acted upon after him, then upon him is the burden of everyone who acted upon it among those who followed him, and that does not diminish their burdens in any way.

﴿And they will surely be questioned on the Day of Resurrection﴾: that is, a questioning of rebuke and reproach.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 29, verses 1–13 (part 1 of 3):

Surat al-'Ankabut has sixty-nine verses and is Meccan.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

[p. 138] ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾ ﴿Do people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and that they will not be tested?﴾ ﴿We certainly tested those before them, and God will surely know those who are truthful, and He will surely know the liars.﴾ ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they will outrun Us? Evil is what they judge.﴾ ﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting with God, then the term of God is surely coming, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And whoever strives, he strives only for himself. Indeed God is Free of need from the worlds.﴾ ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely remove their evil deeds from them and We will surely reward them with the best of what they used to do.﴾ ﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents. But if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them. To Me is your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely admit them among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in God," but when he is harmed for the sake of God, he considers the trial of people like the punishment of God. And if victory comes from your Lord, they will surely say, "Indeed we were with you." Is not God most knowing of what is in the breasts of the worlds?﴾ ﴿And God will surely know those who believe, and He will surely know the hypocrites.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "Follow our way, and we will bear your sins." But they will not bear anything of their sins. Indeed they are liars.﴾ ﴿And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens, and they will surely be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about what they used to fabricate.﴾

This surah is Meccan; this was said by Jabir, 'Ikrimah and al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said it is Madinan. Yahya ibn Salam said it is Meccan except from its beginning up to ﴿and He will surely know the hypocrites﴾. Its opening verses were revealed concerning some Muslims in Mecca who disliked fighting when it was enjoined in Medina; this was said by al-Suddi. Or they were revealed concerning 'Ammar and his like, of those who were tortured for God; this was said by Ibn 'Umar. Or concerning Muslims whom the disbelievers of Quraysh used to harm; this was said by Mujahid, and this is close to what came before. Or concerning Mihja', the freed slave of 'Umar, who was killed at Badr, and his parents and wife grieved over him, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said about him: "Mihja' is the master of the martyrs, and he is the first to be called to the gate of Paradise." Or concerning 'Ayyash, the brother of Abu Jahl, who betrayed and apostatized.

The word "al-nas" (people) has been explained as referring to the one concerning whom the verse was revealed. Al-Hasan said: "al-nas" here means the hypocrites, that is, that they would be left merely for their saying, "We believe."

The verb ﴿ḥasiba﴾ (to think, suppose) requires two objects. Al-Hawfi, Ibn 'Atiyyah and Abu al-Baqa' said: "an" and what follows it, with its complement, takes the place of the two objects. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ﴿an yaqūlū﴾ be a substitute (badal) for ﴿an yutrakū﴾. And "an yakūnū" is in the position of the accusative after the removal of the preposition, and they estimated it as "bi-an yaqūlū" (by their saying) and "li-an yaqūlū" (because they say). Ibn 'Atiyyah and Abu al-Baqa' said: when the preposition "bi" is assumed, it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the meaning with "bi" and with "li" differs. With "bi," it is like your saying: "I left Zayd in his condition." With "li," it means "for the sake of," that is: they supposed that their faith was the cause for leaving them alone. The explanation of the meaning, as the grammarians explain it, is their supposition that the leaving was for the sake of their uttering faith with the tongue.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "Where is the statement that indicates the content which the supposing requires?" I say: it is in His saying ﴿that they will be left to say, "We believe," and that they will not be tested﴾. Its estimate is: they supposed that their being left, while not being tested, was for their saying "We believe." So the leaving (al-tark) is the first of the two objects of ﴿ḥasiba﴾, and their saying "We believe" is the predicate; and as for "not being tested," it is a complement of the leaving, because it is of the leaving which has the meaning of making (al-taṣyīr), like his saying:

"So I left him as prey for the beasts, tearing him."

Do you not see that before bringing the supposing, you could say: "I left them untested because of their saying, 'We believe'," on the estimate of something established and settled before the lam? If you say: "that they say" is the cause of their being left untested, how can it validly occur as the predicate of a subject? I say: just as you say, "His going out was for fear of harm, and his striking him was for discipline." Here "discipline" and "fear" in your saying, "I went out for fear of harm and struck him as discipline," are two causes. And you also say: "I supposed his going out for fear of harm, and I thought his striking him for discipline," so you make them two objects just as you made them subject and predicate. End of quotation. This is a statement which contains confusion.

He first mentioned that the estimate "untested" is a complement [p. 140], meaning that it is a circumstantial clause, because he derived it from His saying ﴿and they are not tested﴾, and this is a circumstantial clause. Then he mentioned ﴿that they will be left﴾ here as the leaving which is of the making type, and this is not valid, because the second object of the making verb cannot be "for their saying": the estimate would become "that they will become for their saying, ﴿and they are not tested﴾," and this statement is not valid. As for the verse of poetry he gave as an example, it is valid, and "jazar al-sibā'" (prey of the beasts) can be the second object of "taraka" with the meaning of "ṣayyara" (made), unlike what was estimated in the verse.

As for his estimate of their leaving "untested because of their saying 'We believe'," on the estimate of something established and settled before the lam, it is not valid: since their leaving has the meaning of making them, "untested" would be a circumstantial clause, because a subject and predicate cannot be formed from their leaving in the sense of making them and their saying, since the leaving in the sense of making needs a second object; because "untested," in his view, is a circumstantial clause, not a second object.

As for his saying: "If you say, 'that they say,' to the end," it requires some understanding. That is because his saying "that they say" is the cause of their leaving; this is not so, because if it were a cause of it, it would be dependent, as it depends on the verb. But it is the cause of the omitted predicate, which is established or existing, and the predicate is other than the subject. If "for their saying" were a cause of the leaving, it would be part of its completion, and then it would need its predicate. As for his saying, "just as you say, 'His going out was for fear of harm'," then "for fear" is not a cause of the going out, but of the omitted predicate, which is established or existing.

﴿And they are not tested﴾. Al-Sha'bi said: the trial here is what the believers were charged with of migration, from which they were not left exempt. Al-Kalbi said: it is like His saying ﴿or He will confuse you into factions﴾ [al-An'am: 65]. Mujahid said: they are tested in their souls and their wealth.

﴿Those who were before them﴾: the believers, the followers of the prophets, who suffered from the trials by which a believer was split in two with a saw, and was combed with iron combs, and did not turn back from his religion.

﴿God will surely know﴾ through testing ﴿those who are truthful﴾ in their faith, ﴿and He will surely know the liars﴾. In it, "'ilm" is of the transitive type which takes one object in each of the two places. It is impossible for knowledge to newly arise in God, exalted is He. So the meaning is: His knowledge will be related to it as existing, just as it was related to it when it did not exist. The meaning is: the truthful will be distinguished from the liars among them. Or the knowledge is used to express the recompense, that is: He will make apparent the truthful and will punish the liar. The meaning of "they were truthful in their faith" is that their saying and belief agree with their deeds, and "the liars" is the opposite of that. 'Ali and Ja'far ibn Muhammad read ﴿fa-la-yu'lamanna﴾, the causative form of the verb "'alima" (to know), which takes one object by the transitive prefix hamza; the second object is omitted, that is: their ranks in the Hereafter, of reward and punishment; or the first object is omitted, that is: "He will make the people know those who are truthful," that is, He will publicize these in good and those in evil, and this will be in this world and the Hereafter; or it is from "'alāma" (to mark), which takes one object, that is: He will mark them with a sign suited to them, like His saying (ﷺ): "Whoever keeps a secret, God will clothe him in its mantle." Al-Zuhri read the first as the reading of the majority, and the second as the reading of 'Ali.

﴿Or do they think﴾: Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "am" is a counterpart (mu'āddilah) to the alif in His saying ﴿Do they think?﴾, and as if He, glorified and majestic, established both groups: He established the believers in their supposition that they will not be tested, and He established the disbelievers who commit evil deeds in harming the believers and other things, in their supposition that they will outrun the vengeance of God and make Him unable. End of quotation. But "am" here is not a counterpart to the alif in "ḥasiba," as was mentioned, because in that case it would be connected (muttaṣilah), and it has two conditions. One: a question particle (hamzat al-istifhām) must come before it, and this condition is present here. The second: a single noun must come after it, or something that has the status of a single noun. Example of a single noun: "Is Zayd standing, or 'Amr?" Example of something with the status of a single noun: "Did Zayd stand or sit?" Its answer is the specification of one of the two things, if the equivalence is between two things; or among things, if it is between more than two. Here after "am" there is a clause, and the answer cannot be one of the two things; rather "am" here is disjunctive (munqaṭi'ah), with the meaning of "bal" (rather), which is used for transition, meaning a shift from one matter to another, not for cancellation. The interrogative particle and the questioning here serve reproach, rebuke and denial, so they do not require an answer, because it means: how did this supposing occur?

﴿Those who commit evil deeds﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: he means al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Jahl, al-Aswad, al-'As ibn Hisham, Shayba, 'Utba, al-Walid ibn 'Utba, 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'it, Handhala ibn Abi Sufyan, al-'As ibn Wa'il, and their likes among the notables of Quraysh. End of quotation [p. 141]. Even if the verse was revealed because of a particular cause, it includes all who commit evil deeds, whether disbeliever or Muslim. Mujahid said: ﴿that they will outrun us﴾ means: that they will make us unable, so we will not be able to take vengeance. It was also said: that they will hasten the decree that is determined, and it was said: that they will flee from us and escape by themselves. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿that they will outrun us﴾ means that they will escape us; that is, the recompense will certainly reach them, while they did not hope to escape, nor did they entertain it in their minds; but because of their heedlessness, their little reflection on the outcome, and their persistence in sins, they are like one who anticipates it and hopes for it. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿and you will not be able to frustrate Him on earth﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 22], and ﴿Let not those who disbelieved think that they have outrun; indeed they will not frustrate Him﴾ [al-Anfal: 59]. If you ask: where are the two objects of "ḥasiba"? I say: the clause of "an," containing a predicate and a subject, takes the place of the two objects, like their saying: ﴿Or did you suppose that you would enter Paradise?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214]. It is also permissible that "ḥasiba" be taken to mean "qaddara" (estimated), and "am" be disjunctive. The meaning of the transition in it is that this first supposing is that one estimates he will not be tested for his faith, and this one thinks he will not be repaid for his evil deeds. End of quotation.

As for his saying: "they did not hope to escape," up to his saying "and hope for it," it is not as he mentioned. Rather, they believe that there is no resurrection and no recompense; especially the secret matter about which Ibn 'Abbas explicitly stated. What al-Zamakhshari mentioned is based on the belief of one who knows that God will repay him, but who hopes for God's pardon. As for his saying: "the clause of 'an' contains," up to the end of it, it should have been estimated in His saying ﴿that they will be left﴾, so that would take the place of the two objects; but he did not estimate what cannot validly be estimated. As for his saying: "It is also permissible that 'ḥasiba' be taken to mean 'qaddara'," then it is determined that "an" and what follows it are in the position of one object. Transitivization (al-tadmīn, i.e., the implicit borrowing of meaning) is not a regular analogical rule, and one does not resort to it except when there is a need for it, and there is no need for it here.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on surah 29, verses 1–13 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Evil is what they judge.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya said, in substance: "ما" (ma) is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul) and "يَحْكُمُونَ" (yahkumun) is its relative clause (silah). Or it is a specifier (tamyiz) in the sense of "شيء" (thing), and "يَحْكُمُونَ" is a descriptive clause. The object of the blame (al-makhsus bil-dhamm) is omitted, so the sense is: "that is, their judgment." End of quote. Whether "ما" is a relative pronoun in the nominative after "ساء" (sa'a), or an accusative specifier, is a known disagreement in grammar. Ibn Kaysan said: "ما" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), so the sense is "evil is their judgment." On this view the specifier is omitted, meaning: "evil in judgment is their judgment." Here "ساء" (sa'a) has the sense of "بئس" (bi'sa, "evil"). The rule for "بئس" when followed by "ما" and a verb was already discussed in full in al-Baqarah, in the words of God: ﴿Evil is that for which they sold themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:90]. The verb is in the present tense, "يَحْكُمُونَ" (yahkumun). It is said this signals that their judgment is blameworthy both now and in the future. It is also said that the present tense is used in place of the past for the sake of the verse-ending (fasilah), as a license of usage.

The apparent meaning is that "يَرْجُو" (yarju, "hopes") retains its ordinary sense. "لِقَاءَ اللَّهِ" (liqa'a Allah, "meeting God") means reaching the final outcome of the matter: death, resurrection and recompense. His case is compared to a servant who returns to his master from a long journey, and the master has learned what he did in his absence. If he did good, he is received with kindness, and if he did evil, he is met with the opposite of kindness.

﴿Surely the term of God is coming﴾: this means the term God has appointed and set for it, not the Self (of God) itself, which is inevitable. So let him hasten to do what fulfils his hope. Abu 'Ubayda said: "يَرْجُو" (yarju) means "يَخَافُ" (yakhafu, "fears"). The apodosis (jawab) of the conditional is evidently omitted, meaning: ﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting of God﴾ should hasten to good works that realise his hope, for what God has appointed of the meeting with His recompense is coming.

The apparent meaning of ﴿And whoever strives﴾ is: whoever strives against his own self by patience in acts of obedience, the fruit of his striving, which is the reward prepared for him, belongs only to him, not to God. God is free of need of him and of all the worlds. He imposed these duties only as a kindness to them.

﴿We shall surely remove from them their misdeeds﴾: this includes one who was an unbeliever and then believed and did good, for God drops the punishment for what he did before faith of unbelief and disobedience. It also includes one who grew up as a believer doing righteous deeds but who erred in some of his acts; God expiates that from him, and his misdeeds are overwhelmed by his good deeds.

﴿And We shall recompense them with the best of what﴾: that is, the best recompense for their deeds. Ibn 'Atiyya said: there is an omitted noun (mudaf) here, and the sense is: "the reward of the best of what they used to do." End of quote. This reading is not acceptable, because it implies that they are recompensed only for their best deeds, and nothing is said of the reward for their lesser good deeds, whereas they are recompensed for both the best and the good. The only way out is to remove "أَحْسَن" (ahsan) from its usual sense of comparative and take it to mean "حَسَن" (hasan, "good"), which is permissible. As for the reading given before, its sense is that they are recompensed with the best recompense for the deed. Since their deed merits a good deed being repaid with its like, they are given the best of its recompense, which is that it is multiplied tenfold.

These verses contain a stirring and spur to those who held back from the emigration (hijrah), to hasten to make up for what they neglected of it. They also praise the believers who hastened to emigrate, and honour their rank.

﴿And We enjoined upon man﴾: In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi it is related that it was revealed about Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, whose mother swore that she would neither eat nor drink until she died, or until he disbelieved. It was also said to be about 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a, who embraced Islam and emigrated with 'Umar. His mother loved him intensely and swore a similar oath. Abu Jahl and his brother al-Harith tricked him, and when he went out with them from Medina to see his mother, they bound him in chains. Each of them flogged him a hundred lashes, and they brought him back to his mother. She said: "He will remain in punishment until he disbelieves in Muhammad." This is in a long narration mentioned in the biographies (siyar).

﴿And We enjoined upon man concerning his parents﴾: that is, We commanded him to care for them and to show consideration toward them. The word "حُسْنًا" (husnan, "goodly") is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), described by the verbal noun of "وَصَّيْنَا" (wassayna, "We enjoined"), meaning: an enjoining of goodness, that is, enjoining that is good. Or it is in the accusative for emphasis (mubalaghah), meaning: it is in itself goodness.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: it may be in the accusative as an object (maf'ul), and this carries an encouragement that it be general in its meanings, as you say: "وَصَّيْتُكَ خَيْرًا" (wassaytuka khayran, "I enjoined you to good") and "أَوْصَيْتُكَ شَرًّا" (awsaytuka sharran, "I enjoined you to evil"), and by this he expresses the totality of what I said to him. It is better to do this without a preposition. The preposition in ﴿concerning his parents﴾ has the meaning: "We enjoined man concerning goodness towards his parents." A similar example is the verse of the poet:

"I marvelled at Dahma'a when she complains about us,
and at Abu Dahma'a when he enjoins us."

End of quote. The same is the saying of al-Hutay'a, enjoining his daughter Barra:

"I have enjoined upon Barra, a free-hearted one,
good concerning the dog, and evil concerning the mother-in-law."

On this reading the original is "بِخَيْرٍ" (bikhayr, "with good"), which is the second object. The "ba'" (ب) in ﴿bi-walidayhi﴾ and in "بِالْحَمَاةِ" (bil-hamah) and "بِالْكَلْبِ" (bil-kalb) is adverbial of place (zarfiyyah), meaning "in", that is: We enjoined man, in the matter of his parents, with good.

Ibn 'Atiyya also said: it is possible that the second object in ﴿bi-walidayhi﴾ is the second object, and "حُسْنًا" (husnan) is in the accusative by an implied verb whose sense is: "he should behave with goodness," and it is in the accusative like a verbal noun. In al-Tahrir it is said: "حُسْنًا" (husnan) is in the accusative according to the Basrans by repetition, meaning "We enjoined him goodness." It is also said to be in the accusative by detachment from the preposition, the sense being: "We enjoined goodness," meaning that it is accusative when the preposition is removed. The people of Kufa said: "We enjoined man that he do goodness," so a verb is supposed for it. End of quote. In this view there is an omission of "أن" (an, "that") and its clause while the operand is retained, which is not permissible according to the Basrans.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "We enjoined him to show kindness to his parents, or to bestow goodness upon his parents," that is, an act that is good, and something that is in itself good because of its surpassing goodness, as in His words: ﴿And speak to people goodly﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:83]. End of quote. This reading involves the governing of an omitted verbal noun while retaining its operand, which is not permissible according to the Basrans.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: "حُسْنًا" (husnan) may be taken as in the saying "زَيْدًا" (Zaydan), with an implied "اضْرِبْ" (idrib, "strike"), when you see him ready to be struck. You govern it by an implied first of the two, or "افْعَلْ بِهِمَا" (if' bihima, "do to both of them"), because the enjoining of the two is indicative of it, and what follows corresponds to it. It is as if he had said: "We said: Do good to both of them." End of quote.

'Isa and al-Jahdari read "حَسَنًا" (hasanan) with two fatHas. The majority read it with a damma on the ha' and sukun on the sin, and the two are like "البُخْل" (al-bukhl) and "البَخَل" (al-bakhal, both meaning "miserliness"). Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: its accusative is by a verb other than the earlier enjoining, because the enjoining has already taken its two objects together, unrestricted and in a prepositional phrase. So "حُسْن" (husn) here is an adjective set in place of the noun it describes, meaning "a matter that is good". End of quote. That is, "أَمْرًا حَسَنًا" (amran hasanan, "a good matter"), with "أمرًا" omitted and "حُسْن" put in its place. His saying "unrestricted" (mutlaqan) refers to the human being, and there is looseness in this, for it is rather an object (maf'ul bih). The unrestricted object is the verbal noun, because it is an object that is not restricted, in terms of its explanation, by a preposition, unlike the other objects. For you say: object of the verb (maf'ul bih), object of place (maf'ul fihi), object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ahu), object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). In the codex of Ubayy it reads: "إحسانًا" (ihsanan, "kindness").

﴿And if they strive with you﴾: that is, and We said: if they strive with you ﴿to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge﴾, that is, of its divinity. The negation of knowledge here means the negation of the object of knowledge: that is, to associate with Him something that cannot be a god and is not fit to be one. ﴿Then do not obey them﴾ in what they strive with you about, which is association. ﴿To Me is your return﴾ includes the enjoiner, the enjoined, the striver and the one striven against. ﴿Then I will inform you﴾, that is, I will recompense you ﴿of what you used to do﴾, whether of righteousness, or disobedience, or obedience, or rebellion.

God repeated what He has prepared for the believers, their entry ﴿among the righteous﴾, to stir souls to attain their ranks. The meaning of ﴿among the righteous﴾ is among their number. The rank of righteousness is noble. God reported it of Abraham, and Solomon asked for it, peace be upon them both. God also said that He would place those who obey God and His Messenger together with them. It is possible that the sense is: "in the reward of the righteous," which is Paradise.

When God had mentioned what He prepared for the sincere believers, He mentioned the condition of the hypocrites, people who believed with their tongues. When the unbelievers harmed them, they made that harm, which is the trial of people, a deterrent from faith, just as God's punishment deters believers from unbelief. That these verses were revealed about hypocrites is the view of Ibn Zayd. Al-Zajjaj said: they became anxious as one becomes anxious at God's punishment. This is the sense of the saying of Mujahid and al-Dahhak. Qatada said: it concerns those who emigrated, whom the polytheists returned to Mecca. It was also said: it concerns believers whom the polytheists took out to Badr, and they apostatised. These are the ones of whom God said: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:97].

﴿And if there comes a victory from your Lord﴾: that is, for the believers, ﴿they will surely say﴾, that is, the speakers will say: "We were harmed for God's sake," ﴿We are with you﴾, that is, following you in your religion, or fighting with you, supporting you, sharing with you in the spoils you obtain. This sworn clause exposes their deception, for if their faith were sound they would have endured the harm of the unbelievers. Even if these were about those who emigrated, they would have scheming in their affairs and would have faced every peril in their emigration.

It was read "لَيَقُولَنَّ" (layaqulanna) with a fatha on the lam. This was mentioned by Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi and al-Zamakhshari. "أَعْلَمَ" (a'lam) is a superlative (ism tafdil) meaning "more knowing of themselves," that is, of what is in their breasts. "بِمَا فِي صُدُورِهِمْ" (bima fi sudurihim, "of what is in their breasts") means: of what their breasts conceal of faith and hypocrisy. This is a question whose meaning is affirmation: God has already known what the hearts hide of good and evil.

﴿And God will surely know the hypocrites﴾ evidently means that what precedes this sentence concerns the hypocrites, as Ibn Zayd said. His knowledge of the believer is a promise to him of reward, and of the hypocrite a threat of punishment. Having mentioned the condition of believers and hypocrites, He mentioned the speech of the unbelievers, both their words and their belief. They were the leaders of Quraysh. Mujahid said: they used to say to those among them who believed: "We will not be raised, nor will you. If there is any sin upon you, it is upon us." It was also said that the speaker of this was Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and Umayya ibn Khalaf, who said to 'Umar: "If remaining in the religion of the fathers is a sin, then we will bear it on your behalf." It was also said that the speaker was al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: His words ﴿And let us bear﴾ inform that they will bear their sins, in the manner of a comparison with transfer. But they expressed it in the form of a command, because the command is more binding and stronger in confirmation in the soul of the hearer than a mere conditional statement. Of this kind is the saying of the poet:

"I said: call, and I will call, for more resonant
is the voice when two callers call."

End of quote.

Because it is a statement (khabar), their lying in it is apt. Al-Zamakhshari said: They told them to follow their way, which is their path that they were upon in their religion, and they told themselves to carry their sins, so the command was placed upon the command, and they meant: so that these two commands may be combined in their realization, that they follow our way and that we carry your sins. The meaning is that carrying the burden is made conditional upon following, and this is the statement of the chieftains of Quraysh, who used to say to those among them who believed: "We will not be resurrected, nor will you. If that should happen, then we will bear your sin on your behalf." End of quote.

His saying "fa-in 'asā" (then if perhaps) is a non-Arabic construction, not an Arabic one, because the conditional particle "in" does not enter upon "'asā," since it is a rigid verb (fi'l jāmid, a verb that does not inflect). Conditional particles do not enter upon a rigid verb. Also, "'asā" is not followed by "kāna," and he used "'asā" without a subject or predicate, and he did not use it as a complete verb.

Al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā, and Nūḥ al-Qāriʾ recited "wa-linaḥmil" with a kasra on the lam of the imperative (lām al-amr). It is also transmitted from ʿAlī, and it is the dialect of al-Ḥasan regarding the lam of the imperative. The word "al-ḥaml" (carrying) here is figurative: he likened bearing the consequences that result from sin to carrying a load on the back, and the sins to the thing carried. Mujāhid said: "naḥmil" here is from ḥimāla (surety, taking responsibility for another), not from ḥaml (carrying).

The majority reading is ﴿min khaṭāyāhum﴾ (from their sins). Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind, as mentioned by Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī, recited "min khaṭī'atihim" in the singular, and he said: its meaning is the category (jins), and what indicates this is that it is described by a plural pronoun. Ibn Khālawayh and Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī mentioned that this Dāwūd recited "min khaṭī'ātihim," using the sound plural of khaṭī'a with alif and ta'. Ibn ʿAṭiyya mentioned from him that he recited "min khaṭa'ihim," with a fatha on the ṭāʾ and a kasra on the yāʾ. The kasra on the yāʾ should be understood as a hamza that was softened to an intermediate sound (bayn bayn, a sound between hamza and the vowel it resembles), so it resembled a yāʾ, because the standard way of softening it is this.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how did He call them liars, when they only guaranteed something which God knew they could not fulfill? And whoever guarantees something he cannot fulfill is not called a liar, neither when he guaranteed it nor when he failed, because in both states he does not fall under the category of liars, who are those who report about a thing not as it is? I say: God likened their state, since He knew that what they guaranteed had no way for them to fulfill it, so their guarantee in His sight was like the guarantee of liars, whose report about the subject of the report is not as it is. It is also possible that He meant: they are liars, because they said that while their hearts were contrary to it, like the liars who affirm a thing while there is disagreement in their hearts about it. End of quote.

It was mentioned earlier from Ibn ʿAṭiyya that "wa-l-naḥmil" is a statement (khabar), meaning a command, but its meaning is a report. These two commands take the place of a condition and its consequence, since the meaning is: if you follow our way, and sin reaches you in that according to what you claim, then we will bear your sins. If the meaning is this, then it becomes a report about a consequence that does not correspond, and it would be a lie.

﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens﴾: the burdens of their own selves from their disbelief and their sins, ﴿and burdens along with their burdens﴾: that is, other burdens, which are the burdens of those whom they misled, so they became the cause of their disbelief. He did not specify who will bear His burdens, so it is possible for the burdens of the wronged to be included in the burden being carried by the wrongdoer, as came in the hadith: "He will retaliate against the wrongdoer on behalf of the wronged by giving to the wronged from the good deeds of the wrongdoer. If the wrongdoer has no good deed left, then something is taken from the bad deeds of the wronged and cast upon him." In Sahih Muslim there is something with the meaning: Whoever calls to misguidance, and is followed in it and acted upon after him, then upon him is the burden of everyone who acted upon it among those who followed him, and that does not diminish their burdens in any way.

﴿And they will surely be questioned on the Day of Resurrection﴾: that is, a questioning of rebuke and reproach.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 29, verses 1–13 (part 1 of 3):

Surat al-'Ankabut has sixty-nine verses and is Meccan.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

[p. 138] ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾ ﴿Do people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and that they will not be tested?﴾ ﴿We certainly tested those before them, and God will surely know those who are truthful, and He will surely know the liars.﴾ ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they will outrun Us? Evil is what they judge.﴾ ﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting with God, then the term of God is surely coming, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And whoever strives, he strives only for himself. Indeed God is Free of need from the worlds.﴾ ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely remove their evil deeds from them and We will surely reward them with the best of what they used to do.﴾ ﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents. But if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them. To Me is your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely admit them among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in God," but when he is harmed for the sake of God, he considers the trial of people like the punishment of God. And if victory comes from your Lord, they will surely say, "Indeed we were with you." Is not God most knowing of what is in the breasts of the worlds?﴾ ﴿And God will surely know those who believe, and He will surely know the hypocrites.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "Follow our way, and we will bear your sins." But they will not bear anything of their sins. Indeed they are liars.﴾ ﴿And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens, and they will surely be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about what they used to fabricate.﴾

This surah is Meccan; this was said by Jabir, 'Ikrimah and al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said it is Madinan. Yahya ibn Salam said it is Meccan except from its beginning up to ﴿and He will surely know the hypocrites﴾. Its opening verses were revealed concerning some Muslims in Mecca who disliked fighting when it was enjoined in Medina; this was said by al-Suddi. Or they were revealed concerning 'Ammar and his like, of those who were tortured for God; this was said by Ibn 'Umar. Or concerning Muslims whom the disbelievers of Quraysh used to harm; this was said by Mujahid, and this is close to what came before. Or concerning Mihja', the freed slave of 'Umar, who was killed at Badr, and his parents and wife grieved over him, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said about him: "Mihja' is the master of the martyrs, and he is the first to be called to the gate of Paradise." Or concerning 'Ayyash, the brother of Abu Jahl, who betrayed and apostatized.

The word "al-nas" (people) has been explained as referring to the one concerning whom the verse was revealed. Al-Hasan said: "al-nas" here means the hypocrites, that is, that they would be left merely for their saying, "We believe."

The verb ﴿ḥasiba﴾ (to think, suppose) requires two objects. Al-Hawfi, Ibn 'Atiyyah and Abu al-Baqa' said: "an" and what follows it, with its complement, takes the place of the two objects. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ﴿an yaqūlū﴾ be a substitute (badal) for ﴿an yutrakū﴾. And "an yakūnū" is in the position of the accusative after the removal of the preposition, and they estimated it as "bi-an yaqūlū" (by their saying) and "li-an yaqūlū" (because they say). Ibn 'Atiyyah and Abu al-Baqa' said: when the preposition "bi" is assumed, it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the meaning with "bi" and with "li" differs. With "bi," it is like your saying: "I left Zayd in his condition." With "li," it means "for the sake of," that is: they supposed that their faith was the cause for leaving them alone. The explanation of the meaning, as the grammarians explain it, is their supposition that the leaving was for the sake of their uttering faith with the tongue.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "Where is the statement that indicates the content which the supposing requires?" I say: it is in His saying ﴿that they will be left to say, "We believe," and that they will not be tested﴾. Its estimate is: they supposed that their being left, while not being tested, was for their saying "We believe." So the leaving (al-tark) is the first of the two objects of ﴿ḥasiba﴾, and their saying "We believe" is the predicate; and as for "not being tested," it is a complement of the leaving, because it is of the leaving which has the meaning of making (al-taṣyīr), like his saying:

"So I left him as prey for the beasts, tearing him."

Do you not see that before bringing the supposing, you could say: "I left them untested because of their saying, 'We believe'," on the estimate of something established and settled before the lam? If you say: "that they say" is the cause of their being left untested, how can it validly occur as the predicate of a subject? I say: just as you say, "His going out was for fear of harm, and his striking him was for discipline." Here "discipline" and "fear" in your saying, "I went out for fear of harm and struck him as discipline," are two causes. And you also say: "I supposed his going out for fear of harm, and I thought his striking him for discipline," so you make them two objects just as you made them subject and predicate. End of quotation. This is a statement which contains confusion.

He first mentioned that the estimate "untested" is a complement [p. 140], meaning that it is a circumstantial clause, because he derived it from His saying ﴿and they are not tested﴾, and this is a circumstantial clause. Then he mentioned ﴿that they will be left﴾ here as the leaving which is of the making type, and this is not valid, because the second object of the making verb cannot be "for their saying": the estimate would become "that they will become for their saying, ﴿and they are not tested﴾," and this statement is not valid. As for the verse of poetry he gave as an example, it is valid, and "jazar al-sibā'" (prey of the beasts) can be the second object of "taraka" with the meaning of "ṣayyara" (made), unlike what was estimated in the verse.

As for his estimate of their leaving "untested because of their saying 'We believe'," on the estimate of something established and settled before the lam, it is not valid: since their leaving has the meaning of making them, "untested" would be a circumstantial clause, because a subject and predicate cannot be formed from their leaving in the sense of making them and their saying, since the leaving in the sense of making needs a second object; because "untested," in his view, is a circumstantial clause, not a second object.

As for his saying: "If you say, 'that they say,' to the end," it requires some understanding. That is because his saying "that they say" is the cause of their leaving; this is not so, because if it were a cause of it, it would be dependent, as it depends on the verb. But it is the cause of the omitted predicate, which is established or existing, and the predicate is other than the subject. If "for their saying" were a cause of the leaving, it would be part of its completion, and then it would need its predicate. As for his saying, "just as you say, 'His going out was for fear of harm'," then "for fear" is not a cause of the going out, but of the omitted predicate, which is established or existing.

﴿And they are not tested﴾. Al-Sha'bi said: the trial here is what the believers were charged with of migration, from which they were not left exempt. Al-Kalbi said: it is like His saying ﴿or He will confuse you into factions﴾ [al-An'am: 65]. Mujahid said: they are tested in their souls and their wealth.

﴿Those who were before them﴾: the believers, the followers of the prophets, who suffered from the trials by which a believer was split in two with a saw, and was combed with iron combs, and did not turn back from his religion.

﴿God will surely know﴾ through testing ﴿those who are truthful﴾ in their faith, ﴿and He will surely know the liars﴾. In it, "'ilm" is of the transitive type which takes one object in each of the two places. It is impossible for knowledge to newly arise in God, exalted is He. So the meaning is: His knowledge will be related to it as existing, just as it was related to it when it did not exist. The meaning is: the truthful will be distinguished from the liars among them. Or the knowledge is used to express the recompense, that is: He will make apparent the truthful and will punish the liar. The meaning of "they were truthful in their faith" is that their saying and belief agree with their deeds, and "the liars" is the opposite of that. 'Ali and Ja'far ibn Muhammad read ﴿fa-la-yu'lamanna﴾, the causative form of the verb "'alima" (to know), which takes one object by the transitive prefix hamza; the second object is omitted, that is: their ranks in the Hereafter, of reward and punishment; or the first object is omitted, that is: "He will make the people know those who are truthful," that is, He will publicize these in good and those in evil, and this will be in this world and the Hereafter; or it is from "'alāma" (to mark), which takes one object, that is: He will mark them with a sign suited to them, like His saying (ﷺ): "Whoever keeps a secret, God will clothe him in its mantle." Al-Zuhri read the first as the reading of the majority, and the second as the reading of 'Ali.

﴿Or do they think﴾: Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "am" is a counterpart (mu'āddilah) to the alif in His saying ﴿Do they think?﴾, and as if He, glorified and majestic, established both groups: He established the believers in their supposition that they will not be tested, and He established the disbelievers who commit evil deeds in harming the believers and other things, in their supposition that they will outrun the vengeance of God and make Him unable. End of quotation. But "am" here is not a counterpart to the alif in "ḥasiba," as was mentioned, because in that case it would be connected (muttaṣilah), and it has two conditions. One: a question particle (hamzat al-istifhām) must come before it, and this condition is present here. The second: a single noun must come after it, or something that has the status of a single noun. Example of a single noun: "Is Zayd standing, or 'Amr?" Example of something with the status of a single noun: "Did Zayd stand or sit?" Its answer is the specification of one of the two things, if the equivalence is between two things; or among things, if it is between more than two. Here after "am" there is a clause, and the answer cannot be one of the two things; rather "am" here is disjunctive (munqaṭi'ah), with the meaning of "bal" (rather), which is used for transition, meaning a shift from one matter to another, not for cancellation. The interrogative particle and the questioning here serve reproach, rebuke and denial, so they do not require an answer, because it means: how did this supposing occur?

﴿Those who commit evil deeds﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: he means al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Jahl, al-Aswad, al-'As ibn Hisham, Shayba, 'Utba, al-Walid ibn 'Utba, 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'it, Handhala ibn Abi Sufyan, al-'As ibn Wa'il, and their likes among the notables of Quraysh. End of quotation [p. 141]. Even if the verse was revealed because of a particular cause, it includes all who commit evil deeds, whether disbeliever or Muslim. Mujahid said: ﴿that they will outrun us﴾ means: that they will make us unable, so we will not be able to take vengeance. It was also said: that they will hasten the decree that is determined, and it was said: that they will flee from us and escape by themselves.
