'Ali and Ja'far ibn Muhammad read ﴿fa-la-yu'lamanna﴾, the causative form of the verb "'alima" (to know), which takes one object by the transitive prefix hamza; the second object is omitted, that is: their ranks in the Hereafter, of reward and punishment; or the first object is omitted, that is: "He will make the people know those who are truthful," that is, He will publicize these in good and those in evil, and this will be in this world and the Hereafter; or it is from "'alāma" (to mark), which takes one object, that is: He will mark them with a sign suited to them, like His saying (ﷺ): "Whoever keeps a secret, God will clothe him in its mantle." Al-Zuhri read the first as the reading of the majority, and the second as the reading of 'Ali.

﴿Or do they think﴾: Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "am" is a counterpart (mu'āddilah) to the alif in His saying ﴿Do they think?﴾, and as if He, glorified and majestic, established both groups: He established the believers in their supposition that they will not be tested, and He established the disbelievers who commit evil deeds in harming the believers and other things, in their supposition that they will outrun the vengeance of God and make Him unable. End of quotation. But "am" here is not a counterpart to the alif in "ḥasiba," as was mentioned, because in that case it would be connected (muttaṣilah), and it has two conditions. One: a question particle (hamzat al-istifhām) must come before it, and this condition is present here. The second: a single noun must come after it, or something that has the status of a single noun. Example of a single noun: "Is Zayd standing, or 'Amr?" Example of something with the status of a single noun: "Did Zayd stand or sit?" Its answer is the specification of one of the two things, if the equivalence is between two things; or among things, if it is between more than two. Here after "am" there is a clause, and the answer cannot be one of the two things; rather "am" here is disjunctive (munqaṭi'ah), with the meaning of "bal" (rather), which is used for transition, meaning a shift from one matter to another, not for cancellation. The interrogative particle and the questioning here serve reproach, rebuke and denial, so they do not require an answer, because it means: how did this supposing occur?

﴿Those who commit evil deeds﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: he means al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Jahl, al-Aswad, al-'As ibn Hisham, Shayba, 'Utba, al-Walid ibn 'Utba, 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'it, Handhala ibn Abi Sufyan, al-'As ibn Wa'il, and their likes among the notables of Quraysh. End of quotation [p. 141]. Even if the verse was revealed because of a particular cause, it includes all who commit evil deeds, whether disbeliever or Muslim. Mujahid said: ﴿that they will outrun us﴾ means: that they will make us unable, so we will not be able to take vengeance. It was also said: that they will hasten the decree that is determined, and it was said: that they will flee from us and escape by themselves. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿that they will outrun us﴾ means that they will escape us; that is, the recompense will certainly reach them, while they did not hope to escape, nor did they entertain it in their minds; but because of their heedlessness, their little reflection on the outcome, and their persistence in sins, they are like one who anticipates it and hopes for it. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿and you will not be able to frustrate Him on earth﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 22], and ﴿Let not those who disbelieved think that they have outrun; indeed they will not frustrate Him﴾ [al-Anfal: 59]. If you ask: where are the two objects of "ḥasiba"? I say: the clause of "an," containing a predicate and a subject, takes the place of the two objects, like their saying: ﴿Or did you suppose that you would enter Paradise?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214]. It is also permissible that "ḥasiba" be taken to mean "qaddara" (estimated), and "am" be disjunctive. The meaning of the transition in it is that this first supposing is that one estimates he will not be tested for his faith, and this one thinks he will not be repaid for his evil deeds. End of quotation.

As for his saying: "they did not hope to escape," up to his saying "and hope for it," it is not as he mentioned. Rather, they believe that there is no resurrection and no recompense; especially the secret matter about which Ibn 'Abbas explicitly stated. What al-Zamakhshari mentioned is based on the belief of one who knows that God will repay him, but who hopes for God's pardon. As for his saying: "the clause of 'an' contains," up to the end of it, it should have been estimated in His saying ﴿that they will be left﴾, so that would take the place of the two objects; but he did not estimate what cannot validly be estimated. As for his saying: "It is also permissible that 'ḥasiba' be taken to mean 'qaddara'," then it is determined that "an" and what follows it are in the position of one object. Transitivization (al-tadmīn, i.e., the implicit borrowing of meaning) is not a regular analogical rule, and one does not resort to it except when there is a need for it, and there is no need for it here.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on surah 29, verses 1–13 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Evil is what they judge.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya said, in substance: "ما" (ma) is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul) and "يَحْكُمُونَ" (yahkumun) is its relative clause (silah). Or it is a specifier (tamyiz) in the sense of "شيء" (thing), and "يَحْكُمُونَ" is a descriptive clause. The object of the blame (al-makhsus bil-dhamm) is omitted, so the sense is: "that is, their judgment." End of quote. Whether "ما" is a relative pronoun in the nominative after "ساء" (sa'a), or an accusative specifier, is a known disagreement in grammar. Ibn Kaysan said: "ما" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), so the sense is "evil is their judgment." On this view the specifier is omitted, meaning: "evil in judgment is their judgment." Here "ساء" (sa'a) has the sense of "بئس" (bi'sa, "evil"). The rule for "بئس" when followed by "ما" and a verb was already discussed in full in al-Baqarah, in the words of God: ﴿Evil is that for which they sold themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:90]. The verb is in the present tense, "يَحْكُمُونَ" (yahkumun). It is said this signals that their judgment is blameworthy both now and in the future. It is also said that the present tense is used in place of the past for the sake of the verse-ending (fasilah), as a license of usage.

The apparent meaning is that "يَرْجُو" (yarju, "hopes") retains its ordinary sense. "لِقَاءَ اللَّهِ" (liqa'a Allah, "meeting God") means reaching the final outcome of the matter: death, resurrection and recompense. His case is compared to a servant who returns to his master from a long journey, and the master has learned what he did in his absence. If he did good, he is received with kindness, and if he did evil, he is met with the opposite of kindness.

﴿Surely the term of God is coming﴾: this means the term God has appointed and set for it, not the Self (of God) itself, which is inevitable. So let him hasten to do what fulfils his hope. Abu 'Ubayda said: "يَرْجُو" (yarju) means "يَخَافُ" (yakhafu, "fears"). The apodosis (jawab) of the conditional is evidently omitted, meaning: ﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting of God﴾ should hasten to good works that realise his hope, for what God has appointed of the meeting with His recompense is coming.

The apparent meaning of ﴿And whoever strives﴾ is: whoever strives against his own self by patience in acts of obedience, the fruit of his striving, which is the reward prepared for him, belongs only to him, not to God. God is free of need of him and of all the worlds. He imposed these duties only as a kindness to them.

﴿We shall surely remove from them their misdeeds﴾: this includes one who was an unbeliever and then believed and did good, for God drops the punishment for what he did before faith of unbelief and disobedience. It also includes one who grew up as a believer doing righteous deeds but who erred in some of his acts; God expiates that from him, and his misdeeds are overwhelmed by his good deeds.

﴿And We shall recompense them with the best of what﴾: that is, the best recompense for their deeds. Ibn 'Atiyya said: there is an omitted noun (mudaf) here, and the sense is: "the reward of the best of what they used to do." End of quote. This reading is not acceptable, because it implies that they are recompensed only for their best deeds, and nothing is said of the reward for their lesser good deeds, whereas they are recompensed for both the best and the good. The only way out is to remove "أَحْسَن" (ahsan) from its usual sense of comparative and take it to mean "حَسَن" (hasan, "good"), which is permissible. As for the reading given before, its sense is that they are recompensed with the best recompense for the deed. Since their deed merits a good deed being repaid with its like, they are given the best of its recompense, which is that it is multiplied tenfold.

These verses contain a stirring and spur to those who held back from the emigration (hijrah), to hasten to make up for what they neglected of it. They also praise the believers who hastened to emigrate, and honour their rank.

﴿And We enjoined upon man﴾: In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi it is related that it was revealed about Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, whose mother swore that she would neither eat nor drink until she died, or until he disbelieved. It was also said to be about 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a, who embraced Islam and emigrated with 'Umar. His mother loved him intensely and swore a similar oath. Abu Jahl and his brother al-Harith tricked him, and when he went out with them from Medina to see his mother, they bound him in chains. Each of them flogged him a hundred lashes, and they brought him back to his mother. She said: "He will remain in punishment until he disbelieves in Muhammad." This is in a long narration mentioned in the biographies (siyar).

﴿And We enjoined upon man concerning his parents﴾: that is, We commanded him to care for them and to show consideration toward them. The word "حُسْنًا" (husnan, "goodly") is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), described by the verbal noun of "وَصَّيْنَا" (wassayna, "We enjoined"), meaning: an enjoining of goodness, that is, enjoining that is good. Or it is in the accusative for emphasis (mubalaghah), meaning: it is in itself goodness.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: it may be in the accusative as an object (maf'ul), and this carries an encouragement that it be general in its meanings, as you say: "وَصَّيْتُكَ خَيْرًا" (wassaytuka khayran, "I enjoined you to good") and "أَوْصَيْتُكَ شَرًّا" (awsaytuka sharran, "I enjoined you to evil"), and by this he expresses the totality of what I said to him. It is better to do this without a preposition. The preposition in ﴿concerning his parents﴾ has the meaning: "We enjoined man concerning goodness towards his parents." A similar example is the verse of the poet:

"I marvelled at Dahma'a when she complains about us,
and at Abu Dahma'a when he enjoins us."

End of quote. The same is the saying of al-Hutay'a, enjoining his daughter Barra:

"I have enjoined upon Barra, a free-hearted one,
good concerning the dog, and evil concerning the mother-in-law."

On this reading the original is "بِخَيْرٍ" (bikhayr, "with good"), which is the second object. The "ba'" (ب) in ﴿bi-walidayhi﴾ and in "بِالْحَمَاةِ" (bil-hamah) and "بِالْكَلْبِ" (bil-kalb) is adverbial of place (zarfiyyah), meaning "in", that is: We enjoined man, in the matter of his parents, with good.

Ibn 'Atiyya also said: it is possible that the second object in ﴿bi-walidayhi﴾ is the second object, and "حُسْنًا" (husnan) is in the accusative by an implied verb whose sense is: "he should behave with goodness," and it is in the accusative like a verbal noun. In al-Tahrir it is said: "حُسْنًا" (husnan) is in the accusative according to the Basrans by repetition, meaning "We enjoined him goodness." It is also said to be in the accusative by detachment from the preposition, the sense being: "We enjoined goodness," meaning that it is accusative when the preposition is removed. The people of Kufa said: "We enjoined man that he do goodness," so a verb is supposed for it. End of quote. In this view there is an omission of "أن" (an, "that") and its clause while the operand is retained, which is not permissible according to the Basrans.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "We enjoined him to show kindness to his parents, or to bestow goodness upon his parents," that is, an act that is good, and something that is in itself good because of its surpassing goodness, as in His words: ﴿And speak to people goodly﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:83]. End of quote. This reading involves the governing of an omitted verbal noun while retaining its operand, which is not permissible according to the Basrans.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: "حُسْنًا" (husnan) may be taken as in the saying "زَيْدًا" (Zaydan), with an implied "اضْرِبْ" (idrib, "strike"), when you see him ready to be struck. You govern it by an implied first of the two, or "افْعَلْ بِهِمَا" (if' bihima, "do to both of them"), because the enjoining of the two is indicative of it, and what follows corresponds to it. It is as if he had said: "We said: Do good to both of them." End of quote.

'Isa and al-Jahdari read "حَسَنًا" (hasanan) with two fatHas. The majority read it with a damma on the ha' and sukun on the sin, and the two are like "البُخْل" (al-bukhl) and "البَخَل" (al-bakhal, both meaning "miserliness"). Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: its accusative is by a verb other than the earlier enjoining, because the enjoining has already taken its two objects together, unrestricted and in a prepositional phrase. So "حُسْن" (husn) here is an adjective set in place of the noun it describes, meaning "a matter that is good". End of quote. That is, "أَمْرًا حَسَنًا" (amran hasanan, "a good matter"), with "أمرًا" omitted and "حُسْن" put in its place. His saying "unrestricted" (mutlaqan) refers to the human being, and there is looseness in this, for it is rather an object (maf'ul bih). The unrestricted object is the verbal noun, because it is an object that is not restricted, in terms of its explanation, by a preposition, unlike the other objects. For you say: object of the verb (maf'ul bih), object of place (maf'ul fihi), object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ahu), object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). In the codex of Ubayy it reads: "إحسانًا" (ihsanan, "kindness").

﴿And if they strive with you﴾: that is, and We said: if they strive with you ﴿to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge﴾, that is, of its divinity. The negation of knowledge here means the negation of the object of knowledge: that is, to associate with Him something that cannot be a god and is not fit to be one. ﴿Then do not obey them﴾ in what they strive with you about, which is association. ﴿To Me is your return﴾ includes the enjoiner, the enjoined, the striver and the one striven against. ﴿Then I will inform you﴾, that is, I will recompense you ﴿of what you used to do﴾, whether of righteousness, or disobedience, or obedience, or rebellion.

God repeated what He has prepared for the believers, their entry ﴿among the righteous﴾, to stir souls to attain their ranks. The meaning of ﴿among the righteous﴾ is among their number. The rank of righteousness is noble. God reported it of Abraham, and Solomon asked for it, peace be upon them both. God also said that He would place those who obey God and His Messenger together with them. It is possible that the sense is: "in the reward of the righteous," which is Paradise.

When God had mentioned what He prepared for the sincere believers, He mentioned the condition of the hypocrites, people who believed with their tongues. When the unbelievers harmed them, they made that harm, which is the trial of people, a deterrent from faith, just as God's punishment deters believers from unbelief. That these verses were revealed about hypocrites is the view of Ibn Zayd. Al-Zajjaj said: they became anxious as one becomes anxious at God's punishment. This is the sense of the saying of Mujahid and al-Dahhak. Qatada said: it concerns those who emigrated, whom the polytheists returned to Mecca. It was also said: it concerns believers whom the polytheists took out to Badr, and they apostatised. These are the ones of whom God said: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:97].

﴿And if there comes a victory from your Lord﴾: that is, for the believers, ﴿they will surely say﴾, that is, the speakers will say: "We were harmed for God's sake," ﴿We are with you﴾, that is, following you in your religion, or fighting with you, supporting you, sharing with you in the spoils you obtain. This sworn clause exposes their deception, for if their faith were sound they would have endured the harm of the unbelievers. Even if these were about those who emigrated, they would have scheming in their affairs and would have faced every peril in their emigration.

It was read "لَيَقُولَنَّ" (layaqulanna) with a fatha on the lam. This was mentioned by Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi and al-Zamakhshari. "أَعْلَمَ" (a'lam) is a superlative (ism tafdil) meaning "more knowing of themselves," that is, of what is in their breasts. "بِمَا فِي صُدُورِهِمْ" (bima fi sudurihim, "of what is in their breasts") means: of what their breasts conceal of faith and hypocrisy. This is a question whose meaning is affirmation: God has already known what the hearts hide of good and evil.

﴿And God will surely know the hypocrites﴾ evidently means that what precedes this sentence concerns the hypocrites, as Ibn Zayd said. His knowledge of the believer is a promise to him of reward, and of the hypocrite a threat of punishment. Having mentioned the condition of believers and hypocrites, He mentioned the speech of the unbelievers, both their words and their belief. They were the leaders of Quraysh. Mujahid said: they used to say to those among them who believed: "We will not be raised, nor will you. If there is any sin upon you, it is upon us." It was also said that the speaker of this was Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and Umayya ibn Khalaf, who said to 'Umar: "If remaining in the religion of the fathers is a sin, then we will bear it on your behalf." It was also said that the speaker was al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: His words ﴿And let us bear﴾ inform that they will bear their sins, in the manner of a comparison with transfer. But they expressed it in the form of a command, because the command is more binding and stronger in confirmation in the soul of the hearer than a mere conditional statement. Of this kind is the saying of the poet:

"I said: call, and I will call, for more resonant
is the voice when two callers call."

End of quote.

Because it is a statement (khabar), their lying in it is apt. Al-Zamakhshari said: They told them to follow their way, which is their path that they were upon in their religion, and they told themselves to carry their sins, so the command was placed upon the command, and they meant: so that these two commands may be combined in their realization, that they follow our way and that we carry your sins. The meaning is that carrying the burden is made conditional upon following, and this is the statement of the chieftains of Quraysh, who used to say to those among them who believed: "We will not be resurrected, nor will you. If that should happen, then we will bear your sin on your behalf." End of quote.

His saying "fa-in 'asā" (then if perhaps) is a non-Arabic construction, not an Arabic one, because the conditional particle "in" does not enter upon "'asā," since it is a rigid verb (fi'l jāmid, a verb that does not inflect). Conditional particles do not enter upon a rigid verb. Also, "'asā" is not followed by "kāna," and he used "'asā" without a subject or predicate, and he did not use it as a complete verb.

Al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā, and Nūḥ al-Qāriʾ recited "wa-linaḥmil" with a kasra on the lam of the imperative (lām al-amr). It is also transmitted from ʿAlī, and it is the dialect of al-Ḥasan regarding the lam of the imperative. The word "al-ḥaml" (carrying) here is figurative: he likened bearing the consequences that result from sin to carrying a load on the back, and the sins to the thing carried. Mujāhid said: "naḥmil" here is from ḥimāla (surety, taking responsibility for another), not from ḥaml (carrying).

The majority reading is ﴿min khaṭāyāhum﴾ (from their sins). Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind, as mentioned by Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī, recited "min khaṭī'atihim" in the singular, and he said: its meaning is the category (jins), and what indicates this is that it is described by a plural pronoun. Ibn Khālawayh and Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī mentioned that this Dāwūd recited "min khaṭī'ātihim," using the sound plural of khaṭī'a with alif and ta'. Ibn ʿAṭiyya mentioned from him that he recited "min khaṭa'ihim," with a fatha on the ṭāʾ and a kasra on the yāʾ. The kasra on the yāʾ should be understood as a hamza that was softened to an intermediate sound (bayn bayn, a sound between hamza and the vowel it resembles), so it resembled a yāʾ, because the standard way of softening it is this.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how did He call them liars, when they only guaranteed something which God knew they could not fulfill? And whoever guarantees something he cannot fulfill is not called a liar, neither when he guaranteed it nor when he failed, because in both states he does not fall under the category of liars, who are those who report about a thing not as it is? I say: God likened their state, since He knew that what they guaranteed had no way for them to fulfill it, so their guarantee in His sight was like the guarantee of liars, whose report about the subject of the report is not as it is. It is also possible that He meant: they are liars, because they said that while their hearts were contrary to it, like the liars who affirm a thing while there is disagreement in their hearts about it. End of quote.

It was mentioned earlier from Ibn ʿAṭiyya that "wa-l-naḥmil" is a statement (khabar), meaning a command, but its meaning is a report. These two commands take the place of a condition and its consequence, since the meaning is: if you follow our way, and sin reaches you in that according to what you claim, then we will bear your sins. If the meaning is this, then it becomes a report about a consequence that does not correspond, and it would be a lie.

﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens﴾: the burdens of their own selves from their disbelief and their sins, ﴿and burdens along with their burdens﴾: that is, other burdens, which are the burdens of those whom they misled, so they became the cause of their disbelief. He did not specify who will bear His burdens, so it is possible for the burdens of the wronged to be included in the burden being carried by the wrongdoer, as came in the hadith: "He will retaliate against the wrongdoer on behalf of the wronged by giving to the wronged from the good deeds of the wrongdoer. If the wrongdoer has no good deed left, then something is taken from the bad deeds of the wronged and cast upon him." In Sahih Muslim there is something with the meaning: Whoever calls to misguidance, and is followed in it and acted upon after him, then upon him is the burden of everyone who acted upon it among those who followed him, and that does not diminish their burdens in any way.

﴿And they will surely be questioned on the Day of Resurrection﴾: that is, a questioning of rebuke and reproach.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 29, verses 14–23 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people, and he remained among them for a thousand years less fifty years. Then the flood seized them while they were wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿So We saved him and the people of the ship, and made it a sign for the worlds.﴾ ﴿And Abraham, when he said to his people: "Worship God and fear Him. That is better for you, if you only knew.﴾ ﴿You worship, apart from God, only idols, and you invent a lie. Those whom you worship apart from God do not possess any provision for you. So seek provision from God, worship Him, and give thanks to Him. To Him you will be returned.﴾ ﴿And if you deny, then nations before you have denied. And upon the Messenger is only the clear delivery (of the message).﴾ ﴿Have they not seen how God originates creation and then repeats it? Indeed, that is easy for God.﴾ ﴿Say: "Travel through the earth and observe how He originated creation. Then God will produce the final creation. Indeed, God is competent over all things."﴾ ﴿He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wills, and to Him you will be turned back.﴾ ﴿You cannot escape (Him) on earth or in the heaven, and you have no protector or helper other than God.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of God and in His meeting—those have despaired of My mercy, and for those is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Kill him or burn him." But God saved him from the fire. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 24] ﴿And he said: "You have taken, apart from God, only idols out of affection among yourselves in the worldly life. Then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disavow others and some of you will curse others, and your refuge will be the Fire, and you will have no helpers.﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 25].

(p-145) He mentioned this story as consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), because of the harm he suffered from the disbelievers. He mentioned what the first of the messengers, Noah, suffered from his people during long periods, as consolation for the seal of the messengers, may the blessings of God be upon him. The waw in (wa-laqad) is a conjunctive waw, joining one sentence to another. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The oath in it is remote," meaning that the sworn-by element has been omitted while its particle and its response remain. In this there is the omission of the genitive object while the preposition is retained, and a preposition does not get detached from its government; rather, its object must be mentioned. The apparent meaning is that he remained among his people for this stated period, calling them to God. Ibn 'Atiyya also said: "It is possible that the stated period is the period of his residence among his people, from his birth until the drowning of his people." End of quote. But this is not, in my view, a possibility, because the remaining (labitha) is followed by the particle fa- which indicates sequence. There has been disagreement about the length of his lifespan, both when he was sent and when he died, a disagreement that is confused and contradictory, and we have left its recounting in our book, as it is found in the books of tafsir. Whether this is established in the language of the Arabs is a disputed matter in grammar. The jurists have built rulings on the permissibility of this. Also, expressing the stated period in this way, by mentioning the head of the number which has no larger head, is more effective and more conducive to the purpose than leaving the listener to feel the length of the duration of patience. It also removes the misconception that might arise from saying "nine hundred and fifty years," that this is by way of exaggeration rather than exact count; the exception removes this figurative misconception.

The event of Noah was mentioned in a more complete form than here, and there is disagreement about the number of those who believed and boarded the ship. The pronoun in (wa-ja'alnaha) may refer to the ship (al-safina) and may refer to the event and the story. He used the singular (ayah) and followed it with the closing (li-l-'alamin) because the rescue by ships is a familiar matter. So the sign is His, may He be exalted, rescuing the people of the ship at the time of need, and because it remained for years until people passed by it and saw it, so knowledge of it was attained by them, and this fits His saying (for the worlds). Abraham (Ibrahim) is in the accusative as a conjunction upon Noah (Nuhan). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Or upon the pronoun in (fa-anjaynahu)." He and al-Zamakhshari said: by supposing "udhkuru" (remember) as a substitute for it, being a badal al-ishtimal (inclusion apposition), since the times include what is in them. It has previously been established for us that (idh) is an adverb that is not used as an object, so it cannot be a direct object. The grammarians have often given the example that the governing element in it is udhkur (remember), because the Qur'an contains it. If it is an adverb of past time, then even if it were in the nominative, it would not be permissible for it to be governed by "udhkur," because the future does not occur within the past; it is not permissible to say "thumma amsi." But if it has been removed from past adverbial function and has been made subject to inflection, then it is permissible for it to be a direct object governed by "udhkur." Al-Nakha'i, Abu Ja'far, Abu Hanifa, and Ibrahim read (Ibrahimu) in the nominative, meaning: "And among the messengers is Ibrahim." This story is an illustration for the Quraysh and a reminder of the condition of their forefather Abraham in rejecting idols and calling to the worship of God. Nimrod and the people of his city were worshippers of idols.

The majority read (wa-takhluqna) as the imperfect of khalaqa, and (ifkan) with a kasra on the hamza and sukun on the fa'. Ali, al-Sulami, Awn al-'Uqayli, Ubada, Ibn Abi Layla, and Zayd ibn Ali read it with a fatha on the ta', the kha', and the lam, with shadda. Ibn Mujahid said: it is related from Ibn al-Zubayr, its origin being (tatakhalaqna), with two ta's, and one of them was deleted, according to the disagreement about which one is deleted. Zayd ibn Ali also read, according to what al-Ahwazi mentioned: (tukhalliquna), from the intensive form khallaqa. Ibn al-Zubayr and Fudayl ibn Zurqan read (afikan), with a fatha on the hamza and a kasra on the fa', and it is a verbal noun like al-kidhb (lie). Ibn 'Abbas said: (wa-takhluqna ifkan) is the carving of idols and their creation; he called them ifkan (falsehood) figuratively, from the perspective that they fabricate falsehood about them in that they are gods. Mujahid said: it is the fabrication of lies regarding the matter of the idols and other things. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ifkan" has two aspects: one of them is that it is a verbal noun like kidhb and li'b (play), and al-ifk is its lighter form, as kidhb and li'b are from their origins; and the other is that it is an adjective of the pattern fi'l, meaning: a creation that is falsehood, possessing falsehood and untruth. Their fabrication of falsehood is naming the idols as gods and partners with God and intercessors to Him; or he named the idols falsehood, and their work on them and carving them is a creation for falsehood. End of quote.

This alternating explanation by him regarding (wa-takhluqna ifkan) represents two opinions of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, and we have previously cited them from them. And their negation by His saying (who do not possess provision for you) is an argument based on a matter understood by both their common people and their elite: that idols are not provided with sustenance. Provision (rizq) may mean the verbal noun: they do not possess the ability to provide you with any of the provision. It may also mean the thing provided, i.e., they do not possess for you the giving or acquiring of provision. Provision was singled out for its place among creation. Then He commanded them to seek provision from the One who possesses it and gives it. He mentioned provision because the point is that they are unable to do anything about it, and He then specified it with the definite article because it indicates generality, since with Him are all the sustenances.

(and give thanks to Him) for His abundant blessings of provision and other things.

(and to Him you will be returned) that is, to His recompense; He informed them of the return and the gathering. Then He said: (and if you deny), that is: this is not something you originated, and nations of the messengers before you denied the same. It was said: they were the people of Seth, Idris, and others. It is related that Idris, peace be upon him, lived among his people for a thousand years, and a thousand people believed in him, corresponding to the number of his years, while the rest of them remained in denial.

(and upon the Messenger is only the clear delivery) The discussion of a similar sentence has already been given. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr, with a variant from him, read (tarawa) with the ta' of address. The rest of the seven read it with the ya'. The majority read (yubdi'u), the imperfect of abda'a; al-Zubayr, Isa, and Abu 'Amr, with a variant from him, read (yabda'u), the imperfect of bada'a. Al-Zuhri read (kayfa bada'a al-khalq) with the hamza lightened by converting it into an alif, so it disappeared in connected speech. This is a non-analogical lightening, as the poet said:

*Graze, O Fazara, may your pasture not be pleasant.*

The analogical lightening of this would be to make it between-between (bayna bayn). The fixing of their seeing the beginning of creation in His saying (have they not seen) and in (fa-unzuru kayfa bada'a al-khalq) is only for their witnessing the revival of the earth with vegetation and the bringing forth of things from non-existence into existence. His saying (then He repeats it) and His saying (then God produces the final creation) are not included within the seeing or the looking. So (thumma yu'iduhu) is not coordinated upon (yubdi'u), nor is (thumma yunshi'u) included within the manner of looking at the beginning; rather they are two independent sentences, informing from God, may He be exalted, about the return after death. What precedes these two sentences has been placed first as a way of indicating the possibility of that; so when it is possible, and the Truthful One has informed of its occurrence, it becomes necessary and definitively certain without doubt. Qatada said: (have they not seen) through evidences and reflection, how it is possible that God should restore bodies after death? Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: the meaning is: how He originates the creation of man and then returns him to other states, even to dust? Muqatil said: the creation here is the night and the day. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read al-nash'a here and in (al-Najm) and (al-Waqi'a) on the pattern fa'ala; the rest of the seven read al-nash'a on the pattern fa'la. They are like al-ra'afa and al-ra'fa, and they are two dialects, the shortened form being more common. Its accusative placement is as a verbal noun, either as a verbal noun not of the same root that fills the role of the act of creating, or by supposing its verb, meaning: "then you will be brought into being a bringing into being."

In the first verse He explicitly mentioned His name in (how God originates creation), then the pronoun was used in (then He repeats it). Here, the pattern is reversed: the pronoun was used for "originates," then He made it explicit in (then God produces), so that the two sentences would not be devoid of explicit mention of His name. Making it explicit here indicates the magnification of the final creation, the exalting of its matter, and the affirming of its existence, since the disbelievers disputed it. It is as if it were said: "then that same One who originated creation is the One who produces the final creation." So mentioning His name explicitly is more majestic in attributing the creation to Him. "Final" is an adjective of the creation; so there are two creations: a creation of origination from non-existence, and a creation of restoration. Then He mentioned an attribute of which the creation is part of His capabilities. Then He informed that He (punishes whom He wills), that is, His punishment, (and has mercy on whom He wills), His mercy. He began with punishment because the discourse is with the disbelievers who deny the messengers.

(and to Him you will be turned) that is, you will be sent back. Al-Zamakhshari said: The object of the two wills is explained and clarified in several places in the Qur'an, and it requires both of them from the disbeliever and the sinner if they do not repent, and from the one who is protected from sin and the penitent. End of quote. This is according to the path of Mu'tazilism (the rationalist school which holds that God is bound by justice and reason).

(and you cannot escape) that is, you cannot outrun what God wills for you. (on earth or in the heaven). If "the heaven" is taken to mean height, it is permissible, meaning: in towers and fortresses that rise high, and it would be specification after generalization. Or it is taken to mean the sky, in which case it needs a supposition: "if you were in it." A similar example is the saying of al-A'sha:

*Even if you were in a pit eighty cubits deep, and were raised up by the ladders of heaven,*
*The speech would surely surround you until you shake it, and you would know that I am not forbidden to you.*

And His saying: (If you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through) [al-Rahman: 33], on the supposition of judgment if you were in them. Ibn Zayd and al-Farra' said: the supposition is: "nor whoever is in the heaven," meaning: he would be unable if he disobeyed. Al-Farra' said: this is one of the subtleties of Arabic, and he recited the verse of Hassan:

*So whoever among you satirizes the Messenger of God and praises him and supports him, they are equal.*

That is, "and who will help him." According to the Basrī grammarians, this is only permissible in poetry, because it involves omitting the relative pronoun while retaining its clause. Even further from this view is the opinion of those who claimed that the implied meaning is: "You cannot escape from those on earth, among humans and jinn, nor from those in heaven, among the angels, so how could you overpower God?"

The majority of reciters read ﴿يَئِسُوا﴾ (yaʾisū, "they despair") with a hamza. Al-Dhimārī and Abū Jaʿfar read it without a hamza, replacing the hamza with a yāʾ. It is a threat, meaning: they will despair on the Day of Resurrection. It has been said that the meaning is "from My mercy." It has also been said that it means "from My religion," so I will not guide them. It has further been said that it describes their state, because the believer is always hopeful and fearful, whereas the disbeliever does not entertain such thoughts. Their situation, in the absence of His mercy towards them, is compared to the situation of one who has despaired of mercy.

The apparent view is that the statement ﴿وَإِن تُكَذِّبُوا﴾ (and if you deny) is part of God's speech, reporting Abraham's words, up to His statement ﴿عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾ (a painful punishment). It has also been said that these verses are a parenthetical interjection (iʿtirāḍ) within the speech of God, placed between the words of Abraham, and that they report the answer of his people. In that case the meaning is: "And if you deny Muḥammad..." The placing of this sentence as a parenthetical interjection refutes Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī, who claimed that an interjection cannot consist of two or more sentences. The purpose of this interjection is to console the Messenger (ﷺ), since he had been tested with the same kind of trials that his forefather Abraham had faced: the polytheism of his people, their worship of idols, their denial of him, and their attempts to kill him. The verses that come after the conditional sentence confirm what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought: the Oneness of God, His signs, a mention of the evidence of His power, and the return (to God).

*Graze, O Fazara, may your pasture not be pleasant.*

(and to Him you will be turned) that is, you will be sent back. Al-Zamakhshari said: The object of the two wills is explained and clarified in several places in the Qur'an, and it requires both of them from the disbeliever and the sinner if they do not repent, and from the one who is protected from sin and the penitent. (and you cannot escape) that is, you cannot outrun what God wills for you. (on earth or in the heaven). If "the heaven" is taken to mean height, it is permissible, meaning: in towers and fortresses that rise high, and it would be specification after generalization. Or it is taken to mean the sky, in which case it needs a supposition: "if you were in it." A similar example is the saying of al-A'sha:

*Even if you were in a pit eighty cubits deep, and were raised up by the ladders of heaven,*
*The speech would surely surround you until you shake it, and you would know that I am not forbidden to you.*

And His saying: (If you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through) [al-Rahman: 33], on the supposition of judgment if you were in them. That is, "and who will help him." According to the Basrī grammarians, this is only permissible in poetry, because it involves omitting the relative pronoun while retaining its clause. It has also been said that it means "from My religion," so I will not guide them. The majority read (wa-takhluqna) as the imperfect of khalaqa, and (ifkan) with a kasra on the hamza and sukun on the fa'. Ibn Mujahid said: it is related from Ibn al-Zubayr, its origin being (tatakhalaqna), with two ta's, and one of them was deleted, according to the disagreement about which one is deleted. Zayd ibn Ali also read, according to what al-Ahwazi mentioned: (tukhalliquna), from the intensive form khallaqa. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ifkan" has two aspects: one of them is that it is a verbal noun like kidhb and li'b (play), and al-ifk is its lighter form, as kidhb and li'b are from their origins; and the other is that it is an adjective of the pattern fi'l, meaning: a creation that is falsehood, possessing falsehood and untruth. Their fabrication of falsehood is naming the idols as gods and partners with God and intercessors to Him; or he named the idols falsehood, and their work on them and carving them is a creation for falsehood. End of quote.

This alternating explanation by him regarding (wa-takhluqna ifkan) represents two opinions of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, and we have previously cited them from them. Then He commanded them to seek provision from the One who possesses it and gives it. He mentioned provision because the point is that they are unable to do anything about it, and He then specified it with the definite article because it indicates generality, since with Him are all the sustenances.

The pronoun in (wa-ja'alnaha) may refer to the ship (al-safina) and may refer to the event and the story. He used the singular (ayah) and followed it with the closing (li-l-'alamin) because the rescue by ships is a familiar matter. He and al-Zamakhshari said: by supposing "udhkuru" (remember) as a substitute for it, being a badal al-ishtimal (inclusion apposition), since the times include what is in them. End of quote.

(and give thanks to Him) for His abundant blessings of provision and other things.

*Graze, O Fazara, may your pasture not be pleasant.*

It has also been said that it means "from My religion," so I will not guide them. It has further been said that it describes their state, because the believer is always hopeful and fearful, whereas the disbeliever does not entertain such thoughts. Their situation, in the absence of His mercy towards them, is compared to the situation of one who has despaired of mercy.

The apparent view is that the statement ﴿وَإِن تُكَذِّبُوا﴾ (and if you deny) is part of God's speech, reporting Abraham's words, up to His statement ﴿عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾ (a painful punishment). The verses that come after the conditional sentence confirm what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought: the Oneness of God, His signs, a mention of the evidence of His power, and the return (to God).

Even further from this view is the opinion of those who claimed that the implied meaning is: "You cannot escape from those on earth, among humans and jinn, nor from those in heaven, among the angels, so how could you overpower God?"

The majority of reciters read ﴿يَئِسُوا﴾ (yaʾisū, "they despair") with a hamza. Al-Dhimārī and Abū Jaʿfar read it without a hamza, replacing the hamza with a yāʾ. It is a threat, meaning: they will despair on the Day of Resurrection. It has been said that the meaning is "from My mercy." It has also been said that it means "from My religion," so I will not guide them. It has further been said that it describes their state, because the believer is always hopeful and fearful, whereas the disbeliever does not entertain such thoughts. Their situation, in the absence of His mercy towards them, is compared to the situation of one who has despaired of mercy.

The apparent view is that the statement ﴿وَإِن تُكَذِّبُوا﴾ (and if you deny) is part of God's speech, reporting Abraham's words, up to His statement ﴿عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾ (a painful punishment). It has also been said that these verses are a parenthetical interjection (iʿtirāḍ) within the speech of God, placed between the words of Abraham, and that they report the answer of his people. In that case the meaning is: "And if you deny Muḥammad..." The placing of this sentence as a parenthetical interjection refutes Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī, who claimed that an interjection cannot consist of two or more sentences. The purpose of this interjection is to console the Messenger (ﷺ), since he had been tested with the same kind of trials that his forefather Abraham had faced: the polytheism of his people, their worship of idols, their denial of him, and their attempts to kill him. The verses that come after the conditional sentence confirm what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought: the Oneness of God, His signs, a mention of the evidence of His power, and the return (to God).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 29, verses 14–23 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people, and he remained among them for a thousand years less fifty years. Then the flood seized them while they were wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿So We saved him and the people of the ship, and made it a sign for the worlds.﴾ ﴿And Abraham, when he said to his people: "Worship God and fear Him. That is better for you, if you only knew.﴾ ﴿You worship, apart from God, only idols, and you invent a lie. Those whom you worship apart from God do not possess any provision for you. So seek provision from God, worship Him, and give thanks to Him. To Him you will be returned.﴾ ﴿And if you deny, then nations before you have denied. And upon the Messenger is only the clear delivery (of the message).﴾ ﴿Have they not seen how God originates creation and then repeats it? Indeed, that is easy for God.﴾ ﴿Say: "Travel through the earth and observe how He originated creation. Then God will produce the final creation. Indeed, God is competent over all things."﴾ ﴿He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wills, and to Him you will be turned back.﴾ ﴿You cannot escape (Him) on earth or in the heaven, and you have no protector or helper other than God.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of God and in His meeting—those have despaired of My mercy, and for those is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Kill him or burn him." But God saved him from the fire. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 24] ﴿And he said: "You have taken, apart from God, only idols out of affection among yourselves in the worldly life. Then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disavow others and some of you will curse others, and your refuge will be the Fire, and you will have no helpers.﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 25].

(p-145) He mentioned this story as consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), because of the harm he suffered from the disbelievers. He mentioned what the first of the messengers, Noah, suffered from his people during long periods, as consolation for the seal of the messengers, may the blessings of God be upon him. The waw in (wa-laqad) is a conjunctive waw, joining one sentence to another. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The oath in it is remote," meaning that the sworn-by element has been omitted while its particle and its response remain. In this there is the omission of the genitive object while the preposition is retained, and a preposition does not get detached from its government; rather, its object must be mentioned. The apparent meaning is that he remained among his people for this stated period, calling them to God. Ibn 'Atiyya also said: "It is possible that the stated period is the period of his residence among his people, from his birth until the drowning of his people." End of quote. But this is not, in my view, a possibility, because the remaining (labitha) is followed by the particle fa- which indicates sequence. There has been disagreement about the length of his lifespan, both when he was sent and when he died, a disagreement that is confused and contradictory, and we have left its recounting in our book, as it is found in the books of tafsir. The exception from the thousand (al-istithna') has been used as evidence for the permissibility of exception from a number. Whether this is established in the language of the Arabs is a disputed matter in grammar. The jurists have built rulings on the permissibility of this. He distinguished between the specification (tamyiz) of the number from which the exception is made and the specification of the excepted number, because repetition within a single utterance is avoided in eloquence unless it serves a purpose such as magnification, awe, or emphasis. Also, expressing the stated period in this way, by mentioning the head of the number which has no larger head, is more effective and more conducive to the purpose than leaving the listener to feel the length of the duration of patience. It also removes the misconception that might arise from saying "nine hundred and fifty years," that this is by way of exaggeration rather than exact count; the exception removes this figurative misconception.

The event of Noah was mentioned in a more complete form than here, and there is disagreement about the number of those who believed and boarded the ship. The pronoun in (wa-ja'alnaha) may refer to the ship (al-safina) and may refer to the event and the story. He used the singular (ayah) and followed it with the closing (li-l-'alamin) because the rescue by ships is a familiar matter. So the sign is His, may He be exalted, rescuing the people of the ship at the time of need, and because it remained for years until people passed by it and saw it, so knowledge of it was attained by them, and this fits His saying (for the worlds). Abraham (Ibrahim) is in the accusative as a conjunction upon Noah (Nuhan). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Or upon the pronoun in (fa-anjaynahu)." He and al-Zamakhshari said: by supposing "udhkuru" (remember) as a substitute for it, being a badal al-ishtimal (inclusion apposition), since the times include what is in them. It has previously been established for us that (idh) is an adverb that is not used as an object, so it cannot be a direct object. The grammarians have often given the example that the governing element in it is udhkur (remember), because the Qur'an contains it. If it is an adverb of past time, then even if it were in the nominative, it would not be permissible for it to be governed by "udhkur," because the future does not occur within the past; it is not permissible to say "thumma amsi." But if it has been removed from past adverbial function and has been made subject to inflection, then it is permissible for it to be a direct object governed by "udhkur." Al-Nakha'i, Abu Ja'far, Abu Hanifa, and Ibrahim read (Ibrahimu) in the nominative, meaning: "And among the messengers is Ibrahim." This story is an illustration for the Quraysh and a reminder of the condition of their forefather Abraham in rejecting idols and calling to the worship of God. Nimrod and the people of his city were worshippers of idols.

The majority read (wa-takhluqna) as the imperfect of khalaqa, and (ifkan) with a kasra on the hamza and sukun on the fa'. Ali, al-Sulami, Awn al-'Uqayli, Ubada, Ibn Abi Layla, and Zayd ibn Ali read it with a fatha on the ta', the kha', and the lam, with shadda. Ibn Mujahid said: it is related from Ibn al-Zubayr, its origin being (tatakhalaqna), with two ta's, and one of them was deleted, according to the disagreement about which one is deleted. Zayd ibn Ali also read, according to what al-Ahwazi mentioned: (tukhalliquna), from the intensive form khallaqa. Ibn al-Zubayr and Fudayl ibn Zurqan read (afikan), with a fatha on the hamza and a kasra on the fa', and it is a verbal noun like al-kidhb (lie). Ibn 'Abbas said: (wa-takhluqna ifkan) is the carving of idols and their creation; he called them ifkan (falsehood) figuratively, from the perspective that they fabricate falsehood about them in that they are gods. Mujahid said: it is the fabrication of lies regarding the matter of the idols and other things. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ifkan" has two aspects: one of them is that it is a verbal noun like kidhb and li'b (play), and al-ifk is its lighter form, as kidhb and li'b are from their origins; and the other is that it is an adjective of the pattern fi'l, meaning: a creation that is falsehood, possessing falsehood and untruth. Their fabrication of falsehood is naming the idols as gods and partners with God and intercessors to Him; or he named the idols falsehood, and their work on them and carving them is a creation for falsehood. End of quote.

This alternating explanation by him regarding (wa-takhluqna ifkan) represents two opinions of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, and we have previously cited them from them. And their negation by His saying (who do not possess provision for you) is an argument based on a matter understood by both their common people and their elite: that idols are not provided with sustenance. Provision (rizq) may mean the verbal noun: they do not possess the ability to provide you with any of the provision. It may also mean the thing provided, i.e., they do not possess for you the giving or acquiring of provision. Provision was singled out for its place among creation. Then He commanded them to seek provision from the One who possesses it and gives it. He mentioned provision because the point is that they are unable to do anything about it, and He then specified it with the definite article because it indicates generality, since with Him are all the sustenances.

(and give thanks to Him) for His abundant blessings of provision and other things.

(and to Him you will be returned) that is, to His recompense; He informed them of the return and the gathering. Then He said: (and if you deny), that is: this is not something you originated, and nations of the messengers before you denied the same. It was said: they were the people of Seth, Idris, and others. It is related that Idris, peace be upon him, lived among his people for a thousand years, and a thousand people believed in him, corresponding to the number of his years, while the rest of them remained in denial.

(and upon the Messenger is only the clear delivery) The discussion of a similar sentence has already been given. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr, with a variant from him, read (tarawa) with the ta' of address. The rest of the seven read it with the ya'. The majority read (yubdi'u), the imperfect of abda'a; al-Zubayr, Isa, and Abu 'Amr, with a variant from him, read (yabda'u), the imperfect of bada'a. Al-Zuhri read (kayfa bada'a al-khalq) with the hamza lightened by converting it into an alif, so it disappeared in connected speech. This is a non-analogical lightening, as the poet said:

*Graze, O Fazara, may your pasture not be pleasant.*

The analogical lightening of this would be to make it between-between (bayna bayn). The fixing of their seeing the beginning of creation in His saying (have they not seen) and in (fa-unzuru kayfa bada'a al-khalq) is only for their witnessing the revival of the earth with vegetation and the bringing forth of things from non-existence into existence. His saying (then He repeats it) and His saying (then God produces the final creation) are not included within the seeing or the looking. So (thumma yu'iduhu) is not coordinated upon (yubdi'u), nor is (thumma yunshi'u) included within the manner of looking at the beginning; rather they are two independent sentences, informing from God, may He be exalted, about the return after death. What precedes these two sentences has been placed first as a way of indicating the possibility of that; so when it is possible, and the Truthful One has informed of its occurrence, it becomes necessary and definitively certain without doubt. Qatada said: (have they not seen) through evidences and reflection, how it is possible that God should restore bodies after death? Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: the meaning is: how He originates the creation of man and then returns him to other states, even to dust? Muqatil said: the creation here is the night and the day. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read al-nash'a here and in (al-Najm) and (al-Waqi'a) on the pattern fa'ala; the rest of the seven read al-nash'a on the pattern fa'la. They are like al-ra'afa and al-ra'fa, and they are two dialects, the shortened form being more common. Its accusative placement is as a verbal noun, either as a verbal noun not of the same root that fills the role of the act of creating, or by supposing its verb, meaning: "then you will be brought into being a bringing into being."

In the first verse He explicitly mentioned His name in (how God originates creation), then the pronoun was used in (then He repeats it). Here, the pattern is reversed: the pronoun was used for "originates," then He made it explicit in (then God produces), so that the two sentences would not be devoid of explicit mention of His name. Making it explicit here indicates the magnification of the final creation, the exalting of its matter, and the affirming of its existence, since the disbelievers disputed it. It is as if it were said: "then that same One who originated creation is the One who produces the final creation." So mentioning His name explicitly is more majestic in attributing the creation to Him. "Final" is an adjective of the creation; so there are two creations: a creation of origination from non-existence, and a creation of restoration. Then He mentioned an attribute of which the creation is part of His capabilities. Then He informed that He (punishes whom He wills), that is, His punishment, (and has mercy on whom He wills), His mercy. He began with punishment because the discourse is with the disbelievers who deny the messengers.

(and to Him you will be turned) that is, you will be sent back. Al-Zamakhshari said: The object of the two wills is explained and clarified in several places in the Qur'an, and it requires both of them from the disbeliever and the sinner if they do not repent, and from the one who is protected from sin and the penitent. End of quote. This is according to the path of Mu'tazilism (the rationalist school which holds that God is bound by justice and reason).

(and you cannot escape) that is, you cannot outrun what God wills for you. (on earth or in the heaven). If "the heaven" is taken to mean height, it is permissible, meaning: in towers and fortresses that rise high, and it would be specification after generalization. Or it is taken to mean the sky, in which case it needs a supposition: "if you were in it." A similar example is the saying of al-A'sha:

*Even if you were in a pit eighty cubits deep, and were raised up by the ladders of heaven,*
*The speech would surely surround you until you shake it, and you would know that I am not forbidden to you.*

And His saying: (If you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through) [al-Rahman: 33], on the supposition of judgment if you were in them. Ibn Zayd and al-Farra' said: the supposition is: "nor whoever is in the heaven," meaning: he would be unable if he disobeyed. Al-Farra' said: this is one of the subtleties of Arabic, and he recited the verse of Hassan:

*So whoever among you satirizes the Messenger of God and praises him and supports him, they are equal.*

That is, "and who will help him." According to the Basrī grammarians, this is only permissible in poetry, because it involves omitting the relative pronoun while retaining its clause. Even further from this view is the opinion of those who claimed that the implied meaning is: "You cannot escape from those on earth, among humans and jinn, nor from those in heaven, among the angels, so how could you overpower God?"

The majority of reciters read ﴿يَئِسُوا﴾ (yaʾisū, "they despair") with a hamza. Al-Dhimārī and Abū Jaʿfar read it without a hamza, replacing the hamza with a yāʾ. It is a threat, meaning: they will despair on the Day of Resurrection. It has been said that the meaning is "from My mercy." It has also been said that it means "from My religion," so I will not guide them. It has further been said that it describes their state, because the believer is always hopeful and fearful, whereas the disbeliever does not entertain such thoughts. Their situation, in the absence of His mercy towards them, is compared to the situation of one who has despaired of mercy.

The apparent view is that the statement ﴿وَإِن تُكَذِّبُوا﴾ (and if you deny) is part of God's speech, reporting Abraham's words, up to His statement ﴿عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾ (a painful punishment). It has also been said that these verses are a parenthetical interjection (iʿtirāḍ) within the speech of God, placed between the words of Abraham, and that they report the answer of his people. In that case the meaning is: "And if you deny Muḥammad..." The placing of this sentence as a parenthetical interjection refutes Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī, who claimed that an interjection cannot consist of two or more sentences. The purpose of this interjection is to console the Messenger (ﷺ), since he had been tested with the same kind of trials that his forefather Abraham had faced: the polytheism of his people, their worship of idols, their denial of him, and their attempts to kill him. The verses that come after the conditional sentence confirm what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought: the Oneness of God, His signs, a mention of the evidence of His power, and the return (to God).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 29, verses 24–35 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Kill him or burn him." But Allah saved him from the fire. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿And he said, "You have taken only idols instead of Allah, out of affection among yourselves in the life of this world. Then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disown others and some of you will curse others, and your refuge will be the Fire, and you will have no helpers."﴾ ﴿So Lot believed him, and he said, "I am emigrating to my Lord. Indeed He is the Almighty, the Wise."﴾ ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book, and We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And Lot, when he said to his people, "Indeed you commit an abomination which no one in the worlds preceded you in."﴾ ﴿"Do you really approach men, and cut off the way, and commit wickedness in your gatherings?" But the answer of his people was only that they said, "Bring us the punishment of Allah if you are among the truthful."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, help me against the corrupt people."﴾ ﴿And when Our messengers came to Abraham with good news, they said, "Indeed we are going to destroy the people of this town, for its people have been wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed Lot is in it." They said, "We know best who is in it. We will surely save him and his family, except his wife; she is among those who remain behind."﴾ ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed by them and felt helpless for them, and they said, "Do not fear and do not grieve. Indeed we will save you and your family, except your wife; she is among those who remain behind."﴾ ﴿"Indeed we will send down upon the people of this town a punishment from the sky because of what they have been doing of wickedness."﴾ ﴿And We have left from it a clear sign for a people who reason.﴾.

(p-148) When he commanded them to worship Allah, and explained their foolishness in worshipping idols, and his proof against them became manifest, they resorted to force. So they made their saying "Kill him or burn him" stand in place of an answer to what he had told them. Those who gave this order were either some of them to others, or their leaders said to their followers, "Kill him, so that you may be rid of him quickly," or "Burn him with fire," for either he would return to your religion if the fire put him out, or he would die in it if he persisted in his saying and his religion. There is an omission in the speech, meaning: "Burn him in the fire," ﴿so Allah saved him from the fire﴾. His story of being burned has already been mentioned in the surah ﴿The Hour of their reckoning has drawn near for the people﴾ [al-Anbiya': 1]. Here He used the plural "signs" (al-ayat), saying "in that are signs," because his deliverance from the fire, the fire being made cool and safe for him, and that it was only in the rope with which they had bound him and not in his body, and even if it is true what is reported, that the place where he was thrown became a flourishing garden, all of this is a collection of signs, so the plural fits. This is unlike his deliverance from the ship, which is one single sign, and the discussion of that has already passed. In this there is also an indication of his escape from the fire after being thrown into it, according to what Ka'b said: "Only the rope with which they had bound him was burned." Here the alternation between killing him and burning him appears. This may have come from speakers, some of whom pointed to killing and some pointed to burning. In "The Hour has drawn near," they said "Burn him," limiting themselves to one of the two things, which is what they did: they threw him into the fire and did not kill him.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read jawāba with the accusative (naṣb), and al-Hasan and Salim al-Afṭas read it with the nominative (raf'), as the noun of kāna. Al-Hasan, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi Ablah, Abu 'Amr in the transmission of al-Asma'i, and al-A'mash from Abu Bakr read "mawaddatun" with the nominative and "baynakum" with the accusative. The nominative is then the predicate of inna, and "mā" is a relative pronoun meaning "those," i.e., indeed the idols which you have taken are objects of affection, or a cause of affection; or it is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), i.e., indeed your taking idols is an affection; or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "they are an affection among you," and in that case "mā" is preparatory (muhayyi'ah). It is reported from 'Asim: "mawaddatu" with the nominative without tanwin, and "baynakum" with fatḥa, meaning with the fatḥa of the nūn; he made it indeclinable because it is attached to an indeclinable word, and it is in the position of the genitive by annexation, and for this reason the tanwin dropped from "mawaddatu." Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and Ibn Kathir did likewise, except that he read the nūn of "baynikum" with kasra. Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read "mawaddatan" with tanwin and the accusative, and "baynakum" with the accusative; Hamzah did likewise, except that he made "mawaddatan" annexed to "baynakum" and read it with the genitive, as in the reading of the one who read "mawaddatan" as an accusative with the sense of "preparatory" (muhayyi'ah). The verb "ittakhadha" may be among those that take two objects, and the second object is "mawadda," meaning you took the idols because of the affection among you, with an omitted noun, or you took them as an affection among you, like His saying: ﴿And among people are those who take, besides Allah, equals whom they love as they love Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165]. Or it may be among those that take one object, and "mawaddata" is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning so that they may be affectionate toward one another, be connected, and gather in the worship of them, as a people gather upon a single doctrine, so that love arises among them. They mentioned from Ibn Mas'ud an anomalous reading that contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf, although it has been transmitted from him what is in the consonantal text by a sound and widely attested transmission; for this reason I have not mentioned that reading.

﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection﴾ mutual cursing will take place among you, meaning the worshippers and the worshipped idols will curse one another, as in His saying ﴿and they will become opponents to them﴾ [Maryam: 82]. "Baynakum" and "fi'l-ḥayah" may be attached to the word "mawadda," and one verb has governed two adverbials (ẓarfayn) because they differ, being an adverb of place and an adverb of time. It is also possible that both are attached to omitted words, so that they are in the position of a qualifier, meaning "existing among you in the life of this world," being a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun hidden in "baynikum." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "fi'l-ḥayah" be attached to "ittakhadhtum" with "mā" being a restrictive particle (kāffah) and "mawadda" in the accusative, not making "mā" a relative pronoun meaning "those," nor a verbal-noun particle, and the "mawadda" in the nominative, lest it lead to separating the relative from its clause by the predicate. Some people, including Ibn 'Atiyyah, permitted that "fi'l-ḥayah" be attached to "mawadda," and that "baynikum" be a qualifier of "mawadda," and this is not permissible, for a verbal noun, if it is qualified before its complements are taken, does not govern; the basis of their argument is that latitude is allowed with adverbials, unlike the direct object. Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that it be attached to "baynikum" itself, and he said: because its meaning is "your gathering or your connection." He also permitted making it a circumstantial clause from "baynikum," and he said: because it is definite through annexation. He said: "These are two forms of parsing that cannot be understood."

﴿So Lot believed him.﴾ No one from his people believed in Abraham except Lot, peace be upon him, when he saw that the fire did not burn him. He was the son of Sarah's brother, or he was her uncle's daughter's son. The pronoun in "wa-qala" refers to Abraham, which is the apparent meaning, so that it harmonizes with His saying: ﴿And We gave him Isaac﴾. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Nakha'i. A group said: it refers to Lot, and Hajar, and Abraham, peace be upon them, who emigrated from their town of Kuthā, which is in the countryside of Iraq, in the land of Babylon, to Palestine in the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria). Abraham was seventy-five years old, and he was the first to emigrate for the sake of Allah. Ibn Jurayj said: he emigrated to Harran, then to al-Sham, and during this emigration Sarah was with him. The muhājir is one who is free of something, and in the terminology of the Shari'ah it is one who leaves his homeland seeking the pleasure of Allah. The name was known for the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun), before the conquest of Mecca. ("To my Lord") means: to the direction to which my Lord commanded me to emigrate. It was said: to where I will not be prevented from worshipping my Lord. It was said: emigrating from those among my people who opposed me, drawing near to my Lord. Abraham settled in a town in the land of Palestine, and left Lot in Sodom, which is the overturned city, at a distance of one day and night from the town of Abraham, peace be upon them both.

﴿Indeed He is the Almighty﴾ whom no one who worships Him is humiliated, ﴿the Wise﴾ who places things in their proper places. The pronoun in "dhurriyyatihi" refers to Abraham. "The prophethood" includes Isaac, Jacob, the prophets of the Children of Israel, Ishmael, and Muhammad, the seal of them, may Allah bless them all. "The Book" is a generic noun which includes the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel, and the Furqan.

﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾, meaning during his life. Mujahid said: his deliverance from the fire and from the tyrant king, and good deeds, and a good praise, such that every nation takes him as their leader. Ibn Jurayj said: and a child in whom his eye is comforted. al-Hasan said this. al-Suddi said: he saw his place in Paradise. Ibn Abi Burdah said: what he was granted success in of the deeds of the Hereafter. al-Mawardi said: the continuance of his hospitality at his grave, and this is not for any prophet other than him. It was said: prophethood and wisdom. It was said: the prayer upon him until the end of time.

"Lūtan" is in the accusative by an implied "remember" (udhkur), or by coordination with Abraham, or by coordination with what Abraham was coordinated with. The majority read "a-innakum" with the interrogative in both places together. It was also read as "annakum" in the declarative, and the second with the interrogative. Abu 'Ubayd said: I found it in the Imam (the standard codex) with one letter without a yā', and I saw the second with two letters, the yā' and the nūn. In the story of Lot it is not stated that he called his people to the worship of Allah, as it is in the story of Abraham and the story of Shu'ayb; because Lot was from the people of Abraham and in his time, and Abraham had preceded him in calling to the worship of Allah and to His oneness, and his matter had become well known among the creation for that, so Lot mentioned what was specific to him, namely the prohibition of indecency and other things. As for Abraham and Shu'ayb, they came after those who worshipped Allah had died out, and for that reason they called to the worship of Allah.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "mā sabaqakum bihā" is a resumptive sentence (jumlah mustaʾnafah) confirming the indecency of that act, as if someone had asked: why was it indecent? It was said: because no one before them had undertaken it, shrinking from it in their natures because of its extreme ugliness, until the people of Lot came forward to it because of the wickedness of their nature. They said: no male had mounted a male before the people of Lot. End of quote.
