He asked first and second as questions of denial, rebuke and reproach, and clarified what that vague indecency was in His saying "indeed you commit an indecency," though it is specific, namely the mounting of males in the anus, by His saying "mā sabaqakum bihā." Then He said: "Do you really approach men," meaning in the anus, "and cut off the way," meaning the offspring, by leaving the womb idle and having intercourse with the anuses of men; or by detaining strangers for that act until the roads were cut off; or by killing and taking property; or by the ugliness of the reputation, until the paths of people in trade were cut off.

﴿And you commit in your gatherings﴾, meaning in your assembly where you gather. It is a generic noun, since their gatherings are many in their cities, and it is not called a nādī (gathering) except so long as its people are in it; when they rise from it, the term nādī is not applied to it except figuratively.

"Al-munkar" is what intellects, laws and manly honor reject: throwing pebbles at people, and making light of a stranger who passes by. "Umm Hani narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), or the mounting of men in their assemblies while they watch one another," said by Mansur, Mujahid, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, and Qatadah ibn Zayd; or their passing wind openly; or their slapping one another in them, said by Ibn 'Abbas; or pigeon-playing; or dyeing the fingers with henna, whistling, pebble-throwing, and casting off modesty in all their affairs, said by Mujahid also; or throwing pebbles, shooting with pellets, snapping of fingers, chewing gum, using a toothstick among people, undoing buttons, insults, and obscenity in joking, said by Ibn 'Abbas also, together with their polytheism toward Allah. Among them there were sins other than indecency: injustice among themselves, vulgarity, buffoonery in their assemblies, pebble-throwing, gambling with dice and chess, wearing dyed garments, women's clothing worn by men, and tolls imposed on every passer-by; and they were the first to commit sodomy and the first to practise female homosexuality.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 29, verse 24–35 (part 2 of 2):

When Lut (peace be upon him) reproached them for these abominations, they persisted stubbornly in denial, so their answer to him was: ﴿They said, "Bring us the punishment of Allah, if you are of the truthful"﴾, meaning regarding what you threaten us with of the descent of punishment. They said this while being firmly convinced of his lying in what he promised them. In another verse: ﴿But their people's only answer was that they said, "Expel the family of Lut"﴾ [an-Naml: 56]. The combination of the two is that they first said: ﴿"Bring us the punishment of Allah"﴾, then his denunciation was repeated, and this was repeated from him as prohibition, admonition and warning, so ﴿they said, "Expel the family of Lut"﴾ [an-Naml: 56]. Since he was only commanding them to abandon the indecencies and the vile sins they were committing, and promising punishment for them, and they used to say that Allah had not forbidden this and does not punish for it, while he said that Allah had forbidden it and punishes for it, ﴿they said, "Bring us the punishment of Allah"﴾. Thus they were more courteous in their answer than the people of Ibrahim, who said: ﴿"Kill him or burn him"﴾, because he did not disparage their gods, and he had resolved against their idols and broke them, so his act with them was greater than Lut's word to his people. Hence their answer to him was: ﴿"Kill him or burn him"﴾.

Then Lut (peace be upon him) sought help, so angels were sent to punish them, to pelt them with stones, and to corrupt them by compelling people to the sins they were engaged in, willingly and unwillingly, especially that innovated vice. (With the good tidings) refers to his good news of his son Ishaq, and of his grandson Ya'qub, and of Lut's victory over his people and their destruction. (The town) is Sodom, and concerning it it is said: "More unjust than the judge of Sodom." (They were wrongdoers) meaning: wrongdoing had already preceded from them. They persisted in it over the former days while they were persistent, and their wrongdoing was: their disbelief and kinds of their sins. When they mentioned to Ibrahim: ﴿"We are going to destroy the people of this town"﴾, he was concerned for Lut and said: ﴿"Indeed, Lut is in it"﴾. When they attributed the destruction to wrongdoing, he said to them: in it is one who is innocent of wrongdoing. ﴿They said, "We know best who is in it"﴾, meaning: better than you, and they informed him of his condition. Then they informed him of their saving him ﴿and his family, except his wife﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿لَنُنَجِّيَنَّهُ﴾ as the imperfect of anjā; the rest of the seven read it as the imperfect of najjā; the majority read it with the shadda on the nun; and a group read it with the shadda removed.

﴿And when Our messengers came to Lut, he was distressed on their account and felt helpless for them⁠﴾. The discussion of this same sentence has already passed, except that here ﴿أَنْ﴾ has been added after ﴿لَمَّا﴾, and this is a regular analogical usage. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Anna is a connective particle that emphasizes the existence of the two verbs, one following the other in two adjacent times with no separation between them, as if they occurred in a single part of time; as if it were said: when he sensed their coming, the distress struck without delay, out of fear for them from his people." End of quote. What he mentioned regarding the sequence is the view of Sibawayh, since his view is that lamma is a particle, not an adverb, contrary to al-Farisi; this is mentioned in the science of grammar. ﴿مُنَجُّوكَ﴾ was read with a shadda by the two Arabs (Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr), Nafi' and Hafs; the rest of the seven read it without shadda. The kaf, in Sibawayh's view, is in the position of a genitive. (And your family) is in the accusative by implying a verb, meaning: and We shall save your family. Whoever takes this position into account, conjoins it to the position of the kaf; the kaf, according to al-Akhfash and Hisham, is in the accusative position, and "ahlaka" is conjoined to it, because this nun is like tanwin, and both of them, in their view, are elided for the delicacy of the pronoun and its strong need to connect with what precedes it. The majority read ﴿سِيءَ﴾ with a kasra on the sin; Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma. 'Isa and Talha read ﴿سُوءَ﴾ with a damma, and it is the dialect of Banu Hudhayl; and Banu Wubayr say qula and bu'a for qila and biya' and the like. It was read "munzilun" with and without shadda; Ibn Muhaysin read "rujzan" with a damma on the ra'; and Abu Haywa and al-A'mash read with a kasra on the sin of "yafsuqun". The apparent view is that the pronoun in "minha" refers to the town. Ibn 'Abbas said: their dwellings that are in ruins. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi related that the sign is in their town, except that its foundations are at the top and its roofs at the bottom until now. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is that We left it as a sign, saying: indeed in the sky there is a sign, meaning that it is a sign. End of quote. This does not hold except on the basis of adding "min" in an obligatory position, like his saying: "I gave her in dowry a robe and a he-goat," meaning: I gave her dowry; and likewise: "And We have indeed left it as a sign." It was said: the pronoun in "minha" refers to the deed done to them; so it was said: the sign is the stones which the first of this nation encountered, said by Qatadah; it was said: the black water on the face of the earth, said by Mujahid; and it was said: He completed what He did to them. And ﴿لِقَوْمٍ﴾ is related to ﴿تَرَكْنَا﴾, or to ﴿بَيِّنَةً﴾.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 29, verses 24–35 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Kill him or burn him." But Allah saved him from the fire. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿And he said, "You have taken only idols instead of Allah, out of affection among yourselves in the life of this world. Then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disown others and some of you will curse others, and your refuge will be the Fire, and you will have no helpers."﴾ ﴿So Lot believed him, and he said, "I am emigrating to my Lord. Indeed He is the Almighty, the Wise."﴾ ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book, and We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And Lot, when he said to his people, "Indeed you commit an abomination which no one in the worlds preceded you in."﴾ ﴿"Do you really approach men, and cut off the way, and commit wickedness in your gatherings?" But the answer of his people was only that they said, "Bring us the punishment of Allah if you are among the truthful."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, help me against the corrupt people."﴾ ﴿And when Our messengers came to Abraham with good news, they said, "Indeed we are going to destroy the people of this town, for its people have been wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed Lot is in it." They said, "We know best who is in it. We will surely save him and his family, except his wife; she is among those who remain behind."﴾ ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed by them and felt helpless for them, and they said, "Do not fear and do not grieve. Indeed we will save you and your family, except your wife; she is among those who remain behind."﴾ ﴿"Indeed we will send down upon the people of this town a punishment from the sky because of what they have been doing of wickedness."﴾ ﴿And We have left from it a clear sign for a people who reason.﴾.

(p-148) When he commanded them to worship Allah, and explained their foolishness in worshipping idols, and his proof against them became manifest, they resorted to force. So they made their saying "Kill him or burn him" stand in place of an answer to what he had told them. Those who gave this order were either some of them to others, or their leaders said to their followers, "Kill him, so that you may be rid of him quickly," or "Burn him with fire," for either he would return to your religion if the fire put him out, or he would die in it if he persisted in his saying and his religion. There is an omission in the speech, meaning: "Burn him in the fire," ﴿so Allah saved him from the fire﴾. His story of being burned has already been mentioned in the surah ﴿The Hour of their reckoning has drawn near for the people﴾ [al-Anbiya': 1]. Here He used the plural "signs" (al-ayat), saying "in that are signs," because his deliverance from the fire, the fire being made cool and safe for him, and that it was only in the rope with which they had bound him and not in his body, and even if it is true what is reported, that the place where he was thrown became a flourishing garden, all of this is a collection of signs, so the plural fits. This is unlike his deliverance from the ship, which is one single sign, and the discussion of that has already passed. In this there is also an indication of his escape from the fire after being thrown into it, according to what Ka'b said: "Only the rope with which they had bound him was burned." Here the alternation between killing him and burning him appears. This may have come from speakers, some of whom pointed to killing and some pointed to burning. In "The Hour has drawn near," they said "Burn him," limiting themselves to one of the two things, which is what they did: they threw him into the fire and did not kill him.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read jawāba with the accusative (naṣb), and al-Hasan and Salim al-Afṭas read it with the nominative (raf'), as the noun of kāna. Al-Hasan, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi Ablah, Abu 'Amr in the transmission of al-Asma'i, and al-A'mash from Abu Bakr read "mawaddatun" with the nominative and "baynakum" with the accusative. The nominative is then the predicate of inna, and "mā" is a relative pronoun meaning "those," i.e., indeed the idols which you have taken are objects of affection, or a cause of affection; or it is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), i.e., indeed your taking idols is an affection; or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "they are an affection among you," and in that case "mā" is preparatory (muhayyi'ah). It is reported from 'Asim: "mawaddatu" with the nominative without tanwin, and "baynakum" with fatḥa, meaning with the fatḥa of the nūn; he made it indeclinable because it is attached to an indeclinable word, and it is in the position of the genitive by annexation, and for this reason the tanwin dropped from "mawaddatu." Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and Ibn Kathir did likewise, except that he read the nūn of "baynikum" with kasra. Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read "mawaddatan" with tanwin and the accusative, and "baynakum" with the accusative; Hamzah did likewise, except that he made "mawaddatan" annexed to "baynakum" and read it with the genitive, as in the reading of the one who read "mawaddatan" as an accusative with the sense of "preparatory" (muhayyi'ah). The verb "ittakhadha" may be among those that take two objects, and the second object is "mawadda," meaning you took the idols because of the affection among you, with an omitted noun, or you took them as an affection among you, like His saying: ﴿And among people are those who take, besides Allah, equals whom they love as they love Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165]. Or it may be among those that take one object, and "mawaddata" is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning so that they may be affectionate toward one another, be connected, and gather in the worship of them, as a people gather upon a single doctrine, so that love arises among them. They mentioned from Ibn Mas'ud an anomalous reading that contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf, although it has been transmitted from him what is in the consonantal text by a sound and widely attested transmission; for this reason I have not mentioned that reading.

﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection﴾ mutual cursing will take place among you, meaning the worshippers and the worshipped idols will curse one another, as in His saying ﴿and they will become opponents to them﴾ [Maryam: 82]. "Baynakum" and "fi'l-ḥayah" may be attached to the word "mawadda," and one verb has governed two adverbials (ẓarfayn) because they differ, being an adverb of place and an adverb of time. It is also possible that both are attached to omitted words, so that they are in the position of a qualifier, meaning "existing among you in the life of this world," being a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun hidden in "baynikum." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "fi'l-ḥayah" be attached to "ittakhadhtum" with "mā" being a restrictive particle (kāffah) and "mawadda" in the accusative, not making "mā" a relative pronoun meaning "those," nor a verbal-noun particle, and the "mawadda" in the nominative, lest it lead to separating the relative from its clause by the predicate. Some people, including Ibn 'Atiyyah, permitted that "fi'l-ḥayah" be attached to "mawadda," and that "baynikum" be a qualifier of "mawadda," and this is not permissible, for a verbal noun, if it is qualified before its complements are taken, does not govern; the basis of their argument is that latitude is allowed with adverbials, unlike the direct object. Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that it be attached to "baynikum" itself, and he said: because its meaning is "your gathering or your connection." He also permitted making it a circumstantial clause from "baynikum," and he said: because it is definite through annexation. He said: "These are two forms of parsing that cannot be understood."

﴿So Lot believed him.﴾ No one from his people believed in Abraham except Lot, peace be upon him, when he saw that the fire did not burn him. He was the son of Sarah's brother, or he was her uncle's daughter's son. The pronoun in "wa-qala" refers to Abraham, which is the apparent meaning, so that it harmonizes with His saying: ﴿And We gave him Isaac﴾. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Nakha'i. A group said: it refers to Lot, and Hajar, and Abraham, peace be upon them, who emigrated from their town of Kuthā, which is in the countryside of Iraq, in the land of Babylon, to Palestine in the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria). Abraham was seventy-five years old, and he was the first to emigrate for the sake of Allah. Ibn Jurayj said: he emigrated to Harran, then to al-Sham, and during this emigration Sarah was with him. The muhājir is one who is free of something, and in the terminology of the Shari'ah it is one who leaves his homeland seeking the pleasure of Allah. The name was known for the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun), before the conquest of Mecca. ("To my Lord") means: to the direction to which my Lord commanded me to emigrate. It was said: to where I will not be prevented from worshipping my Lord. It was said: emigrating from those among my people who opposed me, drawing near to my Lord. Abraham settled in a town in the land of Palestine, and left Lot in Sodom, which is the overturned city, at a distance of one day and night from the town of Abraham, peace be upon them both.

﴿Indeed He is the Almighty﴾ whom no one who worships Him is humiliated, ﴿the Wise﴾ who places things in their proper places. The pronoun in "dhurriyyatihi" refers to Abraham. "The prophethood" includes Isaac, Jacob, the prophets of the Children of Israel, Ishmael, and Muhammad, the seal of them, may Allah bless them all. "The Book" is a generic noun which includes the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel, and the Furqan.

﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾, meaning during his life. Mujahid said: his deliverance from the fire and from the tyrant king, and good deeds, and a good praise, such that every nation takes him as their leader. Ibn Jurayj said: and a child in whom his eye is comforted. al-Hasan said this. al-Suddi said: he saw his place in Paradise. Ibn Abi Burdah said: what he was granted success in of the deeds of the Hereafter. al-Mawardi said: the continuance of his hospitality at his grave, and this is not for any prophet other than him. It was said: prophethood and wisdom. It was said: the prayer upon him until the end of time.

This does not hold except on the basis of adding "min" in an obligatory position, like his saying: "I gave her in dowry a robe and a he-goat," meaning: I gave her dowry; and likewise: "And We have indeed left it as a sign." It was said: the pronoun in "minha" refers to the deed done to them; so it was said: the sign is the stones which the first of this nation encountered, said by Qatadah; it was said: the black water on the face of the earth, said by Mujahid; and it was said: He completed what He did to them. And ﴿لِقَوْمٍ﴾ is related to ﴿تَرَكْنَا﴾, or to ﴿بَيِّنَةً﴾.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 29, verses 24–35 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Kill him or burn him." But Allah saved him from the fire. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿And he said, "You have taken only idols instead of Allah, out of affection among yourselves in the life of this world. Then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disown others and some of you will curse others, and your refuge will be the Fire, and you will have no helpers."﴾ ﴿So Lot believed him, and he said, "I am emigrating to my Lord. Indeed He is the Almighty, the Wise."﴾ ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book, and We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And Lot, when he said to his people, "Indeed you commit an abomination which no one in the worlds preceded you in."﴾ ﴿"Do you really approach men, and cut off the way, and commit wickedness in your gatherings?" But the answer of his people was only that they said, "Bring us the punishment of Allah if you are among the truthful."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, help me against the corrupt people."﴾ ﴿And when Our messengers came to Abraham with good news, they said, "Indeed we are going to destroy the people of this town, for its people have been wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed Lot is in it." They said, "We know best who is in it. We will surely save him and his family, except his wife; she is among those who remain behind."﴾ ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed by them and felt helpless for them, and they said, "Do not fear and do not grieve. Indeed we will save you and your family, except your wife; she is among those who remain behind."﴾ ﴿"Indeed we will send down upon the people of this town a punishment from the sky because of what they have been doing of wickedness."﴾ ﴿And We have left from it a clear sign for a people who reason.﴾.

(p-148) When he commanded them to worship Allah, and explained their foolishness in worshipping idols, and his proof against them became manifest, they resorted to force. So they made their saying "Kill him or burn him" stand in place of an answer to what he had told them. Those who gave this order were either some of them to others, or their leaders said to their followers, "Kill him, so that you may be rid of him quickly," or "Burn him with fire," for either he would return to your religion if the fire put him out, or he would die in it if he persisted in his saying and his religion. There is an omission in the speech, meaning: "Burn him in the fire," ﴿so Allah saved him from the fire﴾. His story of being burned has already been mentioned in the surah ﴿The Hour of their reckoning has drawn near for the people﴾ [al-Anbiya': 1]. Here He used the plural "signs" (al-ayat), saying "in that are signs," because his deliverance from the fire, the fire being made cool and safe for him, and that it was only in the rope with which they had bound him and not in his body, and even if it is true what is reported, that the place where he was thrown became a flourishing garden, all of this is a collection of signs, so the plural fits. This is unlike his deliverance from the ship, which is one single sign, and the discussion of that has already passed. In this there is also an indication of his escape from the fire after being thrown into it, according to what Ka'b said: "Only the rope with which they had bound him was burned." Here the alternation between killing him and burning him appears. This may have come from speakers, some of whom pointed to killing and some pointed to burning. In "The Hour has drawn near," they said "Burn him," limiting themselves to one of the two things, which is what they did: they threw him into the fire and did not kill him.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read jawāba with the accusative (naṣb), and al-Hasan and Salim al-Afṭas read it with the nominative (raf'), as the noun of kāna. Al-Hasan, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi Ablah, Abu 'Amr in the transmission of al-Asma'i, and al-A'mash from Abu Bakr read "mawaddatun" with the nominative and "baynakum" with the accusative. The nominative is then the predicate of inna, and "mā" is a relative pronoun meaning "those," i.e., indeed the idols which you have taken are objects of affection, or a cause of affection; or it is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), i.e., indeed your taking idols is an affection; or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "they are an affection among you," and in that case "mā" is preparatory (muhayyi'ah). It is reported from 'Asim: "mawaddatu" with the nominative without tanwin, and "baynakum" with fatḥa, meaning with the fatḥa of the nūn; he made it indeclinable because it is attached to an indeclinable word, and it is in the position of the genitive by annexation, and for this reason the tanwin dropped from "mawaddatu." Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and Ibn Kathir did likewise, except that he read the nūn of "baynikum" with kasra. Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read "mawaddatan" with tanwin and the accusative, and "baynakum" with the accusative; Hamzah did likewise, except that he made "mawaddatan" annexed to "baynakum" and read it with the genitive, as in the reading of the one who read "mawaddatan" as an accusative with the sense of "preparatory" (muhayyi'ah). The verb "ittakhadha" may be among those that take two objects, and the second object is "mawadda," meaning you took the idols because of the affection among you, with an omitted noun, or you took them as an affection among you, like His saying: ﴿And among people are those who take, besides Allah, equals whom they love as they love Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165]. Or it may be among those that take one object, and "mawaddata" is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning so that they may be affectionate toward one another, be connected, and gather in the worship of them, as a people gather upon a single doctrine, so that love arises among them. They mentioned from Ibn Mas'ud an anomalous reading that contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf, although it has been transmitted from him what is in the consonantal text by a sound and widely attested transmission; for this reason I have not mentioned that reading.

﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection﴾ mutual cursing will take place among you, meaning the worshippers and the worshipped idols will curse one another, as in His saying ﴿and they will become opponents to them﴾ [Maryam: 82]. "Baynakum" and "fi'l-ḥayah" may be attached to the word "mawadda," and one verb has governed two adverbials (ẓarfayn) because they differ, being an adverb of place and an adverb of time. It is also possible that both are attached to omitted words, so that they are in the position of a qualifier, meaning "existing among you in the life of this world," being a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun hidden in "baynikum." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "fi'l-ḥayah" be attached to "ittakhadhtum" with "mā" being a restrictive particle (kāffah) and "mawadda" in the accusative, not making "mā" a relative pronoun meaning "those," nor a verbal-noun particle, and the "mawadda" in the nominative, lest it lead to separating the relative from its clause by the predicate. Some people, including Ibn 'Atiyyah, permitted that "fi'l-ḥayah" be attached to "mawadda," and that "baynikum" be a qualifier of "mawadda," and this is not permissible, for a verbal noun, if it is qualified before its complements are taken, does not govern; the basis of their argument is that latitude is allowed with adverbials, unlike the direct object. Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that it be attached to "baynikum" itself, and he said: because its meaning is "your gathering or your connection." He also permitted making it a circumstantial clause from "baynikum," and he said: because it is definite through annexation. He said: "These are two forms of parsing that cannot be understood."

﴿So Lot believed him.﴾ No one from his people believed in Abraham except Lot, peace be upon him, when he saw that the fire did not burn him. He was the son of Sarah's brother, or he was her uncle's daughter's son. The pronoun in "wa-qala" refers to Abraham, which is the apparent meaning, so that it harmonizes with His saying: ﴿And We gave him Isaac﴾. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Nakha'i. A group said: it refers to Lot, and Hajar, and Abraham, peace be upon them, who emigrated from their town of Kuthā, which is in the countryside of Iraq, in the land of Babylon, to Palestine in the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria). Abraham was seventy-five years old, and he was the first to emigrate for the sake of Allah. Ibn Jurayj said: he emigrated to Harran, then to al-Sham, and during this emigration Sarah was with him. The muhājir is one who is free of something, and in the terminology of the Shari'ah it is one who leaves his homeland seeking the pleasure of Allah. The name was known for the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun), before the conquest of Mecca. ("To my Lord") means: to the direction to which my Lord commanded me to emigrate. It was said: to where I will not be prevented from worshipping my Lord. It was said: emigrating from those among my people who opposed me, drawing near to my Lord. Abraham settled in a town in the land of Palestine, and left Lot in Sodom, which is the overturned city, at a distance of one day and night from the town of Abraham, peace be upon them both.

﴿Indeed He is the Almighty﴾ whom no one who worships Him is humiliated, ﴿the Wise﴾ who places things in their proper places. The pronoun in "dhurriyyatihi" refers to Abraham. "The prophethood" includes Isaac, Jacob, the prophets of the Children of Israel, Ishmael, and Muhammad, the seal of them, may Allah bless them all. "The Book" is a generic noun which includes the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel, and the Furqan.

﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾, meaning during his life. Mujahid said: his deliverance from the fire and from the tyrant king, and good deeds, and a good praise, such that every nation takes him as their leader. Ibn Jurayj said: and a child in whom his eye is comforted. al-Hasan said this. al-Suddi said: he saw his place in Paradise. Ibn Abi Burdah said: what he was granted success in of the deeds of the Hereafter. al-Mawardi said: the continuance of his hospitality at his grave, and this is not for any prophet other than him. It was said: prophethood and wisdom. It was said: the prayer upon him until the end of time.

"Lūtan" is in the accusative by an implied "remember" (udhkur), or by coordination with Abraham, or by coordination with what Abraham was coordinated with. The majority read "a-innakum" with the interrogative in both places together. It was also read as "annakum" in the declarative, and the second with the interrogative. Abu 'Ubayd said: I found it in the Imam (the standard codex) with one letter without a yā', and I saw the second with two letters, the yā' and the nūn. In the story of Lot it is not stated that he called his people to the worship of Allah, as it is in the story of Abraham and the story of Shu'ayb; because Lot was from the people of Abraham and in his time, and Abraham had preceded him in calling to the worship of Allah and to His oneness, and his matter had become well known among the creation for that, so Lot mentioned what was specific to him, namely the prohibition of indecency and other things. As for Abraham and Shu'ayb, they came after those who worshipped Allah had died out, and for that reason they called to the worship of Allah.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "mā sabaqakum bihā" is a resumptive sentence (jumlah mustaʾnafah) confirming the indecency of that act, as if someone had asked: why was it indecent? It was said: because no one before them had undertaken it, shrinking from it in their natures because of its extreme ugliness, until the people of Lot came forward to it because of the wickedness of their nature. They said: no male had mounted a male before the people of Lot. End of quote. It appears that "mā sabaqakum bihā" is a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah), as if he said: do you commit indecency, originating it, not preceded by anyone in it? He asked first and second as questions of denial, rebuke and reproach, and clarified what that vague indecency was in His saying "indeed you commit an indecency," though it is specific, namely the mounting of males in the anus, by His saying "mā sabaqakum bihā." Then He said: "Do you really approach men," meaning in the anus, "and cut off the way," meaning the offspring, by leaving the womb idle and having intercourse with the anuses of men; or by detaining strangers for that act until the roads were cut off; or by killing and taking property; or by the ugliness of the reputation, until the paths of people in trade were cut off.

﴿And you commit in your gatherings﴾, meaning in your assembly where you gather. It is a generic noun, since their gatherings are many in their cities, and it is not called a nādī (gathering) except so long as its people are in it; when they rise from it, the term nādī is not applied to it except figuratively.

"Al-munkar" is what intellects, laws and manly honor reject: throwing pebbles at people, and making light of a stranger who passes by. "Umm Hani narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), or the mounting of men in their assemblies while they watch one another," said by Mansur, Mujahid, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, and Qatadah ibn Zayd; or their passing wind openly; or their slapping one another in them, said by Ibn 'Abbas; or pigeon-playing; or dyeing the fingers with henna, whistling, pebble-throwing, and casting off modesty in all their affairs, said by Mujahid also; or throwing pebbles, shooting with pellets, snapping of fingers, chewing gum, using a toothstick among people, undoing buttons, insults, and obscenity in joking, said by Ibn 'Abbas also, together with their polytheism toward Allah. Among them there were sins other than indecency: injustice among themselves, vulgarity, buffoonery in their assemblies, pebble-throwing, gambling with dice and chess, wearing dyed garments, women's clothing worn by men, and tolls imposed on every passer-by; and they were the first to commit sodomy and the first to practise female homosexuality.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 29, verse 24–35 (part 2 of 2):

When Lut (peace be upon him) reproached them for these abominations, they persisted stubbornly in denial, so their answer to him was: ﴿They said, "Bring us the punishment of Allah, if you are of the truthful"﴾, meaning regarding what you threaten us with of the descent of punishment. They said this while being firmly convinced of his lying in what he promised them. In another verse: ﴿But their people's only answer was that they said, "Expel the family of Lut"﴾ [an-Naml: 56]. The combination of the two is that they first said: ﴿"Bring us the punishment of Allah"﴾, then his denunciation was repeated, and this was repeated from him as prohibition, admonition and warning, so ﴿they said, "Expel the family of Lut"﴾ [an-Naml: 56]. Since he was only commanding them to abandon the indecencies and the vile sins they were committing, and promising punishment for them, and they used to say that Allah had not forbidden this and does not punish for it, while he said that Allah had forbidden it and punishes for it, ﴿they said, "Bring us the punishment of Allah"﴾. Thus they were more courteous in their answer than the people of Ibrahim, who said: ﴿"Kill him or burn him"﴾, because he did not disparage their gods, and he had resolved against their idols and broke them, so his act with them was greater than Lut's word to his people. Hence their answer to him was: ﴿"Kill him or burn him"﴾.

Then Lut (peace be upon him) sought help, so angels were sent to punish them, to pelt them with stones, and to corrupt them by compelling people to the sins they were engaged in, willingly and unwillingly, especially that innovated vice. (With the good tidings) refers to his good news of his son Ishaq, and of his grandson Ya'qub, and of Lut's victory over his people and their destruction. (The town) is Sodom, and concerning it it is said: "More unjust than the judge of Sodom." (They were wrongdoers) meaning: wrongdoing had already preceded from them. They persisted in it over the former days while they were persistent, and their wrongdoing was: their disbelief and kinds of their sins. When they mentioned to Ibrahim: ﴿"We are going to destroy the people of this town"﴾, he was concerned for Lut and said: ﴿"Indeed, Lut is in it"﴾. When they attributed the destruction to wrongdoing, he said to them: in it is one who is innocent of wrongdoing. ﴿They said, "We know best who is in it"﴾, meaning: better than you, and they informed him of his condition. Then they informed him of their saving him ﴿and his family, except his wife﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿لَنُنَجِّيَنَّهُ﴾ as the imperfect of anjā; the rest of the seven read it as the imperfect of najjā; the majority read it with the shadda on the nun; and a group read it with the shadda removed.

﴿And when Our messengers came to Lut, he was distressed on their account and felt helpless for them⁠﴾. The discussion of this same sentence has already passed, except that here ﴿أَنْ﴾ has been added after ﴿لَمَّا﴾, and this is a regular analogical usage. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Anna is a connective particle that emphasizes the existence of the two verbs, one following the other in two adjacent times with no separation between them, as if they occurred in a single part of time; as if it were said: when he sensed their coming, the distress struck without delay, out of fear for them from his people." End of quote. What he mentioned regarding the sequence is the view of Sibawayh, since his view is that lamma is a particle, not an adverb, contrary to al-Farisi; this is mentioned in the science of grammar. ﴿مُنَجُّوكَ﴾ was read with a shadda by the two Arabs (Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr), Nafi' and Hafs; the rest of the seven read it without shadda. The kaf, in Sibawayh's view, is in the position of a genitive. (And your family) is in the accusative by implying a verb, meaning: and We shall save your family. Whoever takes this position into account, conjoins it to the position of the kaf; the kaf, according to al-Akhfash and Hisham, is in the accusative position, and "ahlaka" is conjoined to it, because this nun is like tanwin, and both of them, in their view, are elided for the delicacy of the pronoun and its strong need to connect with what precedes it. The majority read ﴿سِيءَ﴾ with a kasra on the sin; Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma. 'Isa and Talha read ﴿سُوءَ﴾ with a damma, and it is the dialect of Banu Hudhayl; and Banu Wubayr say qula and bu'a for qila and biya' and the like. It was read "munzilun" with and without shadda; Ibn Muhaysin read "rujzan" with a damma on the ra'; and Abu Haywa and al-A'mash read with a kasra on the sin of "yafsuqun". The apparent view is that the pronoun in "minha" refers to the town. Ibn 'Abbas said: their dwellings that are in ruins. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi related that the sign is in their town, except that its foundations are at the top and its roofs at the bottom until now. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is that We left it as a sign, saying: indeed in the sky there is a sign, meaning that it is a sign. End of quote. This does not hold except on the basis of adding "min" in an obligatory position, like his saying: "I gave her in dowry a robe and a he-goat," meaning: I gave her dowry; and likewise: "And We have indeed left it as a sign." It was said: the pronoun in "minha" refers to the deed done to them; so it was said: the sign is the stones which the first of this nation encountered, said by Qatadah; it was said: the black water on the face of the earth, said by Mujahid; and it was said: He completed what He did to them. And ﴿لِقَوْمٍ﴾ is related to ﴿تَرَكْنَا﴾, or to ﴿بَيِّنَةً﴾.

﴿So Lot believed him.﴾ No one from his people believed in Abraham except Lot, peace be upon him, when he saw that the fire did not burn him. He was the son of Sarah's brother, or he was her uncle's daughter's son. A group said: it refers to Lot, and Hajar, and Abraham, peace be upon them, who emigrated from their town of Kuthā, which is in the countryside of Iraq, in the land of Babylon, to Palestine in the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria). Abraham was seventy-five years old, and he was the first to emigrate for the sake of Allah. Ibn Jurayj said: he emigrated to Harran, then to al-Sham, and during this emigration Sarah was with him. The name was known for the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun), before the conquest of Mecca. ("To my Lord") means: to the direction to which my Lord commanded me to emigrate. It was said: to where I will not be prevented from worshipping my Lord. It was said: emigrating from those among my people who opposed me, drawing near to my Lord. Abraham settled in a town in the land of Palestine, and left Lot in Sodom, which is the overturned city, at a distance of one day and night from the town of Abraham, peace be upon them both.

﴿Indeed He is the Almighty﴾ whom no one who worships Him is humiliated, ﴿the Wise﴾ who places things in their proper places. The pronoun in "dhurriyyatihi" refers to Abraham. "The prophethood" includes Isaac, Jacob, the prophets of the Children of Israel, Ishmael, and Muhammad, the seal of them, may Allah bless them all. "The Book" is a generic noun which includes the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel, and the Furqan.

﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾, meaning during his life. Mujahid said: his deliverance from the fire and from the tyrant king, and good deeds, and a good praise, such that every nation takes him as their leader. Ibn Jurayj said: and a child in whom his eye is comforted. al-Hasan said this. al-Suddi said: he saw his place in Paradise. Ibn Abi Burdah said: what he was granted success in of the deeds of the Hereafter. al-Mawardi said: the continuance of his hospitality at his grave, and this is not for any prophet other than him. It was said: prophethood and wisdom. It was said: the prayer upon him until the end of time.

The majority read "a-innakum" with the interrogative in both places together. It was also read as "annakum" in the declarative, and the second with the interrogative. Abu 'Ubayd said: I found it in the Imam (the standard codex) with one letter without a yā', and I saw the second with two letters, the yā' and the nūn. Al-Zamakhshari said: "mā sabaqakum bihā" is a resumptive sentence (jumlah mustaʾnafah) confirming the indecency of that act, as if someone had asked: why was it indecent? It was said: because no one before them had undertaken it, shrinking from it in their natures because of its extreme ugliness, until the people of Lot came forward to it because of the wickedness of their nature. They said: no male had mounted a male before the people of Lot. End of quote. He asked first and second as questions of denial, rebuke and reproach, and clarified what that vague indecency was in His saying "indeed you commit an indecency," though it is specific, namely the mounting of males in the anus, by His saying "mā sabaqakum bihā." Then He said: "Do you really approach men," meaning in the anus, "and cut off the way," meaning the offspring, by leaving the womb idle and having intercourse with the anuses of men; or by detaining strangers for that act until the roads were cut off; or by killing and taking property; or by the ugliness of the reputation, until the paths of people in trade were cut off.

﴿And you commit in your gatherings﴾, meaning in your assembly where you gather. It is a generic noun, since their gatherings are many in their cities, and it is not called a nādī (gathering) except so long as its people are in it; when they rise from it, the term nādī is not applied to it except figuratively.

"Al-munkar" is what intellects, laws and manly honor reject: throwing pebbles at people, and making light of a stranger who passes by. "Umm Hani narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), or the mounting of men in their assemblies while they watch one another," said by Mansur, Mujahid, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, and Qatadah ibn Zayd; or their passing wind openly; or their slapping one another in them, said by Ibn 'Abbas; or pigeon-playing; or dyeing the fingers with henna, whistling, pebble-throwing, and casting off modesty in all their affairs, said by Mujahid also; or throwing pebbles, shooting with pellets, snapping of fingers, chewing gum, using a toothstick among people, undoing buttons, insults, and obscenity in joking, said by Ibn 'Abbas also, together with their polytheism toward Allah. Among them there were sins other than indecency: injustice among themselves, vulgarity, buffoonery in their assemblies, pebble-throwing, gambling with dice and chess, wearing dyed garments, women's clothing worn by men, and tolls imposed on every passer-by; and they were the first to commit sodomy and the first to practise female homosexuality.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 29, verse 24–35 (part 2 of 2):

When Lut (peace be upon him) reproached them for these abominations, they persisted stubbornly in denial, so their answer to him was: ﴿They said, "Bring us the punishment of Allah, if you are of the truthful"﴾, meaning regarding what you threaten us with of the descent of punishment. They said this while being firmly convinced of his lying in what he promised them. In another verse: ﴿But their people's only answer was that they said, "Expel the family of Lut"﴾ [an-Naml: 56]. The combination of the two is that they first said: ﴿"Bring us the punishment of Allah"﴾, then his denunciation was repeated, and this was repeated from him as prohibition, admonition and warning, so ﴿they said, "Expel the family of Lut"﴾ [an-Naml: 56]. Since he was only commanding them to abandon the indecencies and the vile sins they were committing, and promising punishment for them, and they used to say that Allah had not forbidden this and does not punish for it, while he said that Allah had forbidden it and punishes for it, ﴿they said, "Bring us the punishment of Allah"﴾. Thus they were more courteous in their answer than the people of Ibrahim, who said: ﴿"Kill him or burn him"﴾, because he did not disparage their gods, and he had resolved against their idols and broke them, so his act with them was greater than Lut's word to his people. Hence their answer to him was: ﴿"Kill him or burn him"﴾.

Then Lut (peace be upon him) sought help, so angels were sent to punish them, to pelt them with stones, and to corrupt them by compelling people to the sins they were engaged in, willingly and unwillingly, especially that innovated vice. (With the good tidings) refers to his good news of his son Ishaq, and of his grandson Ya'qub, and of Lut's victory over his people and their destruction. (The town) is Sodom, and concerning it it is said: "More unjust than the judge of Sodom." (They were wrongdoers) meaning: wrongdoing had already preceded from them. They persisted in it over the former days while they were persistent, and their wrongdoing was: their disbelief and kinds of their sins. When they mentioned to Ibrahim: ﴿"We are going to destroy the people of this town"﴾, he was concerned for Lut and said: ﴿"Indeed, Lut is in it"﴾. When they attributed the destruction to wrongdoing, he said to them: in it is one who is innocent of wrongdoing. ﴿They said, "We know best who is in it"﴾, meaning: better than you, and they informed him of his condition. Then they informed him of their saving him ﴿and his family, except his wife﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿لَنُنَجِّيَنَّهُ﴾ as the imperfect of anjā; the rest of the seven read it as the imperfect of najjā; the majority read it with the shadda on the nun; and a group read it with the shadda removed.

﴿And when Our messengers came to Lut, he was distressed on their account and felt helpless for them⁠﴾. The discussion of this same sentence has already passed, except that here ﴿أَنْ﴾ has been added after ﴿لَمَّا﴾, and this is a regular analogical usage. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Anna is a connective particle that emphasizes the existence of the two verbs, one following the other in two adjacent times with no separation between them, as if they occurred in a single part of time; as if it were said: when he sensed their coming, the distress struck without delay, out of fear for them from his people." End of quote. What he mentioned regarding the sequence is the view of Sibawayh, since his view is that lamma is a particle, not an adverb, contrary to al-Farisi; this is mentioned in the science of grammar. ﴿مُنَجُّوكَ﴾ was read with a shadda by the two Arabs (Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr), Nafi' and Hafs; the rest of the seven read it without shadda. The kaf, in Sibawayh's view, is in the position of a genitive. (And your family) is in the accusative by implying a verb, meaning: and We shall save your family. Whoever takes this position into account, conjoins it to the position of the kaf; the kaf, according to al-Akhfash and Hisham, is in the accusative position, and "ahlaka" is conjoined to it, because this nun is like tanwin, and both of them, in their view, are elided for the delicacy of the pronoun and its strong need to connect with what precedes it. The majority read ﴿سِيءَ﴾ with a kasra on the sin; Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma. 'Isa and Talha read ﴿سُوءَ﴾ with a damma, and it is the dialect of Banu Hudhayl; and Banu Wubayr say qula and bu'a for qila and biya' and the like. It was read "munzilun" with and without shadda; Ibn Muhaysin read "rujzan" with a damma on the ra'; and Abu Haywa and al-A'mash read with a kasra on the sin of "yafsuqun". The apparent view is that the pronoun in "minha" refers to the town. Ibn 'Abbas said: their dwellings that are in ruins. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi related that the sign is in their town, except that its foundations are at the top and its roofs at the bottom until now. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is that We left it as a sign, saying: indeed in the sky there is a sign, meaning that it is a sign. End of quote. This does not hold except on the basis of adding "min" in an obligatory position, like his saying: "I gave her in dowry a robe and a he-goat," meaning: I gave her dowry; and likewise: "And We have indeed left it as a sign." It was said: the pronoun in "minha" refers to the deed done to them; so it was said: the sign is the stones which the first of this nation encountered, said by Qatadah; it was said: the black water on the face of the earth, said by Mujahid; and it was said: He completed what He did to them. And ﴿لِقَوْمٍ﴾ is related to ﴿تَرَكْنَا﴾, or to ﴿بَيِّنَةً﴾.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 29, verses 24–35 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Kill him or burn him." But Allah saved him from the fire. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿And he said, "You have taken only idols instead of Allah, out of affection among yourselves in the life of this world. Then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disown others and some of you will curse others, and your refuge will be the Fire, and you will have no helpers."﴾ ﴿So Lot believed him, and he said, "I am emigrating to my Lord. Indeed He is the Almighty, the Wise."﴾ ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book, and We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And Lot, when he said to his people, "Indeed you commit an abomination which no one in the worlds preceded you in."﴾ ﴿"Do you really approach men, and cut off the way, and commit wickedness in your gatherings?" But the answer of his people was only that they said, "Bring us the punishment of Allah if you are among the truthful."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, help me against the corrupt people."﴾ ﴿And when Our messengers came to Abraham with good news, they said, "Indeed we are going to destroy the people of this town, for its people have been wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed Lot is in it." They said, "We know best who is in it. We will surely save him and his family, except his wife; she is among those who remain behind."﴾ ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed by them and felt helpless for them, and they said, "Do not fear and do not grieve. Indeed we will save you and your family, except your wife; she is among those who remain behind."﴾ ﴿"Indeed we will send down upon the people of this town a punishment from the sky because of what they have been doing of wickedness."﴾ ﴿And We have left from it a clear sign for a people who reason.﴾.

So they made their saying "Kill him or burn him" stand in place of an answer to what he had told them. Those who gave this order were either some of them to others, or their leaders said to their followers, "Kill him, so that you may be rid of him quickly," or "Burn him with fire," for either he would return to your religion if the fire put him out, or he would die in it if he persisted in his saying and his religion. There is an omission in the speech, meaning: "Burn him in the fire," ﴿so Allah saved him from the fire﴾. His story of being burned has already been mentioned in the surah ﴿The Hour of their reckoning has drawn near for the people﴾ [al-Anbiya': 1]. Here He used the plural "signs" (al-ayat), saying "in that are signs," because his deliverance from the fire, the fire being made cool and safe for him, and that it was only in the rope with which they had bound him and not in his body, and even if it is true what is reported, that the place where he was thrown became a flourishing garden, all of this is a collection of signs, so the plural fits. This is unlike his deliverance from the ship, which is one single sign, and the discussion of that has already passed. In this there is also an indication of his escape from the fire after being thrown into it, according to what Ka'b said: "Only the rope with which they had bound him was burned." Here the alternation between killing him and burning him appears. This may have come from speakers, some of whom pointed to killing and some pointed to burning. In "The Hour has drawn near," they said "Burn him," limiting themselves to one of the two things, which is what they did: they threw him into the fire and did not kill him.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read jawāba with the accusative (naṣb), and al-Hasan and Salim al-Afṭas read it with the nominative (raf'), as the noun of kāna. Al-Hasan, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi Ablah, Abu 'Amr in the transmission of al-Asma'i, and al-A'mash from Abu Bakr read "mawaddatun" with the nominative and "baynakum" with the accusative. The nominative is then the predicate of inna, and "mā" is a relative pronoun meaning "those," i.e., indeed the idols which you have taken are objects of affection, or a cause of affection; or it is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), i.e., indeed your taking idols is an affection; or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "they are an affection among you," and in that case "mā" is preparatory (muhayyi'ah). It is reported from 'Asim: "mawaddatu" with the nominative without tanwin, and "baynakum" with fatḥa, meaning with the fatḥa of the nūn; he made it indeclinable because it is attached to an indeclinable word, and it is in the position of the genitive by annexation, and for this reason the tanwin dropped from "mawaddatu." ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection﴾ mutual cursing will take place among you, meaning the worshippers and the worshipped idols will curse one another, as in His saying ﴿and they will become opponents to them﴾ [Maryam: 82]. Then they informed him of their saving him ﴿and his family, except his wife﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿لَنُنَجِّيَنَّهُ﴾ as the imperfect of anjā; the rest of the seven read it as the imperfect of najjā; the majority read it with the shadda on the nun; and a group read it with the shadda removed.

﴿And when Our messengers came to Lut, he was distressed on their account and felt helpless for them⁠﴾. The discussion of this same sentence has already passed, except that here ﴿أَنْ﴾ has been added after ﴿لَمَّا﴾, and this is a regular analogical usage. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Anna is a connective particle that emphasizes the existence of the two verbs, one following the other in two adjacent times with no separation between them, as if they occurred in a single part of time; as if it were said: when he sensed their coming, the distress struck without delay, out of fear for them from his people." End of quote. What he mentioned regarding the sequence is the view of Sibawayh, since his view is that lamma is a particle, not an adverb, contrary to al-Farisi; this is mentioned in the science of grammar. ﴿مُنَجُّوكَ﴾ was read with a shadda by the two Arabs (Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr), Nafi' and Hafs; the rest of the seven read it without shadda. The kaf, in Sibawayh's view, is in the position of a genitive. (And your family) is in the accusative by implying a verb, meaning: and We shall save your family. Whoever takes this position into account, conjoins it to the position of the kaf; the kaf, according to al-Akhfash and Hisham, is in the accusative position, and "ahlaka" is conjoined to it, because this nun is like tanwin, and both of them, in their view, are elided for the delicacy of the pronoun and its strong need to connect with what precedes it. The majority read ﴿سِيءَ﴾ with a kasra on the sin; Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma. 'Isa and Talha read ﴿سُوءَ﴾ with a damma, and it is the dialect of Banu Hudhayl; and Banu Wubayr say qula and bu'a for qila and biya' and the like. It was read "munzilun" with and without shadda; Ibn Muhaysin read "rujzan" with a damma on the ra'; and Abu Haywa and al-A'mash read with a kasra on the sin of "yafsuqun". The apparent view is that the pronoun in "minha" refers to the town. Ibn 'Abbas said: their dwellings that are in ruins. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi related that the sign is in their town, except that its foundations are at the top and its roofs at the bottom until now. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is that We left it as a sign, saying: indeed in the sky there is a sign, meaning that it is a sign. End of quote. This does not hold except on the basis of adding "min" in an obligatory position, like his saying: "I gave her in dowry a robe and a he-goat," meaning: I gave her dowry; and likewise: "And We have indeed left it as a sign." It was said: the pronoun in "minha" refers to the deed done to them; so it was said: the sign is the stones which the first of this nation encountered, said by Qatadah; it was said: the black water on the face of the earth, said by Mujahid; and it was said: He completed what He did to them. And ﴿لِقَوْمٍ﴾ is related to ﴿تَرَكْنَا﴾, or to ﴿بَيِّنَةً﴾.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 29, verses 24–35 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Kill him or burn him." But Allah saved him from the fire. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿And he said, "You have taken only idols instead of Allah, out of affection among yourselves in the life of this world. Then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disown others and some of you will curse others, and your refuge will be the Fire, and you will have no helpers."﴾ ﴿So Lot believed him, and he said, "I am emigrating to my Lord. Indeed He is the Almighty, the Wise."﴾ ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book, and We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And Lot, when he said to his people, "Indeed you commit an abomination which no one in the worlds preceded you in."﴾ ﴿"Do you really approach men, and cut off the way, and commit wickedness in your gatherings?" But the answer of his people was only that they said, "Bring us the punishment of Allah if you are among the truthful."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, help me against the corrupt people."﴾ ﴿And when Our messengers came to Abraham with good news, they said, "Indeed we are going to destroy the people of this town, for its people have been wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed Lot is in it." They said, "We know best who is in it. We will surely save him and his family, except his wife; she is among those who remain behind."﴾ ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed by them and felt helpless for them, and they said, "Do not fear and do not grieve. Indeed we will save you and your family, except your wife; she is among those who remain behind."﴾ ﴿"Indeed we will send down upon the people of this town a punishment from the sky because of what they have been doing of wickedness."﴾ ﴿And We have left from it a clear sign for a people who reason.﴾.

(p-148) When he commanded them to worship Allah, and explained their foolishness in worshipping idols, and his proof against them became manifest, they resorted to force. So they made their saying "Kill him or burn him" stand in place of an answer to what he had told them. Those who gave this order were either some of them to others, or their leaders said to their followers, "Kill him, so that you may be rid of him quickly," or "Burn him with fire," for either he would return to your religion if the fire put him out, or he would die in it if he persisted in his saying and his religion. There is an omission in the speech, meaning: "Burn him in the fire," ﴿so Allah saved him from the fire﴾. His story of being burned has already been mentioned in the surah ﴿The Hour of their reckoning has drawn near for the people﴾ [al-Anbiya': 1]. Here He used the plural "signs" (al-ayat), saying "in that are signs," because his deliverance from the fire, the fire being made cool and safe for him, and that it was only in the rope with which they had bound him and not in his body, and even if it is true what is reported, that the place where he was thrown became a flourishing garden, all of this is a collection of signs, so the plural fits. This is unlike his deliverance from the ship, which is one single sign, and the discussion of that has already passed. In this there is also an indication of his escape from the fire after being thrown into it, according to what Ka'b said: "Only the rope with which they had bound him was burned." Here the alternation between killing him and burning him appears. This may have come from speakers, some of whom pointed to killing and some pointed to burning. In "The Hour has drawn near," they said "Burn him," limiting themselves to one of the two things, which is what they did: they threw him into the fire and did not kill him.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read jawāba with the accusative (naṣb), and al-Hasan and Salim al-Afṭas read it with the nominative (raf'), as the noun of kāna. Al-Hasan, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi Ablah, Abu 'Amr in the transmission of al-Asma'i, and al-A'mash from Abu Bakr read "mawaddatun" with the nominative and "baynakum" with the accusative. The nominative is then the predicate of inna, and "mā" is a relative pronoun meaning "those," i.e., indeed the idols which you have taken are objects of affection, or a cause of affection; or it is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), i.e., indeed your taking idols is an affection; or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "they are an affection among you," and in that case "mā" is preparatory (muhayyi'ah). It is reported from 'Asim: "mawaddatu" with the nominative without tanwin, and "baynakum" with fatḥa, meaning with the fatḥa of the nūn; he made it indeclinable because it is attached to an indeclinable word, and it is in the position of the genitive by annexation, and for this reason the tanwin dropped from "mawaddatu." Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and Ibn Kathir did likewise, except that he read the nūn of "baynikum" with kasra. Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read "mawaddatan" with tanwin and the accusative, and "baynakum" with the accusative; Hamzah did likewise, except that he made "mawaddatan" annexed to "baynakum" and read it with the genitive, as in the reading of the one who read "mawaddatan" as an accusative with the sense of "preparatory" (muhayyi'ah). The verb "ittakhadha" may be among those that take two objects, and the second object is "mawadda," meaning you took the idols because of the affection among you, with an omitted noun, or you took them as an affection among you, like His saying: ﴿And among people are those who take, besides Allah, equals whom they love as they love Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165]. Or it may be among those that take one object, and "mawaddata" is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning so that they may be affectionate toward one another, be connected, and gather in the worship of them, as a people gather upon a single doctrine, so that love arises among them. They mentioned from Ibn Mas'ud an anomalous reading that contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf, although it has been transmitted from him what is in the consonantal text by a sound and widely attested transmission; for this reason I have not mentioned that reading.

﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection﴾ mutual cursing will take place among you, meaning the worshippers and the worshipped idols will curse one another, as in His saying ﴿and they will become opponents to them﴾ [Maryam: 82]. "Baynakum" and "fi'l-ḥayah" may be attached to the word "mawadda," and one verb has governed two adverbials (ẓarfayn) because they differ, being an adverb of place and an adverb of time. It is also possible that both are attached to omitted words, so that they are in the position of a qualifier, meaning "existing among you in the life of this world," being a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun hidden in "baynikum." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "fi'l-ḥayah" be attached to "ittakhadhtum" with "mā" being a restrictive particle (kāffah) and "mawadda" in the accusative, not making "mā" a relative pronoun meaning "those," nor a verbal-noun particle, and the "mawadda" in the nominative, lest it lead to separating the relative from its clause by the predicate. Some people, including Ibn 'Atiyyah, permitted that "fi'l-ḥayah" be attached to "mawadda," and that "baynikum" be a qualifier of "mawadda," and this is not permissible, for a verbal noun, if it is qualified before its complements are taken, does not govern; the basis of their argument is that latitude is allowed with adverbials, unlike the direct object. Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that it be attached to "baynikum" itself, and he said: because its meaning is "your gathering or your connection." He also permitted making it a circumstantial clause from "baynikum," and he said: because it is definite through annexation. He said: "These are two forms of parsing that cannot be understood."

﴿So Lot believed him.﴾ No one from his people believed in Abraham except Lot, peace be upon him, when he saw that the fire did not burn him. He was the son of Sarah's brother, or he was her uncle's daughter's son. The pronoun in "wa-qala" refers to Abraham, which is the apparent meaning, so that it harmonizes with His saying: ﴿And We gave him Isaac﴾. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Nakha'i. A group said: it refers to Lot, and Hajar, and Abraham, peace be upon them, who emigrated from their town of Kuthā, which is in the countryside of Iraq, in the land of Babylon, to Palestine in the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria). Abraham was seventy-five years old, and he was the first to emigrate for the sake of Allah. Ibn Jurayj said: he emigrated to Harran, then to al-Sham, and during this emigration Sarah was with him. The muhājir is one who is free of something, and in the terminology of the Shari'ah it is one who leaves his homeland seeking the pleasure of Allah. The name was known for the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun), before the conquest of Mecca. ("To my Lord") means: to the direction to which my Lord commanded me to emigrate. It was said: to where I will not be prevented from worshipping my Lord. It was said: emigrating from those among my people who opposed me, drawing near to my Lord. Abraham settled in a town in the land of Palestine, and left Lot in Sodom, which is the overturned city, at a distance of one day and night from the town of Abraham, peace be upon them both.

﴿Indeed He is the Almighty﴾ whom no one who worships Him is humiliated, ﴿the Wise﴾ who places things in their proper places. The pronoun in "dhurriyyatihi" refers to Abraham. "The prophethood" includes Isaac, Jacob, the prophets of the Children of Israel, Ishmael, and Muhammad, the seal of them, may Allah bless them all. "The Book" is a generic noun which includes the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel, and the Furqan.

﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾, meaning during his life. Mujahid said: his deliverance from the fire and from the tyrant king, and good deeds, and a good praise, such that every nation takes him as their leader. Ibn Jurayj said: and a child in whom his eye is comforted. al-Hasan said this. al-Suddi said: he saw his place in Paradise. Ibn Abi Burdah said: what he was granted success in of the deeds of the Hereafter. al-Mawardi said: the continuance of his hospitality at his grave, and this is not for any prophet other than him. It was said: prophethood and wisdom. It was said: the prayer upon him until the end of time.

"Lūtan" is in the accusative by an implied "remember" (udhkur), or by coordination with Abraham, or by coordination with what Abraham was coordinated with. The majority read "a-innakum" with the interrogative in both places together. It was also read as "annakum" in the declarative, and the second with the interrogative. Abu 'Ubayd said: I found it in the Imam (the standard codex) with one letter without a yā', and I saw the second with two letters, the yā' and the nūn. In the story of Lot it is not stated that he called his people to the worship of Allah, as it is in the story of Abraham and the story of Shu'ayb; because Lot was from the people of Abraham and in his time, and Abraham had preceded him in calling to the worship of Allah and to His oneness, and his matter had become well known among the creation for that, so Lot mentioned what was specific to him, namely the prohibition of indecency and other things. As for Abraham and Shu'ayb, they came after those who worshipped Allah had died out, and for that reason they called to the worship of Allah.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "mā sabaqakum bihā" is a resumptive sentence (jumlah mustaʾnafah) confirming the indecency of that act, as if someone had asked: why was it indecent? It was said: because no one before them had undertaken it, shrinking from it in their natures because of its extreme ugliness, until the people of Lot came forward to it because of the wickedness of their nature. They said: no male had mounted a male before the people of Lot. End of quote. It appears that "mā sabaqakum bihā" is a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah), as if he said: do you commit indecency, originating it, not preceded by anyone in it? He asked first and second as questions of denial, rebuke and reproach, and clarified what that vague indecency was in His saying "indeed you commit an indecency," though it is specific, namely the mounting of males in the anus, by His saying "mā sabaqakum bihā." Then He said: "Do you really approach men," meaning in the anus, "and cut off the way," meaning the offspring, by leaving the womb idle and having intercourse with the anuses of men; or by detaining strangers for that act until the roads were cut off; or by killing and taking property; or by the ugliness of the reputation, until the paths of people in trade were cut off.

﴿And you commit in your gatherings﴾, meaning in your assembly where you gather. It is a generic noun, since their gatherings are many in their cities, and it is not called a nādī (gathering) except so long as its people are in it; when they rise from it, the term nādī is not applied to it except figuratively.

"Al-munkar" is what intellects, laws and manly honor reject: throwing pebbles at people, and making light of a stranger who passes by. "Umm Hani narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), or the mounting of men in their assemblies while they watch one another," said by Mansur, Mujahid, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, and Qatadah ibn Zayd; or their passing wind openly; or their slapping one another in them, said by Ibn 'Abbas; or pigeon-playing; or dyeing the fingers with henna, whistling, pebble-throwing, and casting off modesty in all their affairs, said by Mujahid also; or throwing pebbles, shooting with pellets, snapping of fingers, chewing gum, using a toothstick among people, undoing buttons, insults, and obscenity in joking, said by Ibn 'Abbas also, together with their polytheism toward Allah. Among them there were sins other than indecency: injustice among themselves, vulgarity, buffoonery in their assemblies, pebble-throwing, gambling with dice and chess, wearing dyed garments, women's clothing worn by men, and tolls imposed on every passer-by; and they were the first to commit sodomy and the first to practise female homosexuality.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 29, verse 24–35 (part 2 of 2):

When Lut (peace be upon him) reproached them for these abominations, they persisted stubbornly in denial, so their answer to him was: ﴿They said, "Bring us the punishment of Allah, if you are of the truthful"﴾, meaning regarding what you threaten us with of the descent of punishment. Since he was only commanding them to abandon the indecencies and the vile sins they were committing, and promising punishment for them, and they used to say that Allah had not forbidden this and does not punish for it, while he said that Allah had forbidden it and punishes for it, ﴿they said, "Bring us the punishment of Allah"﴾. Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and Ibn Kathir did likewise, except that he read the nūn of "baynikum" with kasra. Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read "mawaddatan" with tanwin and the accusative, and "baynakum" with the accusative; Hamzah did likewise, except that he made "mawaddatan" annexed to "baynakum" and read it with the genitive, as in the reading of the one who read "mawaddatan" as an accusative with the sense of "preparatory" (muhayyi'ah). The verb "ittakhadha" may be among those that take two objects, and the second object is "mawadda," meaning you took the idols because of the affection among you, with an omitted noun, or you took them as an affection among you, like His saying: ﴿And among people are those who take, besides Allah, equals whom they love as they love Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165]. Or it may be among those that take one object, and "mawaddata" is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning so that they may be affectionate toward one another, be connected, and gather in the worship of them, as a people gather upon a single doctrine, so that love arises among them. They mentioned from Ibn Mas'ud an anomalous reading that contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf, although it has been transmitted from him what is in the consonantal text by a sound and widely attested transmission; for this reason I have not mentioned that reading.

﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection﴾ mutual cursing will take place among you, meaning the worshippers and the worshipped idols will curse one another, as in His saying ﴿and they will become opponents to them﴾ [Maryam: 82]. It is also possible that both are attached to omitted words, so that they are in the position of a qualifier, meaning "existing among you in the life of this world," being a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun hidden in "baynikum." Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that it be attached to "baynikum" itself, and he said: because its meaning is "your gathering or your connection." He also permitted making it a circumstantial clause from "baynikum," and he said: because it is definite through annexation. He said: "These are two forms of parsing that cannot be understood."

﴿So Lot believed him.﴾ No one from his people believed in Abraham except Lot, peace be upon him, when he saw that the fire did not burn him. He was the son of Sarah's brother, or he was her uncle's daughter's son. The pronoun in "wa-qala" refers to Abraham, which is the apparent meaning, so that it harmonizes with His saying: ﴿And We gave him Isaac﴾. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Nakha'i. A group said: it refers to Lot, and Hajar, and Abraham, peace be upon them, who emigrated from their town of Kuthā, which is in the countryside of Iraq, in the land of Babylon, to Palestine in the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria). Abraham was seventy-five years old, and he was the first to emigrate for the sake of Allah. Ibn Jurayj said: he emigrated to Harran, then to al-Sham, and during this emigration Sarah was with him. The muhājir is one who is free of something, and in the terminology of the Shari'ah it is one who leaves his homeland seeking the pleasure of Allah. The name was known for the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun), before the conquest of Mecca. ("To my Lord") means: to the direction to which my Lord commanded me to emigrate. It was said: to where I will not be prevented from worshipping my Lord. It was said: emigrating from those among my people who opposed me, drawing near to my Lord. Abraham settled in a town in the land of Palestine, and left Lot in Sodom, which is the overturned city, at a distance of one day and night from the town of Abraham, peace be upon them both.

﴿Indeed He is the Almighty﴾ whom no one who worships Him is humiliated, ﴿the Wise﴾ who places things in their proper places. The pronoun in "dhurriyyatihi" refers to Abraham. "The prophethood" includes Isaac, Jacob, the prophets of the Children of Israel, Ishmael, and Muhammad, the seal of them, may Allah bless them all. "The Book" is a generic noun which includes the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel, and the Furqan.

﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾, meaning during his life. Mujahid said: his deliverance from the fire and from the tyrant king, and good deeds, and a good praise, such that every nation takes him as their leader. Ibn Jurayj said: and a child in whom his eye is comforted. al-Hasan said this. al-Suddi said: he saw his place in Paradise. Ibn Abi Burdah said: what he was granted success in of the deeds of the Hereafter. al-Mawardi said: the continuance of his hospitality at his grave, and this is not for any prophet other than him. It was said: prophethood and wisdom. It was said: the prayer upon him until the end of time.

"Lūtan" is in the accusative by an implied "remember" (udhkur), or by coordination with Abraham, or by coordination with what Abraham was coordinated with. The majority read "a-innakum" with the interrogative in both places together. It was also read as "annakum" in the declarative, and the second with the interrogative. Abu 'Ubayd said: I found it in the Imam (the standard codex) with one letter without a yā', and I saw the second with two letters, the yā' and the nūn. In the story of Lot it is not stated that he called his people to the worship of Allah, as it is in the story of Abraham and the story of Shu'ayb; because Lot was from the people of Abraham and in his time, and Abraham had preceded him in calling to the worship of Allah and to His oneness, and his matter had become well known among the creation for that, so Lot mentioned what was specific to him, namely the prohibition of indecency and other things. As for Abraham and Shu'ayb, they came after those who worshipped Allah had died out, and for that reason they called to the worship of Allah.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "mā sabaqakum bihā" is a resumptive sentence (jumlah mustaʾnafah) confirming the indecency of that act, as if someone had asked: why was it indecent? It was said: because no one before them had undertaken it, shrinking from it in their natures because of its extreme ugliness, until the people of Lot came forward to it because of the wickedness of their nature. They said: no male had mounted a male before the people of Lot. End of quote.
