Whoever takes this position into account, conjoins it to the position of the kaf; the kaf, according to al-Akhfash and Hisham, is in the accusative position, and "ahlaka" is conjoined to it, because this nun is like tanwin, and both of them, in their view, are elided for the delicacy of the pronoun and its strong need to connect with what precedes it. The majority read ﴿سِيءَ﴾ with a kasra on the sin; Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma. 'Isa and Talha read ﴿سُوءَ﴾ with a damma, and it is the dialect of Banu Hudhayl; and Banu Wubayr say qula and bu'a for qila and biya' and the like. It was read "munzilun" with and without shadda; Ibn Muhaysin read "rujzan" with a damma on the ra'; and Abu Haywa and al-A'mash read with a kasra on the sin of "yafsuqun". The apparent view is that the pronoun in "minha" refers to the town. Ibn 'Abbas said: their dwellings that are in ruins. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi related that the sign is in their town, except that its foundations are at the top and its roofs at the bottom until now. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is that We left it as a sign, saying: indeed in the sky there is a sign, meaning that it is a sign. End of quote. This does not hold except on the basis of adding "min" in an obligatory position, like his saying: "I gave her in dowry a robe and a he-goat," meaning: I gave her dowry; and likewise: "And We have indeed left it as a sign." It was said: the pronoun in "minha" refers to the deed done to them; so it was said: the sign is the stones which the first of this nation encountered, said by Qatadah; it was said: the black water on the face of the earth, said by Mujahid; and it was said: He completed what He did to them. And ﴿لِقَوْمٍ﴾ is related to ﴿تَرَكْنَا﴾, or to ﴿بَيِّنَةً﴾.

And to Midian [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb, and he said: "O my people, worship Allah and hope for the Last Day, and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief." But they denied him, so the earthquake seized them, and they were lying prostrate in their homes. And [We destroyed] 'Ad and Thamud, and it has become clear to you from their dwellings. Satan made their deeds appear fair to them and barred them from the way, though they were discerning. And [We destroyed] Qarun, Pharaoh and Haman. Moses came to them with clear proofs, but they acted arrogantly on the earth, and they could not outrun [Us]. So each of them We seized for his sin: among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of pebbles, among them those seized by the Cry, among them those whom We caused the earth to swallow, and among them those whom We drowned. Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves. The likeness of those who take protectors other than Allah is like the spider that takes a house, and indeed the weakest of houses is the spider's house, if only they knew. Indeed Allah knows what they call upon besides Him, of anything; and He is the Mighty, the Wise. These are the parables We set forth for mankind, but none understands them except the people of knowledge. Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth; indeed in that is a sign for the believers. Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book, and establish the prayer. Indeed the prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of Allah is greater; and Allah knows what you do.

(And to Midian) meaning: and to Midian We sent, or We raised up [a messenger], [verbs] which take the preposition ila (to). He commanded them to worship Allah and to believe in the Resurrection and the Last Day. The command to hope (wa-rjū, "and hope") is a command to do that upon which hope is based; the cause is put in the place of the effect. The meaning is: do the things by which you hope for reward from Allah. Or it is a command to hope on the condition of fulfilling its prerequisite, which is belief in Allah. Abu 'Ubayda said: "wa-rjū" means "fear," i.e., fear the punishment of the Last Day, the vengeance of Allah upon you if you do not worship Him. The command to worship and to hope implies that if they do not do so, punishment will befall them. Thus it came: "but they denied him" (fa-kadhdhabūhu), and the fruit of denial came, which is: "so the earthquake seized them, and they were lying prostrate in their homes." The interpretation of such sentences has already been given. "'Ad and Thamud" is in the accusative by an implied verb, "We destroyed," indicated by "the earthquake seized them." It is also said that it is in the accusative by conjunction with the pronoun in "seized them" (fa-akhadhathumu). Al-Kisa'i went too far in conjoining it with "those who" in His saying: "And We certainly tested those before them" (Q. 29:3). He recited "Thamud" without tanwin (nunation), as did Hamza, Shayba, al-Hasan and Hafs; the rest of the Seven read it with tanwin. Ibn Wathhab recited "wa-'Ādin wa-Thamūdin" with kasra in both and tanwin, conjoined to "Midian," meaning: and We sent to 'Ad and Thamud.

(And it has become clear to you) meaning: that, i.e., what has been described to you of their destruction, from the direction of their dwellings, when you look at them as you pass by them. The people of Mecca used to pass by them on their journeys. Al-A'mash recited "masākinuhum" with ḍamma, without "min," so it is the subject of "tabayyana" (became clear).

(And Satan made their deeds appear fair to them) meaning: by his whispering and misleading, [he made appear fair] their ugly deeds. (And barred them from the way of Allah), which is the path of belief in Allah and His messengers.

(And they were discerning) meaning: in their disbelief they had insight and self-admiration. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak. It is also said: they were intelligent, knowing that the message and the signs are true, but they disbelieved out of obstinacy, and denied them, though their souls were certain of them.

(And Qarun) is conjoined to what precedes it, or is in the accusative by an implied "remember." (They acted arrogantly) meaning: they refused to acknowledge the Creator and to worship Him on the earth, indicating the small extent of their intellect; for whoever is on the earth feels weakness, and whoever is in the heaven feels strength, and those in the heaven do not act arrogantly against worshipping Allah, so how about those on the earth? (And they could not outrun [Us]) meaning: they could not outrun the nations to disbelief; that is the custom of the nations with their messengers.

The "hāṣib" (storm of pebbles) was for the people of Lut; it is a violent wind carrying pebbles. It is also said that it was an angel who used to hurl them. The Cry was for Midian and Thamud; the sinking into the earth was for Qarun; and drowning was for the people of Nuh and for Pharaoh and his people. Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: "It is likely that the people of 'Ad are included under the storm of pebbles, for that wind must have pelted them with harmful things. The hāṣib is the passing cloud or wind when it is struck with something." Among its uses is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Facing the north of Syria, it strikes them with pebbles like cotton fluff scattered."

And the saying of al-Akhtal:

"It hurls the thorn-trees with pebbles of its ice, until it passes the night upon the thorn-trees, scattered."

The spider (al-'ankabūt) is a well-known animal; its form is fa'lalūt; it may be feminine or masculine. Its masculine usage is in the saying of the poet:

"Over their rain-clouds, of them are houses, as if the spider had built them."

Its plural is 'anākib, and its diminutive is 'unaykib. He, exalted is He, likens the disbelievers in their worship of idols, and in their building their affairs upon them, to the spider which builds and strives, yet all its affairs are weak: whenever any small harmful creature or insect touches it, it destroys it. So too is the case of those, and their effort is vanishing, having no strength and no support. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The purpose is to liken what they have taken as a support and reliance in their religion, and whom they have taken as protectors besides Allah, to what is a proverb among people for feebleness and weakness of strength, namely the spider's web. Do you not see the conclusion of the comparison, which is His saying: 'Indeed the weakest of houses is the spider's house'?" End of quote. He means by his saying, "Do you not see the conclusion of the comparison," in accordance with what he mentioned first, that the purpose is to liken the one who takes [protectors] to the house, not to liken the one who takes [protectors] to the spider. But what appears is that the comparison is between the one who takes a protector besides Allah and the spider which takes a house. That is, the one who takes a protector besides Allah has no reliance on his protector, just as the spider has no reliance on its house for shade and dwelling; rather, if it entered it, it would tear it. Then He explained the condition of its house, that it is at the extreme of weakness, such that no benefit can be derived from it. Just as those idols do not benefit or avail anything at all. His saying "if only they knew" is not connected to "indeed the weakest of houses is the spider's house," because everyone knows that. Rather the meaning is: if only they knew that this is their likeness, and that the matter of their religion reaches such an extreme of weakness, they would have abandoned it, and would not have taken the idols as gods.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: "If the comparison of what they rely on in their religion to the spider's house is valid, and it is valid that the weakest of houses is the spider's house, then it is clear that their religion is the weakest of religions, if only they knew. Or the statement, after the validity of the comparison, comes out as a figure of speech, as if He said: 'And indeed the weakest of what is relied upon in religion is the worship of idols, if only they knew.'" One may say: the likeness of the polytheist who worships an idol, compared to the believer who worships Allah, is like a spider that takes a house, compared to a man who built a house of baked brick and plaster or hewed it from rock. Just as the weakest of houses, when you examine houses, is the spider's house, so too the weakest of religions, when you examine religions, is the worship of idols, if only they knew. End of quote.

What he mentioned, "One may say, etc.," is not indicated by the wording of the verse; rather it is an imposition on the wording of what it does not bear, as is his habit in much of his exegesis.

Apparently, (akbar) is an elative (a'far al-tafdil, comparative form). ʿAbd Allah, Salman, Abu al-Darda, Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu Qurra said: its meaning is, "and the remembrance of God of you is greater than your remembrance of Him." Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: greater than everything. It was also said: "and the remembrance of God in prayer is greater than it outside prayer," meaning greater in reward. It was said: greater than the other pillars of prayer. It was said: "and the remembrance of God" means His prohibition is greater than the prohibition of prayer. It was said: greater than all worship (p-154).

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: In my view, the meaning is: "and the remembrance of God is greater absolutely," that is, it is what forbids indecency and wrongdoing. The part of it that occurs in prayer forbids, as it forbids outside prayer, because abstention only comes from one who remembers God and is mindful of Him. The reward of that one who remembers is that God mentions him among an assembly better than his own. The movements of prayer have no effect on the prohibition; the beneficial remembrance is that which comes with knowledge, the heart's attentiveness, and its freedom (from other concerns) except for God. As for what does not go beyond the tongue, it is in a different rank.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He means that prayer is greater than other acts of obedience, and He named it "the remembrance of God," as He said: ﴿So hasten to the remembrance of God﴾ [al-Jumuʿah: 9]. He said "and the remembrance of God" so that it stands alone as a reason, as if He said: "Prayer is greater, because it is the remembrance of God," concerning what you do of good and evil, so that He will recompense you. In this is a warning and an exhortation to mindfulness.

Satan made their deeds appear fair to them and barred them from the way, though they were discerning. And [We destroyed] Qarun, Pharaoh and Haman. Moses came to them with clear proofs, but they acted arrogantly on the earth, and they could not outrun [Us]. So each of them We seized for his sin: among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of pebbles, among them those seized by the Cry, among them those whom We caused the earth to swallow, and among them those whom We drowned. Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves. The likeness of those who take protectors other than Allah is like the spider that takes a house, and indeed the weakest of houses is the spider's house, if only they knew. Indeed Allah knows what they call upon besides Him, of anything; and He is the Mighty, the Wise. These are the parables We set forth for mankind, but none understands them except the people of knowledge. Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth; indeed in that is a sign for the believers. Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book, and establish the prayer. Indeed the prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of Allah is greater; and Allah knows what you do.

The meaning is: do the things by which you hope for reward from Allah. Or it is a command to hope on the condition of fulfilling its prerequisite, which is belief in Allah. (And Qarun) is conjoined to what precedes it, or is in the accusative by an implied "remember." "Facing the north of Syria, it strikes them with pebbles like cotton fluff scattered."

And the saying of al-Akhtal:

"It hurls the thorn-trees with pebbles of its ice, until it passes the night upon the thorn-trees, scattered."

Its plural is 'anākib, and its diminutive is 'unaykib. (And they were discerning) meaning: in their disbelief they had insight and self-admiration. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak. It is also said: they were intelligent, knowing that the message and the signs are true, but they disbelieved out of obstinacy, and denied them, though their souls were certain of them.

(And Qarun) is conjoined to what precedes it, or is in the accusative by an implied "remember." (They acted arrogantly) meaning: they refused to acknowledge the Creator and to worship Him on the earth, indicating the small extent of their intellect; for whoever is on the earth feels weakness, and whoever is in the heaven feels strength, and those in the heaven do not act arrogantly against worshipping Allah, so how about those on the earth? (And they could not outrun [Us]) meaning: they could not outrun the nations to disbelief; that is the custom of the nations with their messengers.

The "hāṣib" (storm of pebbles) was for the people of Lut; it is a violent wind carrying pebbles. It is also said that it was an angel who used to hurl them. The Cry was for Midian and Thamud; the sinking into the earth was for Qarun; and drowning was for the people of Nuh and for Pharaoh and his people. "Facing the north of Syria, it strikes them with pebbles like cotton fluff scattered."

And the saying of al-Akhtal:

"It hurls the thorn-trees with pebbles of its ice, until it passes the night upon the thorn-trees, scattered."

"Over their rain-clouds, of them are houses, as if the spider had built them."

Its plural is 'anākib, and its diminutive is 'unaykib. The people of Mecca used to pass by them on their journeys. Al-A'mash recited "masākinuhum" with ḍamma, without "min," so it is the subject of "tabayyana" (became clear).

(And Satan made their deeds appear fair to them) meaning: by his whispering and misleading, [he made appear fair] their ugly deeds. (And barred them from the way of Allah), which is the path of belief in Allah and His messengers.

(And they were discerning) meaning: in their disbelief they had insight and self-admiration. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak. It is also said: they were intelligent, knowing that the message and the signs are true, but they disbelieved out of obstinacy, and denied them, though their souls were certain of them.

(And Qarun) is conjoined to what precedes it, or is in the accusative by an implied "remember." (They acted arrogantly) meaning: they refused to acknowledge the Creator and to worship Him on the earth, indicating the small extent of their intellect; for whoever is on the earth feels weakness, and whoever is in the heaven feels strength, and those in the heaven do not act arrogantly against worshipping Allah, so how about those on the earth? (And they could not outrun [Us]) meaning: they could not outrun the nations to disbelief; that is the custom of the nations with their messengers.

The "hāṣib" (storm of pebbles) was for the people of Lut; it is a violent wind carrying pebbles. It is also said that it was an angel who used to hurl them. The Cry was for Midian and Thamud; the sinking into the earth was for Qarun; and drowning was for the people of Nuh and for Pharaoh and his people. Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: "It is likely that the people of 'Ad are included under the storm of pebbles, for that wind must have pelted them with harmful things. The hāṣib is the passing cloud or wind when it is struck with something." Among its uses is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Facing the north of Syria, it strikes them with pebbles like cotton fluff scattered."

And the saying of al-Akhtal:

"It hurls the thorn-trees with pebbles of its ice, until it passes the night upon the thorn-trees, scattered."

The spider (al-'ankabūt) is a well-known animal; its form is fa'lalūt; it may be feminine or masculine. Its masculine usage is in the saying of the poet:

"Over their rain-clouds, of them are houses, as if the spider had built them."

Its plural is 'anākib, and its diminutive is 'unaykib. He, exalted is He, likens the disbelievers in their worship of idols, and in their building their affairs upon them, to the spider which builds and strives, yet all its affairs are weak: whenever any small harmful creature or insect touches it, it destroys it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The purpose is to liken what they have taken as a support and reliance in their religion, and whom they have taken as protectors besides Allah, to what is a proverb among people for feebleness and weakness of strength, namely the spider's web. That is, the one who takes a protector besides Allah has no reliance on his protector, just as the spider has no reliance on its house for shade and dwelling; rather, if it entered it, it would tear it. Then He explained the condition of its house, that it is at the extreme of weakness, such that no benefit can be derived from it. Just as those idols do not benefit or avail anything at all. His saying "if only they knew" is not connected to "indeed the weakest of houses is the spider's house," because everyone knows that. Rather the meaning is: if only they knew that this is their likeness, and that the matter of their religion reaches such an extreme of weakness, they would have abandoned it, and would not have taken the idols as gods.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: "If the comparison of what they rely on in their religion to the spider's house is valid, and it is valid that the weakest of houses is the spider's house, then it is clear that their religion is the weakest of religions, if only they knew. One may say: the likeness of the polytheist who worships an idol, compared to the believer who worships Allah, is like a spider that takes a house, compared to a man who built a house of baked brick and plaster or hewed it from rock. Just as the weakest of houses, when you examine houses, is the spider's house, so too the weakest of religions, when you examine religions, is the worship of idols, if only they knew. End of quote.

What he mentioned, "One may say, etc.," is not indicated by the wording of the verse; rather it is an imposition on the wording of what it does not bear, as is his habit in much of his exegesis.

As for one whom you see among those who pray and engages in sins, his prayer is not of the description that has preceded.

The Messenger of God ﷺ then said: "Did I not tell you?"

Apparently, (akbar) is an elative (a'far al-tafdil, comparative form). ʿAbd Allah, Salman, Abu al-Darda, Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu Qurra said: its meaning is, "and the remembrance of God of you is greater than your remembrance of Him." It was said: greater than the other pillars of prayer. It was said: "and the remembrance of God" means His prohibition is greater than the prohibition of prayer. It was said: greater than all worship (p-154).

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: In my view, the meaning is: "and the remembrance of God is greater absolutely," that is, it is what forbids indecency and wrongdoing. The reward of that one who remembers is that God mentions him among an assembly better than his own. The movements of prayer have no effect on the prohibition; the beneficial remembrance is that which comes with knowledge, the heart's attentiveness, and its freedom (from other concerns) except for God. As for what does not go beyond the tongue, it is in a different rank.

In this is a warning and an exhortation to mindfulness.

And to Midian [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb, and he said: "O my people, worship Allah and hope for the Last Day, and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief." But they denied him, so the earthquake seized them, and they were lying prostrate in their homes. And [We destroyed] 'Ad and Thamud, and it has become clear to you from their dwellings. Satan made their deeds appear fair to them and barred them from the way, though they were discerning. And [We destroyed] Qarun, Pharaoh and Haman. Moses came to them with clear proofs, but they acted arrogantly on the earth, and they could not outrun [Us]. So each of them We seized for his sin: among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of pebbles, among them those seized by the Cry, among them those whom We caused the earth to swallow, and among them those whom We drowned. Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves. The likeness of those who take protectors other than Allah is like the spider that takes a house, and indeed the weakest of houses is the spider's house, if only they knew. Indeed Allah knows what they call upon besides Him, of anything; and He is the Mighty, the Wise. These are the parables We set forth for mankind, but none understands them except the people of knowledge. Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth; indeed in that is a sign for the believers. Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book, and establish the prayer. Indeed the prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of Allah is greater; and Allah knows what you do.

[p. 155] **And (Ahl al-Kitab)** means the Jews and the Christians.

**﴿Except with what is best﴾** means with gentleness in calling to God and in drawing attention to His signs.

**﴿Except those of them who did wrong﴾**: those who did not pay the jizya (the poll tax levied on non-Muslim subjects) and who took up war, who declared that God has a son or a partner, or who said that God's hand is chained. The verse is abrogated (mansukh) with regard to treating peacefully those who were not at war. This is the view of Mujahid and of the believers among the People of the Book. **(Except with what is best)** means: by agreeing with what they tell you of the reports of their early predecessors.

**﴿Except those of them who did wrong﴾** means those among them who remained upon their disbelief. This is a promise regarding Qurayza and al-Nadir. Ibn Zayd said this, and according to this view the verse is muhkam (decisive, not abrogated). It has also been said: "except those who harmed the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." Qatada said: the verse is abrogated by His saying: ﴿Fight those who do not believe﴾ [al-Tawba: 29], and so on.

The majority of reciters read **(illa)** as the particle of exception. Ibn Abbas read **"ala"** as a particle of alerting and opening, and its implied sense is: "Ala, argue with them in the best manner." **(And say: "We believe")** is part of arguing in the best manner.

**﴿In what was sent down to us﴾** is the Qur'an, **﴿and what was sent down to you﴾** is the Torah, the Psalms and the Gospel.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from Abu Hurayra: "The People of the Book used to read the Torah in Hebrew and explain it to the people of Islam in Arabic. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Do not believe the People of the Book, nor disbelieve them, but say: We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us and what has been sent down to you.'"

**(And thus)** means: like that sending down which was for the earlier books, **﴿We have sent down to you the Book﴾**, that is, the Qur'an.

**﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾** are Abdullah ibn Salam and those who believed with him.

**﴿And among these﴾** means the people of Makka. It has also been said: **﴿those to whom We have given the Book﴾** means those who preceded the time of the Messenger (ﷺ), **"believe in it"**, that is, in the Qur'an, since it is mentioned in their books that it would be sent down upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

**﴿And among these﴾** means among those of them who were in his time.

**﴿And none deny Our signs﴾** despite their clarity and the removal of doubt from them **﴿except the disbelievers﴾**, that is, from the Children of Israel and others.

Mujahid said: The People of the Book used to read in their books that Muhammad (peace be upon him) neither writes nor reads a book. So it was revealed: **(And you did not recite before it any book)**, that is, before its being sent down to you, **(any book)**: "min" here is extra, because it falls within the scope of negation. **(Nor did you transcribe it)**, that is, you did not read or write, **(with your right hand)**, which is the limb with which one writes. Mentioning it is an added depiction of what was negated from him concerning writing. When He mentioned the sending down of the Book upon him, containing eloquence and rhetorical excellence, reports of earlier nations, and unseen matters, which left humankind unable to produce a surah like it, He went on to confirm that it was sent down from God, by showing that it came from a man who was unlettered, who neither reads nor writes, and who does not mix with the learned. The appearance of this Qur'an, sent down upon him, is the greatest proof of his truthfulness. Most Muslims hold that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) never wrote at all, nor read by looking into a book.

It is reported from al-Sha'bi that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not die until he had written and dictated the (poetry of) al-Niqash. The hadith of Abu Kabsha al-Salouli: that he read a document belonging to Uyayna ibn Hisn and reported its meaning. In Sahih Muslim there is what apparently indicates that he wrote directly. As for their doubting while this proof is so clear, its corruption is evident. **The falsifiers (al-mubtilun)** are the People of the Book, according to Qatada, or the disbelieving Quraysh, according to Mujahid. They were called falsifiers because they disbelieved in him, and he was an unlettered man far from doubt. Since he was neither a reader nor a writer, their doubt had no basis.

**(Rather, it)**, that is, the Qur'an, **﴿is clear signs﴾**, evident in their inimitability, **﴿in the breasts of those given knowledge﴾**, that is, firmly established, believed in, preserved in their breasts. Most of the community recites it openly, unlike other books, which are not miraculous and are only read from scrolls. It was said of this community: their breasts are their gospels. That the Qur'an is this is supported by the reading of Abdullah: **"Rather, they are clear signs."** It has also been said: **"Rather, he,"** that is, the Prophet (ﷺ) and his affairs, **"are clear signs,"** said by Qatada. And one reading is: "Rather, he is a clear sign," in the singular. It has been said: **"Rather, he,"** meaning the fact that he neither reads nor writes. One says: "You denied him" and "you denied in him," and "you disbelieved him" and "you disbelieved in him." It is said that the first denial is linked to Oneness, and the second is linked to prophethood. The first was concluded with "the disbelievers," and because they are the counterpart of the believers in His saying: **﴿Who believe in it, and among these are those who believe﴾**, the latter is concluded with "the wrongdoers," because they denied after the proof had been established that the Messenger (ﷺ) had received the Qur'an sent down upon him, while he was unlettered, neither reading nor writing. So they are the wrongdoers after the miracle had become manifest.

**﴿And they say: "Why were not signs sent down upon him from his Lord?"﴾** means: the Quraysh, and some Jews, who taught the Quraysh this kind of demand, said to him: "Will he not bring us a sign like the signs of Moses, such as the staff and others?" Ibn Amir, Nafi and Hafs read **(ayat)** in the plural. The rest of the seven read it in the singular.

**﴿Say: "The signs are only with God"﴾**, He sends down whichever He wills, and had He willed to send down what they propose, He would have done so.

**﴿And I am only a warner﴾** with what I have been given of the signs. Yahya ibn Ja'da mentions that some Muslims came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with writings in which they had recorded some of what the Jews were saying. When he looked at them he threw them away and said: "It is enough folly for a people, or misguidance for a people, to turn away from what their own prophet brought to what was brought by someone other than their prophet." So it was revealed: **(Is it not sufficient for them)**.

What seems apparent is that it is a response to those who said: **﴿Why was not a sign sent down upon him from his Lord?﴾** [Yunus: 20]. That is: "Is it not sufficient for them as a sign that suffices in place of all other signs, if they are seekers of the truth and not contentious: this Qur'an, whose recitation endures among them in every place and time? There will always remain with them a sign that is established and does not vanish or fade, unlike every sign which disappears after its existence and is found only in one place rather than another." Indeed, in this sign, which exists in every place and time, there is **﴿a mercy﴾**, a great blessing that cannot be denied, **﴿and a reminder﴾** to be remembered.

It has been said: **﴿Is it not sufficient for them﴾**, meaning the Jews, **(that We have sent down to you the Book, recited to them)**, confirming what they have in their hands of your description and the description of your religion. It is reported that Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions said: "O Muhammad, who will testify that you are the Messenger of God?" Then it was revealed: **﴿Say: "God suffices as witness between me and you"﴾**, that is: I have conveyed and warned, and you have denied and rejected, and He is the Knower **﴿of what is in the heavens and the earth﴾**, so He knows my affair and your affair. **﴿And those who believe in falsehood﴾**. Ibn Abbas said: "in other than God." Muqatil said: "in the worship of Satan." It has been said: "in an idol."

**(And they ask you to hasten)**, that is, the disbelievers of Quraysh, in their saying: **﴿Bring us what you threaten us with﴾** [al-A'raf: 77], and the saying of al-Nadr: **﴿Then rain upon us stones from the sky﴾** [al-Anfal: 32]. This is hastening in the manner of challenge, denial and mockery concerning the punishment with which the Messenger (ﷺ) threatened them. **The appointed term (al-ajal al-musamma)** is what God named and recorded in the Preserved Tablet for their punishment, and wisdom required its postponement. Ibn Jubayr said: it is the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Salam said: it is the period between the two blasts (of the trumpet). It has been said: it is the Day of Badr.

**﴿And it will surely come upon them suddenly﴾**, that is, unexpectedly, which is what appeared on the Day of Badr and in the seven years (of famine). Then He repeated their act and denounced it, and informed that Jahannam lies behind them, encompassing them. **﴿The Day the punishment covers them﴾** is governed by **"encompassing" (muhitatun)**. The Kufans and Nafi read **(wa-yaqulu)**, meaning God; the rest of the seven read it with the nun, either the nun of majesty or the nun of the group of angels; Abu al-Barr Huthaym read it with the ta', meaning Jahannam, just as speech is attributed to it in His saying: **﴿And it says: "Are there any more?"﴾** [Qaf: 30]. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abi Abla read **wa-yuqalu** in the passive voice, meaning "and it will be said."

[p. 155] **And (Ahl al-Kitab)** means the Jews and the Christians.

**﴿Except with what is best﴾** means with gentleness in calling to God and in drawing attention to His signs.

**﴿Except those of them who did wrong﴾**: those who did not pay the jizya (the poll tax levied on non-Muslim subjects) and who took up war, who declared that God has a son or a partner, or who said that God's hand is chained. The verse is abrogated (mansukh) with regard to treating peacefully those who were not at war. This is the view of Mujahid and of the believers among the People of the Book. **(Except with what is best)** means: by agreeing with what they tell you of the reports of their early predecessors.

**﴿Except those of them who did wrong﴾** means those among them who remained upon their disbelief. This is a promise regarding Qurayza and al-Nadir. Ibn Zayd said this, and according to this view the verse is muhkam (decisive, not abrogated). It has also been said: "except those who harmed the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." Qatada said: the verse is abrogated by His saying: ﴿Fight those who do not believe﴾ [al-Tawba: 29], and so on.

The majority of reciters read **(illa)** as the particle of exception. Ibn Abbas read **"ala"** as a particle of alerting and opening, and its implied sense is: "Ala, argue with them in the best manner." **(And say: "We believe")** is part of arguing in the best manner.

**﴿In what was sent down to us﴾** is the Qur'an, **﴿and what was sent down to you﴾** is the Torah, the Psalms and the Gospel.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from Abu Hurayra: "The People of the Book used to read the Torah in Hebrew and explain it to the people of Islam in Arabic. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Do not believe the People of the Book, nor disbelieve them, but say: We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us and what has been sent down to you.'"

**(And thus)** means: like that sending down which was for the earlier books, **﴿We have sent down to you the Book﴾**, that is, the Qur'an.

**﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾** are Abdullah ibn Salam and those who believed with him.

**﴿And among these﴾** means the people of Makka. It has also been said: **﴿those to whom We have given the Book﴾** means those who preceded the time of the Messenger (ﷺ), **"believe in it"**, that is, in the Qur'an, since it is mentioned in their books that it would be sent down upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

**﴿And among these﴾** means among those of them who were in his time.

**﴿And none deny Our signs﴾** despite their clarity and the removal of doubt from them **﴿except the disbelievers﴾**, that is, from the Children of Israel and others.

Mujahid said: The People of the Book used to read in their books that Muhammad (peace be upon him) neither writes nor reads a book. So it was revealed: **(And you did not recite before it any book)**, that is, before its being sent down to you, **(any book)**: "min" here is extra, because it falls within the scope of negation. **(Nor did you transcribe it)**, that is, you did not read or write, **(with your right hand)**, which is the limb with which one writes. Mentioning it is an added depiction of what was negated from him concerning writing. When He mentioned the sending down of the Book upon him, containing eloquence and rhetorical excellence, reports of earlier nations, and unseen matters, which left humankind unable to produce a surah like it, He went on to confirm that it was sent down from God, by showing that it came from a man who was unlettered, who neither reads nor writes, and who does not mix with the learned. The appearance of this Qur'an, sent down upon him, is the greatest proof of his truthfulness. Most Muslims hold that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) never wrote at all, nor read by looking into a book.

It is reported from al-Sha'bi that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not die until he had written and dictated the (poetry of) al-Niqash. The hadith of Abu Kabsha al-Salouli: that he read a document belonging to Uyayna ibn Hisn and reported its meaning. In Sahih Muslim there is what apparently indicates that he wrote directly. A group of scholars held this view, among them Abu Dharr Abdullah ibn Ahmad al-Harawi and the judge Abu al-Walid al-Baji, and others. Many scholars of our lands strongly rejected Abu al-Walid al-Baji, to the extent that some of them would revile him and attack him from the pulpit. Most scholars interpreted what was narrated, that he wrote, to mean that he ordered writing, as one says: "The sultan wrote to so-and-so with such-and-such," meaning he ordered the writing.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 29, verses 56–69 (part 1 of 2):**

[p. 157] ﴿O My servants who believe, indeed My earth is vast, so worship Me alone.﴾ ﴿Every soul will taste death; then to Us you will be returned.﴾ ﴿As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely settle them in lofty chambers in Paradise, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. How excellent is the reward of the workers!﴾ ﴿Those who are patient and upon their Lord rely.﴾ ﴿And how many a creature does not carry its provision; Allah provides for it, and for you. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon?" they would surely say, "Allah." Then how are they deluded?﴾ ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing of everything.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who sends down water from the sky and thereby gives life to the earth after its death?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Praise be to Allah." But most of them do not reason.﴾ ﴿And this worldly life is nothing but amusement and play. Indeed, the Last Abode is the true life, if only they knew.﴾ ﴿So when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them safely to land, at once they associate others with Him.﴾ ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them and enjoy themselves; but they will soon know.﴾ ﴿Do they not see that We made a sanctuary secure, while people are being snatched away from around them? Then do they believe in falsehood and deny the favor of Allah?﴾ ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies the truth when it comes to him? Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾ ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths. And indeed, Allah is with the good-doers.﴾

Most of the exegetes (mufassirun, the scholars of tafsir, or Qur'anic exegesis) held that His saying: "O My servants..." up to the end of the verse, was revealed concerning those who were residing in Makkah. They were commanded to emigrate from it to Madinah. That is: distance yourselves from the people of polytheism, and seek out the people of faith. Abu al-Aliyah said: "Travel in search of His allies." Ibn Jubayr, Ata', Mujahid and Malik ibn Anas said: "The land in which injustice and evil are committed, this verse applies to it, and emigration from it to a land of truth becomes obligatory." Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: "Indeed My earth is vast" is a promise of the abundance of provision throughout the whole earth. It was also said: "The earth of Paradise is vast; I shall give it to you." Mujahid said: "Travel to fight His enemies."

As for "so worship Me alone" (fa-iyyaya fa-'budun), it is from the construction of ishtighal (the construction in which the verb is preoccupied with a pronoun referring to the object, so the object is fronted). That is: "So worship Me alone, so worship Me." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the meaning of the fa' in 'fa-'budun', and the fronting of the object?" I (al-Zamakhshari) answer: the fa' is the response to an elided conditional clause, because the meaning is: "If My earth is vast, then if you do not make worship sincere in one land, make it sincere in another." Then the condition was elided, and the fronting of the object was given in its place, along with the fronting conveying the meaning of exclusivity and sincerity. End of quote. This answer requires reflection.

When the Exalted informed of the vastness of His earth, and this was an indication of emigration, and He commanded the worship of Him, one might suppose that whoever leaves his land in which he grew up, for the sake of those who inhabit it from the people of disbelief, to the abode of Islam, will not find things going for him there as they went for him in his own land, and that may perhaps lead to his destruction. So He informed that every soul has a term that it will reach, and it will die wherever it is, and that the return of the gathered to their parts will be on the Day of Resurrection.

Ali read "turja'un" (you will be returned) in the active voice (with the verb built to the subject); the majority read it in the passive voice, with the second-person "ta'" (you). It is narrated from Asim that he read it with the third-person "ya'" (they). Abu Haywah read "dha'iqatu" with tanwin, and "al-mawti" in the accusative. He also read "la-nubawwi'annahum" (we will settle them) from al-mabā'ah (the dwelling). Ali, Abdullah, al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, Zayd ibn Ali, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it from al-thawa' (to dwell); and "bawwa'" (to settle) is transitive to two objects. Allah the Exalted said: "He settles the believers at their stations for battle" (Al 'Imran 3:121). It has also come transitive with the preposition "li-" (for). He the Exalted said: "And when We settled for Ibrahim the place of the House" (Al-Hajj 22:26). The meaning is: He will make for them a place of dwelling, that is, a place of return to which they retreat. "Ghurafan" means lofty chambers. As for "thawa," its meaning is "to stay," and it is an intransitive verb. The hamzah of transitivity (af'ala) was added to it, so it became transitive to one object. It has been read with shaddah as "'addā" with doubling, so "ghurafan" is in the accusative, either by dropping the preposition (in chambers), and then the usage was widened and it was elided; or by the verb being understood to include the meaning of settling, so it is transitive to two objects; or it is like a place-adverb specific to the vague, through which the verb reaches it. It is narrated from Ibn Amir: "ghurufan" with a dammah on the ra'. Ibn Wathhab read "fa-ni'ma" with a fa'; the majority read it without fa'. "Those who are patient" means: patient over leaving their homelands, emigration, and all hardships, from carrying out the commands and avoiding the prohibitions.

"And upon their Lord they rely" — these two are the total of all good: patience, and entrusting affairs to Allah the Exalted.

[p. 158] When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded those who had embraced Islam in Makkah to emigrate, they feared poverty and said: "This is a strangeness in lands where we have no home, no property, and no one to feed us." So He gave them an example from the most common animals that feed themselves without storing, and that do not worry about their sustenance, and do not carry their provision. "Carry" here means: do not transport, and do not look toward storing. This was said by Mujahid, Abu Mijlaz and Ali ibn al-Aqmar. Storing (al-idikhar) has come in a hadith: "How will you be when you remain among the dregs of the people, who store up the provision of a year, due to weakness of certainty?" It was said: it is also possible that it comes from the sense of "hamalah" (surety/guarantee), which does not undertake responsibility for itself and does not worry. Al-Hasan said: "(does not carry its provision)" means does not store; it only rises in the morning and Allah provides for it. Ibn Abbas said: "None store except the human, the ant, the mouse and the magpie." It was said: the nightingale hoards in its lap, and it is said the magpie has hiding places, except that it forgets them. The negation of its carrying of its provision is either due to its weakness and inability to do so, or because it was created without intellect, so it does not plan for what it might store for the future. That is: He provides for it despite its weakness. "And you" means: despite your ability to earn, and your cleverness in obtaining a livelihood, and despite that, your provider is Allah. "He is the All-Hearing" of your saying, "We fear poverty," "the All-Knowing" of what your hearts conceal.

Then the Exalted followed this with their acknowledgment that the originator of the world and the subjector of the two luminaries is Allah. He followed that with the extending and restricting of provision, and said: "Allah extends provision to whom He wills" that He extends it for, "and restricts it" for whom He wills to restrict it. The pronoun in "lahu" (for him) apparently refers back to "whom He wills," so that one individual is extended provision at one time and restricted at another time. It is also possible that the pronoun refers back to him in wording, while the intended meaning is another person whom He wills. This becomes similar to His saying: "And none is granted a long life, nor is his life shortened, except that it is in a Book" (Fatir 35:11), that is, from the life of another person who is granted a long life. And the saying of people: "I have a dirham and half of it," meaning: and half of another dirham. So the one who is given extended provision is other than the one whose provision is restricted. Alqamah al-Himsi read "wa-yuqaddiru" with a dammah on the ya', a fathah on the qaf and a shaddah on the dal. "All-Knowing" means He knows what sets right the servants and what corrupts them.

When He informed that they acknowledge that the Creator of the world, the subjector of the two luminaries, and the giver of life to the earth after its death is Allah, that acknowledgment obligated them that the provider of the servants is Allah, who is the one who guarantees it. He commanded His Messenger to praise Him the Exalted; because in their acknowledgment is the affirmation of Allah's oneness in creation, and the negation of partners from Him in that, and this was a proof against them, since they attributed that to Allah and yet worshipped idols.

﴿But most of them do not reason﴾: since they acknowledge the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life, yet worship other than Him.

﴿And this worldly life﴾: the pointing with "this" is a display of contempt for the world and a belittling of its matter. And how could it not be so? For it does not weigh the wing of a gnat with Allah. That is: in the speed of its passing away from its people, and their death from it, it is nothing but like children playing for an hour and then dispersing. "Al-hayawan" and "al-hayah" (life) have the same meaning, and according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh it is the verbal noun of "hayiya" (to live). The meaning: indeed it is the abode of life, that is, the enduring one that does not cease. Mujahid said: "There is no death in it." It was also said: "al-hayawan" means "the living," and it is as if the verbal noun was applied to the living thing. The Last Abode was described as "life" for emphasis by attributing life to it. The appearance of the waw in "al-hayawan" and in "Hayway" (a proper name of a man) is used as evidence by those who hold that the waw in such a structure is changed to ya' because of the kasrah before it, like "shaqiya" (he was miserable) from "al-shiqwah." As for those who hold that the final radical of the word is ya', they claim that the appearance of the waw in "hayawan" and "hayawa" is a substitute for a ya', as an anomaly. The response of "law" (if) is elided, that is: "if they had known, they would not have preferred the abode of perishing over it." The verbal noun of "hayiya" came in the pattern fa'alan because it indicates movement and agitation, like "ghalayan" (boiling), "nazawan" (leaping), "lahayan" (panting/desire), "jawalan" (roaming), and "tawafan" (circling). And "al-hayy" (the living) is one of much agitation and movement, so this pattern carries the sense of abundant movement.

When the Exalted mentioned that they acknowledge Allah when asked: "Who created the world?" and "Who sends down water from the sky?", He also mentioned another state in which they return to Allah, and acknowledge that He is the one who does what He wills. That occurs when they board the sea, the waves surge and the winds change. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: to what is His saying '"So when they board ships"' connected?" I answer: to an elided element indicated by what He described them with, and explained their situation in terms of what they were described with, of polytheism and obstinacy.

﴿So when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [p. 159] being in the form of those who make religion sincere to Allah from among the believers, since they mention none but Allah and call upon no other with Allah. In "sincere" there is a kind of mockery. "And at once they associate others" is the response to "lamma" (when), meaning: their association with Allah surprised their natural disposition; that is, it did not delay from it even for a moment. The apparent reading of "li-yakfuru" (so that they may deny) is that the lam is the lam of purpose ("kay"), and "wa-li-yatamatta'u" (and that they may enjoy themselves) is coordinated with it in the reading of the one who vocalized the lam with a kasrah, and they are: the two Arabs (Abu 'Amr and Ibn Amir), Nafi' and Asim. The meaning: they returned to their polytheism. "So that they may deny" means: what drives them to polytheism is their denial of what Allah the Exalted has given them, and their pleasure in what they were given of the passing goods of this world. This is unlike the believers, for when they are saved from such hardship, that becomes a cause of gratitude to Allah the Exalted and increased obedience to Him. It was also said: the lam in "li-yakfuru" and "wa-li-yatamatta'u" is the lam of command. This is supported by the reading of the one who made the lam of "wa-li-yatamatta'u" sukun (without vowel), and they are: Ibn Kathir, al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "How is it permissible for God, exalted is He, to command disbelief, and to tell the disobedient to do as they wish, when He forbids that and threatens punishment for it?" I say: this is a figurative usage (majaz) for abandonment (khidhlan) and leaving them alone (takhliyah), and that command is a displeasing one, to a certain end. End of quote. Takhliyah (leaving someone to themselves) and khidhlan (divine abandonment) are terms of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist theological school).

Whoever reads وَلْيَتَمَتَّعُوا with a sukun on the lam, and takes the lam in لِيَكْفُرُوا as the lam of purpose (lam kay), then the waw is coordinating one clause with another clause, not coordinating one verb with another verb.

Ibn Atiyyah reported from Ibn Mas'ud: لَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ, with the lam.

Then God reminded them of His blessings, in that He settled them in a town where they felt secure, where no one raided them or plundered them, despite their being few in number and dwelling in a place with no crops. These are among the greatest blessings they disbelieved, and it is a blessing that none can bestow except God, exalted is He.

(وَالَّذِينَ) is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the omitted oath (qasam), and whose answer is: "We will surely guide them." **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 29, verses 56–69 (part 1 of 2):**

[p. 157] ﴿O My servants who believe, indeed My earth is vast, so worship Me alone.﴾ ﴿Every soul will taste death; then to Us you will be returned.﴾ ﴿As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely settle them in lofty chambers in Paradise, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. How excellent is the reward of the workers!﴾ ﴿Those who are patient and upon their Lord rely.﴾ ﴿And how many a creature does not carry its provision; Allah provides for it, and for you. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon?" they would surely say, "Allah." Then how are they deluded?﴾ ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing of everything.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who sends down water from the sky and thereby gives life to the earth after its death?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Praise be to Allah." But most of them do not reason.﴾ ﴿And this worldly life is nothing but amusement and play. Indeed, the Last Abode is the true life, if only they knew.﴾ ﴿So when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them safely to land, at once they associate others with Him.﴾ ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them and enjoy themselves; but they will soon know.﴾ ﴿Do they not see that We made a sanctuary secure, while people are being snatched away from around them? Then do they believe in falsehood and deny the favor of Allah?﴾ ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies the truth when it comes to him? Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾ ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths. And indeed, Allah is with the good-doers.﴾

Most of the exegetes (mufassirun, the scholars of tafsir, or Qur'anic exegesis) held that His saying: "O My servants..." up to the end of the verse, was revealed concerning those who were residing in Makkah. They were commanded to emigrate from it to Madinah. That is: distance yourselves from the people of polytheism, and seek out the people of faith. Abu al-Aliyah said: "Travel in search of His allies." Ibn Jubayr, Ata', Mujahid and Malik ibn Anas said: "The land in which injustice and evil are committed, this verse applies to it, and emigration from it to a land of truth becomes obligatory." Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: "Indeed My earth is vast" is a promise of the abundance of provision throughout the whole earth. It was also said: "The earth of Paradise is vast; I shall give it to you." Mujahid said: "Travel to fight His enemies."

As for "so worship Me alone" (fa-iyyaya fa-'budun), it is from the construction of ishtighal (the construction in which the verb is preoccupied with a pronoun referring to the object, so the object is fronted). That is: "So worship Me alone, so worship Me." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the meaning of the fa' in 'fa-'budun', and the fronting of the object?" I (al-Zamakhshari) answer: the fa' is the response to an elided conditional clause, because the meaning is: "If My earth is vast, then if you do not make worship sincere in one land, make it sincere in another." Then the condition was elided, and the fronting of the object was given in its place, along with the fronting conveying the meaning of exclusivity and sincerity. End of quote. This answer requires reflection.

When the Exalted informed of the vastness of His earth, and this was an indication of emigration, and He commanded the worship of Him, one might suppose that whoever leaves his land in which he grew up, for the sake of those who inhabit it from the people of disbelief, to the abode of Islam, will not find things going for him there as they went for him in his own land, and that may perhaps lead to his destruction. So He informed that every soul has a term that it will reach, and it will die wherever it is, and that the return of the gathered to their parts will be on the Day of Resurrection.

Ali read "turja'un" (you will be returned) in the active voice (with the verb built to the subject); the majority read it in the passive voice, with the second-person "ta'" (you). It is narrated from Asim that he read it with the third-person "ya'" (they). Abu Haywah read "dha'iqatu" with tanwin, and "al-mawti" in the accusative. He also read "la-nubawwi'annahum" (we will settle them) from al-mabā'ah (the dwelling). Ali, Abdullah, al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, Zayd ibn Ali, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it from al-thawa' (to dwell); and "bawwa'" (to settle) is transitive to two objects. Allah the Exalted said: "He settles the believers at their stations for battle" (Al 'Imran 3:121). It has also come transitive with the preposition "li-" (for). He the Exalted said: "And when We settled for Ibrahim the place of the House" (Al-Hajj 22:26). The meaning is: He will make for them a place of dwelling, that is, a place of return to which they retreat. "Ghurafan" means lofty chambers. As for "thawa," its meaning is "to stay," and it is an intransitive verb. The hamzah of transitivity (af'ala) was added to it, so it became transitive to one object. It has been read with shaddah as "'addā" with doubling, so "ghurafan" is in the accusative, either by dropping the preposition (in chambers), and then the usage was widened and it was elided; or by the verb being understood to include the meaning of settling, so it is transitive to two objects; or it is like a place-adverb specific to the vague, through which the verb reaches it. It is narrated from Ibn Amir: "ghurufan" with a dammah on the ra'. Ibn Wathhab read "fa-ni'ma" with a fa'; the majority read it without fa'. "Those who are patient" means: patient over leaving their homelands, emigration, and all hardships, from carrying out the commands and avoiding the prohibitions.

"And upon their Lord they rely" — these two are the total of all good: patience, and entrusting affairs to Allah the Exalted.

[p. 158] When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded those who had embraced Islam in Makkah to emigrate, they feared poverty and said: "This is a strangeness in lands where we have no home, no property, and no one to feed us." So He gave them an example from the most common animals that feed themselves without storing, and that do not worry about their sustenance, and do not carry their provision. "Carry" here means: do not transport, and do not look toward storing. This was said by Mujahid, Abu Mijlaz and Ali ibn al-Aqmar. Storing (al-idikhar) has come in a hadith: "How will you be when you remain among the dregs of the people, who store up the provision of a year, due to weakness of certainty?" It was said: it is also possible that it comes from the sense of "hamalah" (surety/guarantee), which does not undertake responsibility for itself and does not worry. Al-Hasan said: "(does not carry its provision)" means does not store; it only rises in the morning and Allah provides for it. Ibn Abbas said: "None store except the human, the ant, the mouse and the magpie." It was said: the nightingale hoards in its lap, and it is said the magpie has hiding places, except that it forgets them. The negation of its carrying of its provision is either due to its weakness and inability to do so, or because it was created without intellect, so it does not plan for what it might store for the future. That is: He provides for it despite its weakness. "And you" means: despite your ability to earn, and your cleverness in obtaining a livelihood, and despite that, your provider is Allah. "He is the All-Hearing" of your saying, "We fear poverty," "the All-Knowing" of what your hearts conceal.

Then the Exalted followed this with their acknowledgment that the originator of the world and the subjector of the two luminaries is Allah. He followed that with the extending and restricting of provision, and said: "Allah extends provision to whom He wills" that He extends it for, "and restricts it" for whom He wills to restrict it. The pronoun in "lahu" (for him) apparently refers back to "whom He wills," so that one individual is extended provision at one time and restricted at another time. It is also possible that the pronoun refers back to him in wording, while the intended meaning is another person whom He wills. This becomes similar to His saying: "And none is granted a long life, nor is his life shortened, except that it is in a Book" (Fatir 35:11), that is, from the life of another person who is granted a long life. And the saying of people: "I have a dirham and half of it," meaning: and half of another dirham. So the one who is given extended provision is other than the one whose provision is restricted. Alqamah al-Himsi read "wa-yuqaddiru" with a dammah on the ya', a fathah on the qaf and a shaddah on the dal. "All-Knowing" means He knows what sets right the servants and what corrupts them.

When He informed that they acknowledge that the Creator of the world, the subjector of the two luminaries, and the giver of life to the earth after its death is Allah, that acknowledgment obligated them that the provider of the servants is Allah, who is the one who guarantees it. He commanded His Messenger to praise Him the Exalted; because in their acknowledgment is the affirmation of Allah's oneness in creation, and the negation of partners from Him in that, and this was a proof against them, since they attributed that to Allah and yet worshipped idols.

﴿But most of them do not reason﴾: since they acknowledge the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life, yet worship other than Him.

﴿And this worldly life﴾: the pointing with "this" is a display of contempt for the world and a belittling of its matter. And how could it not be so? For it does not weigh the wing of a gnat with Allah. That is: in the speed of its passing away from its people, and their death from it, it is nothing but like children playing for an hour and then dispersing. "Al-hayawan" and "al-hayah" (life) have the same meaning, and according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh it is the verbal noun of "hayiya" (to live). The meaning: indeed it is the abode of life, that is, the enduring one that does not cease. Mujahid said: "There is no death in it." It was also said: "al-hayawan" means "the living," and it is as if the verbal noun was applied to the living thing. The Last Abode was described as "life" for emphasis by attributing life to it. The appearance of the waw in "al-hayawan" and in "Hayway" (a proper name of a man) is used as evidence by those who hold that the waw in such a structure is changed to ya' because of the kasrah before it, like "shaqiya" (he was miserable) from "al-shiqwah." As for those who hold that the final radical of the word is ya', they claim that the appearance of the waw in "hayawan" and "hayawa" is a substitute for a ya', as an anomaly. The response of "law" (if) is elided, that is: "if they had known, they would not have preferred the abode of perishing over it." The verbal noun of "hayiya" came in the pattern fa'alan because it indicates movement and agitation, like "ghalayan" (boiling), "nazawan" (leaping), "lahayan" (panting/desire), "jawalan" (roaming), and "tawafan" (circling). And "al-hayy" (the living) is one of much agitation and movement, so this pattern carries the sense of abundant movement.

When the Exalted informed of the vastness of His earth, and this was an indication of emigration, and He commanded the worship of Him, one might suppose that whoever leaves his land in which he grew up, for the sake of those who inhabit it from the people of disbelief, to the abode of Islam, will not find things going for him there as they went for him in his own land, and that may perhaps lead to his destruction. So He informed that every soul has a term that it will reach, and it will die wherever it is, and that the return of the gathered to their parts will be on the Day of Resurrection.

Ali read "turja'un" (you will be returned) in the active voice (with the verb built to the subject); the majority read it in the passive voice, with the second-person "ta'" (you). It is narrated from Asim that he read it with the third-person "ya'" (they). Abu Haywah read "dha'iqatu" with tanwin, and "al-mawti" in the accusative. He also read "la-nubawwi'annahum" (we will settle them) from al-mabā'ah (the dwelling). Ali, Abdullah, al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, Zayd ibn Ali, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it from al-thawa' (to dwell); and "bawwa'" (to settle) is transitive to two objects. Allah the Exalted said: "He settles the believers at their stations for battle" (Al 'Imran 3:121). It has also come transitive with the preposition "li-" (for). He the Exalted said: "And when We settled for Ibrahim the place of the House" (Al-Hajj 22:26). The meaning is: He will make for them a place of dwelling, that is, a place of return to which they retreat. "Ghurafan" means lofty chambers. As for "thawa," its meaning is "to stay," and it is an intransitive verb. The hamzah of transitivity (af'ala) was added to it, so it became transitive to one object. It has been read with shaddah as "'addā" with doubling, so "ghurafan" is in the accusative, either by dropping the preposition (in chambers), and then the usage was widened and it was elided; or by the verb being understood to include the meaning of settling, so it is transitive to two objects; or it is like a place-adverb specific to the vague, through which the verb reaches it. It is narrated from Ibn Amir: "ghurufan" with a dammah on the ra'. Ibn Wathhab read "fa-ni'ma" with a fa'; the majority read it without fa'. "Those who are patient" means: patient over leaving their homelands, emigration, and all hardships, from carrying out the commands and avoiding the prohibitions.

"And upon their Lord they rely" — these two are the total of all good: patience, and entrusting affairs to Allah the Exalted.

[p. 158] When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded those who had embraced Islam in Makkah to emigrate, they feared poverty and said: "This is a strangeness in lands where we have no home, no property, and no one to feed us." So He gave them an example from the most common animals that feed themselves without storing, and that do not worry about their sustenance, and do not carry their provision. "Carry" here means: do not transport, and do not look toward storing. This was said by Mujahid, Abu Mijlaz and Ali ibn al-Aqmar. Storing (al-idikhar) has come in a hadith: "How will you be when you remain among the dregs of the people, who store up the provision of a year, due to weakness of certainty?" It was said: it is also possible that it comes from the sense of "hamalah" (surety/guarantee), which does not undertake responsibility for itself and does not worry. Al-Hasan said: "(does not carry its provision)" means does not store; it only rises in the morning and Allah provides for it. Ibn Abbas said: "None store except the human, the ant, the mouse and the magpie." It was said: the nightingale hoards in its lap, and it is said the magpie has hiding places, except that it forgets them. The negation of its carrying of its provision is either due to its weakness and inability to do so, or because it was created without intellect, so it does not plan for what it might store for the future. That is: He provides for it despite its weakness. "And you" means: despite your ability to earn, and your cleverness in obtaining a livelihood, and despite that, your provider is Allah. "He is the All-Hearing" of your saying, "We fear poverty," "the All-Knowing" of what your hearts conceal.

Then the Exalted followed this with their acknowledgment that the originator of the world and the subjector of the two luminaries is Allah. He followed that with the extending and restricting of provision, and said: "Allah extends provision to whom He wills" that He extends it for, "and restricts it" for whom He wills to restrict it. The pronoun in "lahu" (for him) apparently refers back to "whom He wills," so that one individual is extended provision at one time and restricted at another time. It is also possible that the pronoun refers back to him in wording, while the intended meaning is another person whom He wills. This becomes similar to His saying: "And none is granted a long life, nor is his life shortened, except that it is in a Book" (Fatir 35:11), that is, from the life of another person who is granted a long life. And the saying of people: "I have a dirham and half of it," meaning: and half of another dirham. So the one who is given extended provision is other than the one whose provision is restricted. Alqamah al-Himsi read "wa-yuqaddiru" with a dammah on the ya', a fathah on the qaf and a shaddah on the dal. "All-Knowing" means He knows what sets right the servants and what corrupts them.

When He informed that they acknowledge that the Creator of the world, the subjector of the two luminaries, and the giver of life to the earth after its death is Allah, that acknowledgment obligated them that the provider of the servants is Allah, who is the one who guarantees it. He commanded His Messenger to praise Him the Exalted; because in their acknowledgment is the affirmation of Allah's oneness in creation, and the negation of partners from Him in that, and this was a proof against them, since they attributed that to Allah and yet worshipped idols.

﴿But most of them do not reason﴾: since they acknowledge the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life, yet worship other than Him.

﴿And this worldly life﴾: the pointing with "this" is a display of contempt for the world and a belittling of its matter. And how could it not be so? For it does not weigh the wing of a gnat with Allah. That is: in the speed of its passing away from its people, and their death from it, it is nothing but like children playing for an hour and then dispersing. "Al-hayawan" and "al-hayah" (life) have the same meaning, and according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh it is the verbal noun of "hayiya" (to live). The meaning: indeed it is the abode of life, that is, the enduring one that does not cease. Mujahid said: "There is no death in it." It was also said: "al-hayawan" means "the living," and it is as if the verbal noun was applied to the living thing. The Last Abode was described as "life" for emphasis by attributing life to it. The appearance of the waw in "al-hayawan" and in "Hayway" (a proper name of a man) is used as evidence by those who hold that the waw in such a structure is changed to ya' because of the kasrah before it, like "shaqiya" (he was miserable) from "al-shiqwah." As for those who hold that the final radical of the word is ya', they claim that the appearance of the waw in "hayawan" and "hayawa" is a substitute for a ya', as an anomaly. The response of "law" (if) is elided, that is: "if they had known, they would not have preferred the abode of perishing over it." The verbal noun of "hayiya" came in the pattern fa'alan because it indicates movement and agitation, like "ghalayan" (boiling), "nazawan" (leaping), "lahayan" (panting/desire), "jawalan" (roaming), and "tawafan" (circling). And "al-hayy" (the living) is one of much agitation and movement, so this pattern carries the sense of abundant movement.

When the Exalted mentioned that they acknowledge Allah when asked: "Who created the world?" and "Who sends down water from the sky?", He also mentioned another state in which they return to Allah, and acknowledge that He is the one who does what He wills. That occurs when they board the sea, the waves surge and the winds change. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: to what is His saying '"So when they board ships"' connected?" I answer: to an elided element indicated by what He described them with, and explained their situation in terms of what they were described with, of polytheism and obstinacy.

﴿So when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [p. 159] being in the form of those who make religion sincere to Allah from among the believers, since they mention none but Allah and call upon no other with Allah. In "sincere" there is a kind of mockery. "And at once they associate others" is the response to "lamma" (when), meaning: their association with Allah surprised their natural disposition; that is, it did not delay from it even for a moment. The apparent reading of "li-yakfuru" (so that they may deny) is that the lam is the lam of purpose ("kay"), and "wa-li-yatamatta'u" (and that they may enjoy themselves) is coordinated with it in the reading of the one who vocalized the lam with a kasrah, and they are: the two Arabs (Abu 'Amr and Ibn Amir), Nafi' and Asim. The meaning: they returned to their polytheism. "So that they may deny" means: what drives them to polytheism is their denial of what Allah the Exalted has given them, and their pleasure in what they were given of the passing goods of this world. This is unlike the believers, for when they are saved from such hardship, that becomes a cause of gratitude to Allah the Exalted and increased obedience to Him. It was also said: the lam in "li-yakfuru" and "wa-li-yatamatta'u" is the lam of command. This is supported by the reading of the one who made the lam of "wa-li-yatamatta'u" sukun (without vowel), and they are: Ibn Kathir, al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. This command is by way of threat, like His saying: "Do what you will" (Fussilat 41:40).

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "How is it permissible for God, exalted is He, to command disbelief, and to tell the disobedient to do as they wish, when He forbids that and threatens punishment for it?" I say: this is a figurative usage (majaz) for abandonment (khidhlan) and leaving them alone (takhliyah), and that command is a displeasing one, to a certain end. End of quote. Takhliyah (leaving someone to themselves) and khidhlan (divine abandonment) are terms of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist theological school).

Ibn Mas'ud recited ﴿فَتَمَتَّعُوا فَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ [al-Nahl: 55] with the ta' in both places, meaning: it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves, for you will come to know." The same reading appears in the codex of Ubayy (Ubayy ibn Ka'b's mushaf, a copy of the Qur'an). Abu al-Aliyah recited فَيَتَمَتَّعُوا with the ya' and in the passive voice. Whoever reads وَلْيَتَمَتَّعُوا with a sukun on the lam, and takes the lam in لِيَكْفُرُوا as the lam of purpose (lam kay), then the waw is coordinating one clause with another clause, not coordinating one verb with another verb.

Ibn Atiyyah reported from Ibn Mas'ud: لَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ, with the lam.

Then God reminded them of His blessings, in that He settled them in a town where they felt secure, where no one raided them or plundered them, despite their being few in number and dwelling in a place with no crops. These are among the greatest blessings they disbelieved, and it is a blessing that none can bestow except God, exalted is He.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read يُؤْمِنُونَ and يَكْفُرُونَ with the ya' in both. Al-Sulami and al-Hasan read them with the ta' of address in both.

Their "fabrication of lies" (iftira'uhum al-kadhib) is their claim that God has a partner, and their "denial of the truth" (takdhibuhum bil-haqq) is their disbelief in the Messenger and the Qur'an.

In His words ﴿لَمَّا جَاءَهُ﴾ ("when it came to them"), there is an indication that they did not hesitate in denying it at the time the truth reached them, unlike the rational person, who, when news reaches him, examines it and reflects upon it until it becomes clear to him whether it is true or false.

ألَيْسَ (Is it not?) is an affirmation of their abode in Hell, as in the line: "Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts?"

لِلْكَافِرِينَ (for the disbelievers) is the placing of an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun, meaning: their abode.

﴿وَالَّذِينَ جَاهَدُوا فِينَا﴾: He used the word "striving" (mujahadah) without limiting it by an object, so that it would include striving against the commanding self, against Satan, and against the enemies of the religion. What was reported from the scholars' sayings are examples.

Ibn Abbas said: they strove against their desires in obedience to God, in thanking His blessings, and in patience with His trials.

﴿لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا﴾: We will increase them in guidance to the path of good, as in His words: ﴿وَالَّذِينَ اهْتَدَوْا زَادَهُمْ هُدًى وَآتَاهُمْ تَقْوَاهُمْ﴾ [Muhammad: 17].

Al-Suddi said: they strove for Us by remaining steadfast in faith; We will guide them on Our paths to Paradise.

Abu Sulayman al-Darani said: they strove in what they knew, and We will guide them to what they did not know.

It was also said: they strove in battle, and We will guide them to the paths of martyrdom and forgiveness.

Ibn Abbas said: "the good-doers" (al-muhsinin) means the monotheists (al-muwahhidin).

Others said: "the good-doers" means the strivers (al-mujahidun).

Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said: whoever finds a question difficult, let him ask the people of the frontiers (ahl al-thughur) about it, as in God's words: ﴿لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا﴾.

(وَالَّذِينَ) is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the omitted oath (qasam), and whose answer is: "We will surely guide them." By this and its like, the view of Abu al-Abbas Thaʿlab was refuted; he prohibited the clause of the oath and the thing sworn to from being the predicate of the subject. Its parallel is: ﴿وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ لَنُبَوِّئَنَّهُمْ﴾ ("And those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely settle them...").

How excellent is the reward of the workers!﴾ ﴿Those who are patient and upon their Lord rely.﴾ ﴿And how many a creature does not carry its provision; Allah provides for it, and for you. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon?" they would surely say, "Allah." Then how are they deluded?﴾ ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing of everything.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who sends down water from the sky and thereby gives life to the earth after its death?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Praise be to Allah." But most of them do not reason.﴾ ﴿And this worldly life is nothing but amusement and play. Indeed, the Last Abode is the true life, if only they knew.﴾ ﴿So when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them safely to land, at once they associate others with Him.﴾ ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them and enjoy themselves; but they will soon know.﴾ ﴿Do they not see that We made a sanctuary secure, while people are being snatched away from around them? Then do they believe in falsehood and deny the favor of Allah?﴾ ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies the truth when it comes to him? Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾ ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths. And indeed, Allah is with the good-doers.﴾

It was also said: "The earth of Paradise is vast; I shall give it to you." Mujahid said: "Travel to fight His enemies."
