Then God reminded them of His blessings, in that He settled them in a town where they felt secure, where no one raided them or plundered them, despite their being few in number and dwelling in a place with no crops. These are among the greatest blessings they disbelieved, and it is a blessing that none can bestow except God, exalted is He.

Al-Suddi said: they strove for Us by remaining steadfast in faith; We will guide them on Our paths to Paradise.

Abu Sulayman al-Darani said: they strove in what they knew, and We will guide them to what they did not know.

It was also said: they strove in battle, and We will guide them to the paths of martyrdom and forgiveness.

Others said: "the good-doers" means the strivers (al-mujahidun).

(وَالَّذِينَ) is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the omitted oath (qasam), and whose answer is: "We will surely guide them." **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 29, verses 56–69 (part 1 of 2):**

[p. 157] ﴿O My servants who believe, indeed My earth is vast, so worship Me alone.﴾ ﴿Every soul will taste death; then to Us you will be returned.﴾ ﴿As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely settle them in lofty chambers in Paradise, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. How excellent is the reward of the workers!﴾ ﴿Those who are patient and upon their Lord rely.﴾ ﴿And how many a creature does not carry its provision; Allah provides for it, and for you. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon?" they would surely say, "Allah." Then how are they deluded?﴾ ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing of everything.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who sends down water from the sky and thereby gives life to the earth after its death?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Praise be to Allah." But most of them do not reason.﴾ ﴿And this worldly life is nothing but amusement and play. Indeed, the Last Abode is the true life, if only they knew.﴾ ﴿So when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them safely to land, at once they associate others with Him.﴾ ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them and enjoy themselves; but they will soon know.﴾ ﴿Do they not see that We made a sanctuary secure, while people are being snatched away from around them? Then do they believe in falsehood and deny the favor of Allah?﴾ ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies the truth when it comes to him? Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾ ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths. And indeed, Allah is with the good-doers.﴾

Most of the exegetes (mufassirun, the scholars of tafsir, or Qur'anic exegesis) held that His saying: "O My servants..." up to the end of the verse, was revealed concerning those who were residing in Makkah. They were commanded to emigrate from it to Madinah. That is: distance yourselves from the people of polytheism, and seek out the people of faith. Abu al-Aliyah said: "Travel in search of His allies." Ibn Jubayr, Ata', Mujahid and Malik ibn Anas said: "The land in which injustice and evil are committed, this verse applies to it, and emigration from it to a land of truth becomes obligatory." Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: "Indeed My earth is vast" is a promise of the abundance of provision throughout the whole earth. It was also said: "The earth of Paradise is vast; I shall give it to you." Mujahid said: "Travel to fight His enemies."

As for "so worship Me alone" (fa-iyyaya fa-'budun), it is from the construction of ishtighal (the construction in which the verb is preoccupied with a pronoun referring to the object, so the object is fronted). That is: "So worship Me alone, so worship Me." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the meaning of the fa' in 'fa-'budun', and the fronting of the object?" I (al-Zamakhshari) answer: the fa' is the response to an elided conditional clause, because the meaning is: "If My earth is vast, then if you do not make worship sincere in one land, make it sincere in another." Then the condition was elided, and the fronting of the object was given in its place, along with the fronting conveying the meaning of exclusivity and sincerity. End of quote. This answer requires reflection.

When the Exalted informed of the vastness of His earth, and this was an indication of emigration, and He commanded the worship of Him, one might suppose that whoever leaves his land in which he grew up, for the sake of those who inhabit it from the people of disbelief, to the abode of Islam, will not find things going for him there as they went for him in his own land, and that may perhaps lead to his destruction. So He informed that every soul has a term that it will reach, and it will die wherever it is, and that the return of the gathered to their parts will be on the Day of Resurrection.

Ali read "turja'un" (you will be returned) in the active voice (with the verb built to the subject); the majority read it in the passive voice, with the second-person "ta'" (you). It is narrated from Asim that he read it with the third-person "ya'" (they). Abu Haywah read "dha'iqatu" with tanwin, and "al-mawti" in the accusative. He also read "la-nubawwi'annahum" (we will settle them) from al-mabā'ah (the dwelling). Ali, Abdullah, al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, Zayd ibn Ali, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it from al-thawa' (to dwell); and "bawwa'" (to settle) is transitive to two objects. Allah the Exalted said: "He settles the believers at their stations for battle" (Al 'Imran 3:121). It has also come transitive with the preposition "li-" (for). He the Exalted said: "And when We settled for Ibrahim the place of the House" (Al-Hajj 22:26). The meaning is: He will make for them a place of dwelling, that is, a place of return to which they retreat. "Ghurafan" means lofty chambers. As for "thawa," its meaning is "to stay," and it is an intransitive verb. The hamzah of transitivity (af'ala) was added to it, so it became transitive to one object. It has been read with shaddah as "'addā" with doubling, so "ghurafan" is in the accusative, either by dropping the preposition (in chambers), and then the usage was widened and it was elided; or by the verb being understood to include the meaning of settling, so it is transitive to two objects; or it is like a place-adverb specific to the vague, through which the verb reaches it. It is narrated from Ibn Amir: "ghurufan" with a dammah on the ra'. Ibn Wathhab read "fa-ni'ma" with a fa'; the majority read it without fa'. "Those who are patient" means: patient over leaving their homelands, emigration, and all hardships, from carrying out the commands and avoiding the prohibitions.

"And upon their Lord they rely" — these two are the total of all good: patience, and entrusting affairs to Allah the Exalted.

[p. 158] When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded those who had embraced Islam in Makkah to emigrate, they feared poverty and said: "This is a strangeness in lands where we have no home, no property, and no one to feed us." So He gave them an example from the most common animals that feed themselves without storing, and that do not worry about their sustenance, and do not carry their provision. "Carry" here means: do not transport, and do not look toward storing. This was said by Mujahid, Abu Mijlaz and Ali ibn al-Aqmar. Storing (al-idikhar) has come in a hadith: "How will you be when you remain among the dregs of the people, who store up the provision of a year, due to weakness of certainty?" It was said: it is also possible that it comes from the sense of "hamalah" (surety/guarantee), which does not undertake responsibility for itself and does not worry. Al-Hasan said: "(does not carry its provision)" means does not store; it only rises in the morning and Allah provides for it. Ibn Abbas said: "None store except the human, the ant, the mouse and the magpie." It was said: the nightingale hoards in its lap, and it is said the magpie has hiding places, except that it forgets them. The negation of its carrying of its provision is either due to its weakness and inability to do so, or because it was created without intellect, so it does not plan for what it might store for the future. That is: He provides for it despite its weakness. "And you" means: despite your ability to earn, and your cleverness in obtaining a livelihood, and despite that, your provider is Allah. "He is the All-Hearing" of your saying, "We fear poverty," "the All-Knowing" of what your hearts conceal.

Then the Exalted followed this with their acknowledgment that the originator of the world and the subjector of the two luminaries is Allah. He followed that with the extending and restricting of provision, and said: "Allah extends provision to whom He wills" that He extends it for, "and restricts it" for whom He wills to restrict it. The pronoun in "lahu" (for him) apparently refers back to "whom He wills," so that one individual is extended provision at one time and restricted at another time. It is also possible that the pronoun refers back to him in wording, while the intended meaning is another person whom He wills. This becomes similar to His saying: "And none is granted a long life, nor is his life shortened, except that it is in a Book" (Fatir 35:11), that is, from the life of another person who is granted a long life. And the saying of people: "I have a dirham and half of it," meaning: and half of another dirham. So the one who is given extended provision is other than the one whose provision is restricted. Alqamah al-Himsi read "wa-yuqaddiru" with a dammah on the ya', a fathah on the qaf and a shaddah on the dal. "All-Knowing" means He knows what sets right the servants and what corrupts them.

When He informed that they acknowledge that the Creator of the world, the subjector of the two luminaries, and the giver of life to the earth after its death is Allah, that acknowledgment obligated them that the provider of the servants is Allah, who is the one who guarantees it. He commanded His Messenger to praise Him the Exalted; because in their acknowledgment is the affirmation of Allah's oneness in creation, and the negation of partners from Him in that, and this was a proof against them, since they attributed that to Allah and yet worshipped idols.

﴿But most of them do not reason﴾: since they acknowledge the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life, yet worship other than Him.

﴿And this worldly life﴾: the pointing with "this" is a display of contempt for the world and a belittling of its matter. And how could it not be so? For it does not weigh the wing of a gnat with Allah. That is: in the speed of its passing away from its people, and their death from it, it is nothing but like children playing for an hour and then dispersing. "Al-hayawan" and "al-hayah" (life) have the same meaning, and according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh it is the verbal noun of "hayiya" (to live). The meaning: indeed it is the abode of life, that is, the enduring one that does not cease. Mujahid said: "There is no death in it." It was also said: "al-hayawan" means "the living," and it is as if the verbal noun was applied to the living thing. The Last Abode was described as "life" for emphasis by attributing life to it. The appearance of the waw in "al-hayawan" and in "Hayway" (a proper name of a man) is used as evidence by those who hold that the waw in such a structure is changed to ya' because of the kasrah before it, like "shaqiya" (he was miserable) from "al-shiqwah." As for those who hold that the final radical of the word is ya', they claim that the appearance of the waw in "hayawan" and "hayawa" is a substitute for a ya', as an anomaly. The response of "law" (if) is elided, that is: "if they had known, they would not have preferred the abode of perishing over it." The verbal noun of "hayiya" came in the pattern fa'alan because it indicates movement and agitation, like "ghalayan" (boiling), "nazawan" (leaping), "lahayan" (panting/desire), "jawalan" (roaming), and "tawafan" (circling). And "al-hayy" (the living) is one of much agitation and movement, so this pattern carries the sense of abundant movement.

When the Exalted mentioned that they acknowledge Allah when asked: "Who created the world?" and "Who sends down water from the sky?", He also mentioned another state in which they return to Allah, and acknowledge that He is the one who does what He wills. That occurs when they board the sea, the waves surge and the winds change. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: to what is His saying '"So when they board ships"' connected?" I answer: to an elided element indicated by what He described them with, and explained their situation in terms of what they were described with, of polytheism and obstinacy.

﴿So when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [p. 159] being in the form of those who make religion sincere to Allah from among the believers, since they mention none but Allah and call upon no other with Allah. In "sincere" there is a kind of mockery. "And at once they associate others" is the response to "lamma" (when), meaning: their association with Allah surprised their natural disposition; that is, it did not delay from it even for a moment. The apparent reading of "li-yakfuru" (so that they may deny) is that the lam is the lam of purpose ("kay"), and "wa-li-yatamatta'u" (and that they may enjoy themselves) is coordinated with it in the reading of the one who vocalized the lam with a kasrah, and they are: the two Arabs (Abu 'Amr and Ibn Amir), Nafi' and Asim. The meaning: they returned to their polytheism. "So that they may deny" means: what drives them to polytheism is their denial of what Allah the Exalted has given them, and their pleasure in what they were given of the passing goods of this world. This is unlike the believers, for when they are saved from such hardship, that becomes a cause of gratitude to Allah the Exalted and increased obedience to Him. It was also said: the lam in "li-yakfuru" and "wa-li-yatamatta'u" is the lam of command. This is supported by the reading of the one who made the lam of "wa-li-yatamatta'u" sukun (without vowel), and they are: Ibn Kathir, al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. This command is by way of threat, like His saying: "Do what you will" (Fussilat 41:40).

He the Exalted said: "And when We settled for Ibrahim the place of the House" (Al-Hajj 22:26). The meaning is: He will make for them a place of dwelling, that is, a place of return to which they retreat. "Ghurafan" means lofty chambers. As for "thawa," its meaning is "to stay," and it is an intransitive verb. The hamzah of transitivity (af'ala) was added to it, so it became transitive to one object. It has been read with shaddah as "'addā" with doubling, so "ghurafan" is in the accusative, either by dropping the preposition (in chambers), and then the usage was widened and it was elided; or by the verb being understood to include the meaning of settling, so it is transitive to two objects; or it is like a place-adverb specific to the vague, through which the verb reaches it. It is narrated from Ibn Amir: "ghurufan" with a dammah on the ra'. Ibn Wathhab read "fa-ni'ma" with a fa'; the majority read it without fa'. "Those who are patient" means: patient over leaving their homelands, emigration, and all hardships, from carrying out the commands and avoiding the prohibitions.

"And upon their Lord they rely" — these two are the total of all good: patience, and entrusting affairs to Allah the Exalted.

[p. 158] When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded those who had embraced Islam in Makkah to emigrate, they feared poverty and said: "This is a strangeness in lands where we have no home, no property, and no one to feed us." So He gave them an example from the most common animals that feed themselves without storing, and that do not worry about their sustenance, and do not carry their provision. "Carry" here means: do not transport, and do not look toward storing. This was said by Mujahid, Abu Mijlaz and Ali ibn al-Aqmar. Storing (al-idikhar) has come in a hadith: "How will you be when you remain among the dregs of the people, who store up the provision of a year, due to weakness of certainty?" It was said: it is also possible that it comes from the sense of "hamalah" (surety/guarantee), which does not undertake responsibility for itself and does not worry. Al-Hasan said: "(does not carry its provision)" means does not store; it only rises in the morning and Allah provides for it. Ibn Abbas said: "None store except the human, the ant, the mouse and the magpie." It was said: the nightingale hoards in its lap, and it is said the magpie has hiding places, except that it forgets them. The negation of its carrying of its provision is either due to its weakness and inability to do so, or because it was created without intellect, so it does not plan for what it might store for the future. That is: He provides for it despite its weakness. "And you" means: despite your ability to earn, and your cleverness in obtaining a livelihood, and despite that, your provider is Allah. "He is the All-Hearing" of your saying, "We fear poverty," "the All-Knowing" of what your hearts conceal.

Then the Exalted followed this with their acknowledgment that the originator of the world and the subjector of the two luminaries is Allah. He followed that with the extending and restricting of provision, and said: "Allah extends provision to whom He wills" that He extends it for, "and restricts it" for whom He wills to restrict it. The pronoun in "lahu" (for him) apparently refers back to "whom He wills," so that one individual is extended provision at one time and restricted at another time. It is also possible that the pronoun refers back to him in wording, while the intended meaning is another person whom He wills. This becomes similar to His saying: "And none is granted a long life, nor is his life shortened, except that it is in a Book" (Fatir 35:11), that is, from the life of another person who is granted a long life. And the saying of people: "I have a dirham and half of it," meaning: and half of another dirham. So the one who is given extended provision is other than the one whose provision is restricted. Alqamah al-Himsi read "wa-yuqaddiru" with a dammah on the ya', a fathah on the qaf and a shaddah on the dal. "All-Knowing" means He knows what sets right the servants and what corrupts them.

When He informed that they acknowledge that the Creator of the world, the subjector of the two luminaries, and the giver of life to the earth after its death is Allah, that acknowledgment obligated them that the provider of the servants is Allah, who is the one who guarantees it. He commanded His Messenger to praise Him the Exalted; because in their acknowledgment is the affirmation of Allah's oneness in creation, and the negation of partners from Him in that, and this was a proof against them, since they attributed that to Allah and yet worshipped idols.

﴿But most of them do not reason﴾: since they acknowledge the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life, yet worship other than Him.

﴿And this worldly life﴾: the pointing with "this" is a display of contempt for the world and a belittling of its matter. And how could it not be so? For it does not weigh the wing of a gnat with Allah. That is: in the speed of its passing away from its people, and their death from it, it is nothing but like children playing for an hour and then dispersing. "Al-hayawan" and "al-hayah" (life) have the same meaning, and according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh it is the verbal noun of "hayiya" (to live). The meaning: indeed it is the abode of life, that is, the enduring one that does not cease. Mujahid said: "There is no death in it." It was also said: "al-hayawan" means "the living," and it is as if the verbal noun was applied to the living thing. The Last Abode was described as "life" for emphasis by attributing life to it. The appearance of the waw in "al-hayawan" and in "Hayway" (a proper name of a man) is used as evidence by those who hold that the waw in such a structure is changed to ya' because of the kasrah before it, like "shaqiya" (he was miserable) from "al-shiqwah." As for those who hold that the final radical of the word is ya', they claim that the appearance of the waw in "hayawan" and "hayawa" is a substitute for a ya', as an anomaly. The response of "law" (if) is elided, that is: "if they had known, they would not have preferred the abode of perishing over it." The verbal noun of "hayiya" came in the pattern fa'alan because it indicates movement and agitation, like "ghalayan" (boiling), "nazawan" (leaping), "lahayan" (panting/desire), "jawalan" (roaming), and "tawafan" (circling). And "al-hayy" (the living) is one of much agitation and movement, so this pattern carries the sense of abundant movement.

When the Exalted mentioned that they acknowledge Allah when asked: "Who created the world?" and "Who sends down water from the sky?", He also mentioned another state in which they return to Allah, and acknowledge that He is the one who does what He wills. That occurs when they board the sea, the waves surge and the winds change. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: to what is His saying '"So when they board ships"' connected?" I answer: to an elided element indicated by what He described them with, and explained their situation in terms of what they were described with, of polytheism and obstinacy.

﴿So when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [p. 159] being in the form of those who make religion sincere to Allah from among the believers, since they mention none but Allah and call upon no other with Allah. In "sincere" there is a kind of mockery. "And at once they associate others" is the response to "lamma" (when), meaning: their association with Allah surprised their natural disposition; that is, it did not delay from it even for a moment. The apparent reading of "li-yakfuru" (so that they may deny) is that the lam is the lam of purpose ("kay"), and "wa-li-yatamatta'u" (and that they may enjoy themselves) is coordinated with it in the reading of the one who vocalized the lam with a kasrah, and they are: the two Arabs (Abu 'Amr and Ibn Amir), Nafi' and Asim. The meaning: they returned to their polytheism. "So that they may deny" means: what drives them to polytheism is their denial of what Allah the Exalted has given them, and their pleasure in what they were given of the passing goods of this world. This is unlike the believers, for when they are saved from such hardship, that becomes a cause of gratitude to Allah the Exalted and increased obedience to Him. It was also said: the lam in "li-yakfuru" and "wa-li-yatamatta'u" is the lam of command. This is supported by the reading of the one who made the lam of "wa-li-yatamatta'u" sukun (without vowel), and they are: Ibn Kathir, al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. This command is by way of threat, like His saying: "Do what you will" (Fussilat 41:40).

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "How is it permissible for God, exalted is He, to command disbelief, and to tell the disobedient to do as they wish, when He forbids that and threatens punishment for it?" Whoever reads وَلْيَتَمَتَّعُوا with a sukun on the lam, and takes the lam in لِيَكْفُرُوا as the lam of purpose (lam kay), then the waw is coordinating one clause with another clause, not coordinating one verb with another verb.

Ibn Atiyyah reported from Ibn Mas'ud: لَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ, with the lam.

Then God reminded them of His blessings, in that He settled them in a town where they felt secure, where no one raided them or plundered them, despite their being few in number and dwelling in a place with no crops. These are among the greatest blessings they disbelieved, and it is a blessing that none can bestow except God, exalted is He.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read يُؤْمِنُونَ and يَكْفُرُونَ with the ya' in both. Al-Sulami and al-Hasan read them with the ta' of address in both.

Their "fabrication of lies" (iftira'uhum al-kadhib) is their claim that God has a partner, and their "denial of the truth" (takdhibuhum bil-haqq) is their disbelief in the Messenger and the Qur'an.

In His words ﴿لَمَّا جَاءَهُ﴾ ("when it came to them"), there is an indication that they did not hesitate in denying it at the time the truth reached them, unlike the rational person, who, when news reaches him, examines it and reflects upon it until it becomes clear to him whether it is true or false.

ألَيْسَ (Is it not?) is an affirmation of their abode in Hell, as in the line: "Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts?"

لِلْكَافِرِينَ (for the disbelievers) is the placing of an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun, meaning: their abode.

﴿وَالَّذِينَ جَاهَدُوا فِينَا﴾: He used the word "striving" (mujahadah) without limiting it by an object, so that it would include striving against the commanding self, against Satan, and against the enemies of the religion. What was reported from the scholars' sayings are examples.

Ibn Abbas said: they strove against their desires in obedience to God, in thanking His blessings, and in patience with His trials.

﴿لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا﴾: We will increase them in guidance to the path of good, as in His words: ﴿وَالَّذِينَ اهْتَدَوْا زَادَهُمْ هُدًى وَآتَاهُمْ تَقْوَاهُمْ﴾ [Muhammad: 17].

Al-Suddi said: they strove for Us by remaining steadfast in faith; We will guide them on Our paths to Paradise.

Abu Sulayman al-Darani said: they strove in what they knew, and We will guide them to what they did not know.

It was also said: they strove in battle, and We will guide them to the paths of martyrdom and forgiveness.

Ibn Abbas said: "the good-doers" (al-muhsinin) means the monotheists (al-muwahhidin).

Others said: "the good-doers" means the strivers (al-mujahidun).

Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said: whoever finds a question difficult, let him ask the people of the frontiers (ahl al-thughur) about it, as in God's words: ﴿لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا﴾.

(وَالَّذِينَ) is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the omitted oath (qasam), and whose answer is: "We will surely guide them." By this and its like, the view of Abu al-Abbas Thaʿlab was refuted; he prohibited the clause of the oath and the thing sworn to from being the predicate of the subject. Its parallel is: ﴿وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ لَنُبَوِّئَنَّهُمْ﴾ ("And those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely settle them...").

How excellent is the reward of the workers!﴾ ﴿Those who are patient and upon their Lord rely.﴾ ﴿And how many a creature does not carry its provision; Allah provides for it, and for you. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon?" they would surely say, "Allah." Then how are they deluded?﴾ ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing of everything.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who sends down water from the sky and thereby gives life to the earth after its death?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Praise be to Allah." But most of them do not reason.﴾ ﴿And this worldly life is nothing but amusement and play. Indeed, the Last Abode is the true life, if only they knew.﴾ ﴿So when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them safely to land, at once they associate others with Him.﴾ ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them and enjoy themselves; but they will soon know.﴾ ﴿Do they not see that We made a sanctuary secure, while people are being snatched away from around them? Then do they believe in falsehood and deny the favor of Allah?﴾ ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies the truth when it comes to him? Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾ ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths. And indeed, Allah is with the good-doers.﴾

Ibn Jubayr, Ata', Mujahid and Malik ibn Anas said: "The land in which injustice and evil are committed, this verse applies to it, and emigration from it to a land of truth becomes obligatory." Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: "Indeed My earth is vast" is a promise of the abundance of provision throughout the whole earth. It was also said: "The earth of Paradise is vast; I shall give it to you." Mujahid said: "Travel to fight His enemies."

As for "so worship Me alone" (fa-iyyaya fa-'budun), it is from the construction of ishtighal (the construction in which the verb is preoccupied with a pronoun referring to the object, so the object is fronted). Then God reminded them of His blessings, in that He settled them in a town where they felt secure, where no one raided them or plundered them, despite their being few in number and dwelling in a place with no crops. These are among the greatest blessings they disbelieved, and it is a blessing that none can bestow except God, exalted is He.

ألَيْسَ (Is it not?) is an affirmation of their abode in Hell, as in the line: "Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts?"

Ibn Abbas said: they strove against their desires in obedience to God, in thanking His blessings, and in patience with His trials.

﴿لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا﴾: We will increase them in guidance to the path of good, as in His words: ﴿وَالَّذِينَ اهْتَدَوْا زَادَهُمْ هُدًى وَآتَاهُمْ تَقْوَاهُمْ﴾ [Muhammad: 17].

Al-Suddi said: they strove for Us by remaining steadfast in faith; We will guide them on Our paths to Paradise.

Abu Sulayman al-Darani said: they strove in what they knew, and We will guide them to what they did not know.

It was also said: they strove in battle, and We will guide them to the paths of martyrdom and forgiveness.

Ibn Abbas said: "the good-doers" (al-muhsinin) means the monotheists (al-muwahhidin).

Others said: "the good-doers" means the strivers (al-mujahidun).

Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said: whoever finds a question difficult, let him ask the people of the frontiers (ahl al-thughur) about it, as in God's words: ﴿لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا﴾.

(وَالَّذِينَ) is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the omitted oath (qasam), and whose answer is: "We will surely guide them." By this and its like, the view of Abu al-Abbas Thaʿlab was refuted; he prohibited the clause of the oath and the thing sworn to from being the predicate of the subject. Its parallel is: ﴿وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ لَنُبَوِّئَنَّهُمْ﴾ ("And those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely settle them...").

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 29, verses 56–69 (part 1 of 2):**

[p. 157] ﴿O My servants who believe, indeed My earth is vast, so worship Me alone.﴾ ﴿Every soul will taste death; then to Us you will be returned.﴾ ﴿As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely settle them in lofty chambers in Paradise, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. How excellent is the reward of the workers!﴾ ﴿Those who are patient and upon their Lord rely.﴾ ﴿And how many a creature does not carry its provision; Allah provides for it, and for you. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon?" they would surely say, "Allah." Then how are they deluded?﴾ ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing of everything.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who sends down water from the sky and thereby gives life to the earth after its death?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Praise be to Allah." But most of them do not reason.﴾ ﴿And this worldly life is nothing but amusement and play. Indeed, the Last Abode is the true life, if only they knew.﴾ ﴿So when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them safely to land, at once they associate others with Him.﴾ ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them and enjoy themselves; but they will soon know.﴾ ﴿Do they not see that We made a sanctuary secure, while people are being snatched away from around them? Then do they believe in falsehood and deny the favor of Allah?﴾ ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies the truth when it comes to him? Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾ ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths. And indeed, Allah is with the good-doers.﴾

Most of the exegetes (mufassirun, the scholars of tafsir, or Qur'anic exegesis) held that His saying: "O My servants..." up to the end of the verse, was revealed concerning those who were residing in Makkah. They were commanded to emigrate from it to Madinah. That is: distance yourselves from the people of polytheism, and seek out the people of faith. Abu al-Aliyah said: "Travel in search of His allies." Ibn Jubayr, Ata', Mujahid and Malik ibn Anas said: "The land in which injustice and evil are committed, this verse applies to it, and emigration from it to a land of truth becomes obligatory." Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: "Indeed My earth is vast" is a promise of the abundance of provision throughout the whole earth. It was also said: "The earth of Paradise is vast; I shall give it to you." Mujahid said: "Travel to fight His enemies."

As for "so worship Me alone" (fa-iyyaya fa-'budun), it is from the construction of ishtighal (the construction in which the verb is preoccupied with a pronoun referring to the object, so the object is fronted). That is: "So worship Me alone, so worship Me." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the meaning of the fa' in 'fa-'budun', and the fronting of the object?" I (al-Zamakhshari) answer: the fa' is the response to an elided conditional clause, because the meaning is: "If My earth is vast, then if you do not make worship sincere in one land, make it sincere in another." Then the condition was elided, and the fronting of the object was given in its place, along with the fronting conveying the meaning of exclusivity and sincerity. End of quote. This answer requires reflection.

When the Exalted informed of the vastness of His earth, and this was an indication of emigration, and He commanded the worship of Him, one might suppose that whoever leaves his land in which he grew up, for the sake of those who inhabit it from the people of disbelief, to the abode of Islam, will not find things going for him there as they went for him in his own land, and that may perhaps lead to his destruction. So He informed that every soul has a term that it will reach, and it will die wherever it is, and that the return of the gathered to their parts will be on the Day of Resurrection.

Ali read "turja'un" (you will be returned) in the active voice (with the verb built to the subject); the majority read it in the passive voice, with the second-person "ta'" (you). It is narrated from Asim that he read it with the third-person "ya'" (they). Abu Haywah read "dha'iqatu" with tanwin, and "al-mawti" in the accusative. He also read "la-nubawwi'annahum" (we will settle them) from al-mabā'ah (the dwelling). Ali, Abdullah, al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, Zayd ibn Ali, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it from al-thawa' (to dwell); and "bawwa'" (to settle) is transitive to two objects. Allah the Exalted said: "He settles the believers at their stations for battle" (Al 'Imran 3:121). It has also come transitive with the preposition "li-" (for). He the Exalted said: "And when We settled for Ibrahim the place of the House" (Al-Hajj 22:26). The meaning is: He will make for them a place of dwelling, that is, a place of return to which they retreat. "Ghurafan" means lofty chambers. As for "thawa," its meaning is "to stay," and it is an intransitive verb. The hamzah of transitivity (af'ala) was added to it, so it became transitive to one object. It has been read with shaddah as "'addā" with doubling, so "ghurafan" is in the accusative, either by dropping the preposition (in chambers), and then the usage was widened and it was elided; or by the verb being understood to include the meaning of settling, so it is transitive to two objects; or it is like a place-adverb specific to the vague, through which the verb reaches it. It is narrated from Ibn Amir: "ghurufan" with a dammah on the ra'. Ibn Wathhab read "fa-ni'ma" with a fa'; the majority read it without fa'. "Those who are patient" means: patient over leaving their homelands, emigration, and all hardships, from carrying out the commands and avoiding the prohibitions.

"And upon their Lord they rely" — these two are the total of all good: patience, and entrusting affairs to Allah the Exalted.

[p. 158] When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded those who had embraced Islam in Makkah to emigrate, they feared poverty and said: "This is a strangeness in lands where we have no home, no property, and no one to feed us." So He gave them an example from the most common animals that feed themselves without storing, and that do not worry about their sustenance, and do not carry their provision. "Carry" here means: do not transport, and do not look toward storing. This was said by Mujahid, Abu Mijlaz and Ali ibn al-Aqmar. Storing (al-idikhar) has come in a hadith: "How will you be when you remain among the dregs of the people, who store up the provision of a year, due to weakness of certainty?" It was said: it is also possible that it comes from the sense of "hamalah" (surety/guarantee), which does not undertake responsibility for itself and does not worry. Al-Hasan said: "(does not carry its provision)" means does not store; it only rises in the morning and Allah provides for it. Ibn Abbas said: "None store except the human, the ant, the mouse and the magpie." It was said: the nightingale hoards in its lap, and it is said the magpie has hiding places, except that it forgets them. The negation of its carrying of its provision is either due to its weakness and inability to do so, or because it was created without intellect, so it does not plan for what it might store for the future. That is: He provides for it despite its weakness. "And you" means: despite your ability to earn, and your cleverness in obtaining a livelihood, and despite that, your provider is Allah. "He is the All-Hearing" of your saying, "We fear poverty," "the All-Knowing" of what your hearts conceal.

Then the Exalted followed this with their acknowledgment that the originator of the world and the subjector of the two luminaries is Allah. He followed that with the extending and restricting of provision, and said: "Allah extends provision to whom He wills" that He extends it for, "and restricts it" for whom He wills to restrict it. The pronoun in "lahu" (for him) apparently refers back to "whom He wills," so that one individual is extended provision at one time and restricted at another time. It is also possible that the pronoun refers back to him in wording, while the intended meaning is another person whom He wills. This becomes similar to His saying: "And none is granted a long life, nor is his life shortened, except that it is in a Book" (Fatir 35:11), that is, from the life of another person who is granted a long life. And the saying of people: "I have a dirham and half of it," meaning: and half of another dirham. So the one who is given extended provision is other than the one whose provision is restricted. Alqamah al-Himsi read "wa-yuqaddiru" with a dammah on the ya', a fathah on the qaf and a shaddah on the dal. "All-Knowing" means He knows what sets right the servants and what corrupts them.

When He informed that they acknowledge that the Creator of the world, the subjector of the two luminaries, and the giver of life to the earth after its death is Allah, that acknowledgment obligated them that the provider of the servants is Allah, who is the one who guarantees it. He commanded His Messenger to praise Him the Exalted; because in their acknowledgment is the affirmation of Allah's oneness in creation, and the negation of partners from Him in that, and this was a proof against them, since they attributed that to Allah and yet worshipped idols.

﴿But most of them do not reason﴾: since they acknowledge the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life, yet worship other than Him.

﴿And this worldly life﴾: the pointing with "this" is a display of contempt for the world and a belittling of its matter. And how could it not be so? For it does not weigh the wing of a gnat with Allah. That is: in the speed of its passing away from its people, and their death from it, it is nothing but like children playing for an hour and then dispersing. "Al-hayawan" and "al-hayah" (life) have the same meaning, and according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh it is the verbal noun of "hayiya" (to live). The meaning: indeed it is the abode of life, that is, the enduring one that does not cease. Mujahid said: "There is no death in it." It was also said: "al-hayawan" means "the living," and it is as if the verbal noun was applied to the living thing. The Last Abode was described as "life" for emphasis by attributing life to it. The appearance of the waw in "al-hayawan" and in "Hayway" (a proper name of a man) is used as evidence by those who hold that the waw in such a structure is changed to ya' because of the kasrah before it, like "shaqiya" (he was miserable) from "al-shiqwah." As for those who hold that the final radical of the word is ya', they claim that the appearance of the waw in "hayawan" and "hayawa" is a substitute for a ya', as an anomaly. The response of "law" (if) is elided, that is: "if they had known, they would not have preferred the abode of perishing over it." The verbal noun of "hayiya" came in the pattern fa'alan because it indicates movement and agitation, like "ghalayan" (boiling), "nazawan" (leaping), "lahayan" (panting/desire), "jawalan" (roaming), and "tawafan" (circling). And "al-hayy" (the living) is one of much agitation and movement, so this pattern carries the sense of abundant movement.

When the Exalted mentioned that they acknowledge Allah when asked: "Who created the world?" and "Who sends down water from the sky?", He also mentioned another state in which they return to Allah, and acknowledge that He is the one who does what He wills. That occurs when they board the sea, the waves surge and the winds change. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: to what is His saying '"So when they board ships"' connected?" I answer: to an elided element indicated by what He described them with, and explained their situation in terms of what they were described with, of polytheism and obstinacy.

﴿So when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [p. 159] being in the form of those who make religion sincere to Allah from among the believers, since they mention none but Allah and call upon no other with Allah. In "sincere" there is a kind of mockery. "And at once they associate others" is the response to "lamma" (when), meaning: their association with Allah surprised their natural disposition; that is, it did not delay from it even for a moment. The apparent reading of "li-yakfuru" (so that they may deny) is that the lam is the lam of purpose ("kay"), and "wa-li-yatamatta'u" (and that they may enjoy themselves) is coordinated with it in the reading of the one who vocalized the lam with a kasrah, and they are: the two Arabs (Abu 'Amr and Ibn Amir), Nafi' and Asim. The meaning: they returned to their polytheism. "So that they may deny" means: what drives them to polytheism is their denial of what Allah the Exalted has given them, and their pleasure in what they were given of the passing goods of this world. This is unlike the believers, for when they are saved from such hardship, that becomes a cause of gratitude to Allah the Exalted and increased obedience to Him. It was also said: the lam in "li-yakfuru" and "wa-li-yatamatta'u" is the lam of command. This is supported by the reading of the one who made the lam of "wa-li-yatamatta'u" sukun (without vowel), and they are: Ibn Kathir, al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. This command is by way of threat, like His saying: "Do what you will" (Fussilat 41:40).

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "How is it permissible for God, exalted is He, to command disbelief, and to tell the disobedient to do as they wish, when He forbids that and threatens punishment for it?" I say: this is a figurative usage (majaz) for abandonment (khidhlan) and leaving them alone (takhliyah), and that command is a displeasing one, to a certain end. End of quote. Takhliyah (leaving someone to themselves) and khidhlan (divine abandonment) are terms of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist theological school).

Ibn Mas'ud recited ﴿فَتَمَتَّعُوا فَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ [al-Nahl: 55] with the ta' in both places, meaning: it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves, for you will come to know." The same reading appears in the codex of Ubayy (Ubayy ibn Ka'b's mushaf, a copy of the Qur'an). Abu al-Aliyah recited فَيَتَمَتَّعُوا with the ya' and in the passive voice. "And upon their Lord they rely" — these two are the total of all good: patience, and entrusting affairs to Allah the Exalted.

[p. 158] When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded those who had embraced Islam in Makkah to emigrate, they feared poverty and said: "This is a strangeness in lands where we have no home, no property, and no one to feed us." So He gave them an example from the most common animals that feed themselves without storing, and that do not worry about their sustenance, and do not carry their provision. "Carry" here means: do not transport, and do not look toward storing. This was said by Mujahid, Abu Mijlaz and Ali ibn al-Aqmar. Storing (al-idikhar) has come in a hadith: "How will you be when you remain among the dregs of the people, who store up the provision of a year, due to weakness of certainty?" It was said: it is also possible that it comes from the sense of "hamalah" (surety/guarantee), which does not undertake responsibility for itself and does not worry. Al-Hasan said: "(does not carry its provision)" means does not store; it only rises in the morning and Allah provides for it. Ibn Abbas said: "None store except the human, the ant, the mouse and the magpie." It was said: the nightingale hoards in its lap, and it is said the magpie has hiding places, except that it forgets them. The negation of its carrying of its provision is either due to its weakness and inability to do so, or because it was created without intellect, so it does not plan for what it might store for the future. That is: He provides for it despite its weakness. "And you" means: despite your ability to earn, and your cleverness in obtaining a livelihood, and despite that, your provider is Allah. "He is the All-Hearing" of your saying, "We fear poverty," "the All-Knowing" of what your hearts conceal.

Then the Exalted followed this with their acknowledgment that the originator of the world and the subjector of the two luminaries is Allah. He followed that with the extending and restricting of provision, and said: "Allah extends provision to whom He wills" that He extends it for, "and restricts it" for whom He wills to restrict it. The pronoun in "lahu" (for him) apparently refers back to "whom He wills," so that one individual is extended provision at one time and restricted at another time. It is also possible that the pronoun refers back to him in wording, while the intended meaning is another person whom He wills. This becomes similar to His saying: "And none is granted a long life, nor is his life shortened, except that it is in a Book" (Fatir 35:11), that is, from the life of another person who is granted a long life. And the saying of people: "I have a dirham and half of it," meaning: and half of another dirham. So the one who is given extended provision is other than the one whose provision is restricted. Alqamah al-Himsi read "wa-yuqaddiru" with a dammah on the ya', a fathah on the qaf and a shaddah on the dal. "All-Knowing" means He knows what sets right the servants and what corrupts them.

When He informed that they acknowledge that the Creator of the world, the subjector of the two luminaries, and the giver of life to the earth after its death is Allah, that acknowledgment obligated them that the provider of the servants is Allah, who is the one who guarantees it. He commanded His Messenger to praise Him the Exalted; because in their acknowledgment is the affirmation of Allah's oneness in creation, and the negation of partners from Him in that, and this was a proof against them, since they attributed that to Allah and yet worshipped idols.

﴿But most of them do not reason﴾: since they acknowledge the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life, yet worship other than Him.

﴿And this worldly life﴾: the pointing with "this" is a display of contempt for the world and a belittling of its matter. And how could it not be so? For it does not weigh the wing of a gnat with Allah. That is: in the speed of its passing away from its people, and their death from it, it is nothing but like children playing for an hour and then dispersing. "Al-hayawan" and "al-hayah" (life) have the same meaning, and according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh it is the verbal noun of "hayiya" (to live). The meaning: indeed it is the abode of life, that is, the enduring one that does not cease. Mujahid said: "There is no death in it." It was also said: "al-hayawan" means "the living," and it is as if the verbal noun was applied to the living thing. The Last Abode was described as "life" for emphasis by attributing life to it. The appearance of the waw in "al-hayawan" and in "Hayway" (a proper name of a man) is used as evidence by those who hold that the waw in such a structure is changed to ya' because of the kasrah before it, like "shaqiya" (he was miserable) from "al-shiqwah." As for those who hold that the final radical of the word is ya', they claim that the appearance of the waw in "hayawan" and "hayawa" is a substitute for a ya', as an anomaly. The response of "law" (if) is elided, that is: "if they had known, they would not have preferred the abode of perishing over it." The verbal noun of "hayiya" came in the pattern fa'alan because it indicates movement and agitation, like "ghalayan" (boiling), "nazawan" (leaping), "lahayan" (panting/desire), "jawalan" (roaming), and "tawafan" (circling). And "al-hayy" (the living) is one of much agitation and movement, so this pattern carries the sense of abundant movement.

When the Exalted mentioned that they acknowledge Allah when asked: "Who created the world?" and "Who sends down water from the sky?", He also mentioned another state in which they return to Allah, and acknowledge that He is the one who does what He wills. That occurs when they board the sea, the waves surge and the winds change. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: to what is His saying '"So when they board ships"' connected?" I answer: to an elided element indicated by what He described them with, and explained their situation in terms of what they were described with, of polytheism and obstinacy.

﴿So when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [p. 159] being in the form of those who make religion sincere to Allah from among the believers, since they mention none but Allah and call upon no other with Allah. In "sincere" there is a kind of mockery. "And at once they associate others" is the response to "lamma" (when), meaning: their association with Allah surprised their natural disposition; that is, it did not delay from it even for a moment. The apparent reading of "li-yakfuru" (so that they may deny) is that the lam is the lam of purpose ("kay"), and "wa-li-yatamatta'u" (and that they may enjoy themselves) is coordinated with it in the reading of the one who vocalized the lam with a kasrah, and they are: the two Arabs (Abu 'Amr and Ibn Amir), Nafi' and Asim. The meaning: they returned to their polytheism. "So that they may deny" means: what drives them to polytheism is their denial of what Allah the Exalted has given them, and their pleasure in what they were given of the passing goods of this world. This is unlike the believers, for when they are saved from such hardship, that becomes a cause of gratitude to Allah the Exalted and increased obedience to Him. It was also said: the lam in "li-yakfuru" and "wa-li-yatamatta'u" is the lam of command. This is supported by the reading of the one who made the lam of "wa-li-yatamatta'u" sukun (without vowel), and they are: Ibn Kathir, al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. This command is by way of threat, like His saying: "Do what you will" (Fussilat 41:40).

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "How is it permissible for God, exalted is He, to command disbelief, and to tell the disobedient to do as they wish, when He forbids that and threatens punishment for it?" I say: this is a figurative usage (majaz) for abandonment (khidhlan) and leaving them alone (takhliyah), and that command is a displeasing one, to a certain end. End of quote. Whoever reads وَلْيَتَمَتَّعُوا with a sukun on the lam, and takes the lam in لِيَكْفُرُوا as the lam of purpose (lam kay), then the waw is coordinating one clause with another clause, not coordinating one verb with another verb.

Ibn Atiyyah reported from Ibn Mas'ud: لَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ, with the lam.

Then God reminded them of His blessings, in that He settled them in a town where they felt secure, where no one raided them or plundered them, despite their being few in number and dwelling in a place with no crops. These are among the greatest blessings they disbelieved, and it is a blessing that none can bestow except God, exalted is He.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read يُؤْمِنُونَ and يَكْفُرُونَ with the ya' in both. Al-Sulami and al-Hasan read them with the ta' of address in both.

ألَيْسَ (Is it not?) is an affirmation of their abode in Hell, as in the line: "Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts?"

لِلْكَافِرِينَ (for the disbelievers) is the placing of an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun, meaning: their abode.

﴿وَالَّذِينَ جَاهَدُوا فِينَا﴾: He used the word "striving" (mujahadah) without limiting it by an object, so that it would include striving against the commanding self, against Satan, and against the enemies of the religion. What was reported from the scholars' sayings are examples.

Ibn Abbas said: they strove against their desires in obedience to God, in thanking His blessings, and in patience with His trials.

﴿لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا﴾: We will increase them in guidance to the path of good, as in His words: ﴿وَالَّذِينَ اهْتَدَوْا زَادَهُمْ هُدًى وَآتَاهُمْ تَقْوَاهُمْ﴾ [Muhammad: 17].

Al-Suddi said: they strove for Us by remaining steadfast in faith; We will guide them on Our paths to Paradise.

Abu Sulayman al-Darani said: they strove in what they knew, and We will guide them to what they did not know.

It was also said: they strove in battle, and We will guide them to the paths of martyrdom and forgiveness.

Ibn Abbas said: "the good-doers" (al-muhsinin) means the monotheists (al-muwahhidin).

Others said: "the good-doers" means the strivers (al-mujahidun).

Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said: whoever finds a question difficult, let him ask the people of the frontiers (ahl al-thughur) about it, as in God's words: ﴿لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا﴾.

(وَالَّذِينَ) is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the omitted oath (qasam), and whose answer is: "We will surely guide them." By this and its like, the view of Abu al-Abbas Thaʿlab was refuted; he prohibited the clause of the oath and the thing sworn to from being the predicate of the subject. Its parallel is: ﴿وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ لَنُبَوِّئَنَّهُمْ﴾ ("And those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely settle them...").

How excellent is the reward of the workers!﴾ ﴿Those who are patient and upon their Lord rely.﴾ ﴿And how many a creature does not carry its provision; Allah provides for it, and for you. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon?" they would surely say, "Allah." Then how are they deluded?﴾ ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing of everything.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who sends down water from the sky and thereby gives life to the earth after its death?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Praise be to Allah." But most of them do not reason.﴾ ﴿And this worldly life is nothing but amusement and play. Indeed, the Last Abode is the true life, if only they knew.﴾ ﴿So when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them safely to land, at once they associate others with Him.﴾ ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them and enjoy themselves; but they will soon know.﴾ ﴿Do they not see that We made a sanctuary secure, while people are being snatched away from around them? Then do they believe in falsehood and deny the favor of Allah?﴾ ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies the truth when it comes to him? Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾ ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths. And indeed, Allah is with the good-doers.﴾

Ibn Jubayr, Ata', Mujahid and Malik ibn Anas said: "The land in which injustice and evil are committed, this verse applies to it, and emigration from it to a land of truth becomes obligatory." Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: "Indeed My earth is vast" is a promise of the abundance of provision throughout the whole earth. It was also said: "The earth of Paradise is vast; I shall give it to you." Mujahid said: "Travel to fight His enemies."

As for "so worship Me alone" (fa-iyyaya fa-'budun), it is from the construction of ishtighal (the construction in which the verb is preoccupied with a pronoun referring to the object, so the object is fronted). That is: "So worship Me alone, so worship Me." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the meaning of the fa' in 'fa-'budun', and the fronting of the object?" I (al-Zamakhshari) answer: the fa' is the response to an elided conditional clause, because the meaning is: "If My earth is vast, then if you do not make worship sincere in one land, make it sincere in another." Then the condition was elided, and the fronting of the object was given in its place, along with the fronting conveying the meaning of exclusivity and sincerity. End of quote. This answer requires reflection.

When the Exalted informed of the vastness of His earth, and this was an indication of emigration, and He commanded the worship of Him, one might suppose that whoever leaves his land in which he grew up, for the sake of those who inhabit it from the people of disbelief, to the abode of Islam, will not find things going for him there as they went for him in his own land, and that may perhaps lead to his destruction. So He informed that every soul has a term that it will reach, and it will die wherever it is, and that the return of the gathered to their parts will be on the Day of Resurrection.

لِلْكَافِرِينَ (for the disbelievers) is the placing of an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun, meaning: their abode.

﴿وَالَّذِينَ جَاهَدُوا فِينَا﴾: He used the word "striving" (mujahadah) without limiting it by an object, so that it would include striving against the commanding self, against Satan, and against the enemies of the religion. What was reported from the scholars' sayings are examples.

Ibn Abbas said: they strove against their desires in obedience to God, in thanking His blessings, and in patience with His trials.

﴿لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا﴾: We will increase them in guidance to the path of good, as in His words: ﴿وَالَّذِينَ اهْتَدَوْا زَادَهُمْ هُدًى وَآتَاهُمْ تَقْوَاهُمْ﴾ [Muhammad: 17].

Al-Suddi said: they strove for Us by remaining steadfast in faith; We will guide them on Our paths to Paradise.

Abu Sulayman al-Darani said: they strove in what they knew, and We will guide them to what they did not know.

It was also said: they strove in battle, and We will guide them to the paths of martyrdom and forgiveness.

Ibn Abbas said: "the good-doers" (al-muhsinin) means the monotheists (al-muwahhidin).

Others said: "the good-doers" means the strivers (al-mujahidun).

Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said: whoever finds a question difficult, let him ask the people of the frontiers (ahl al-thughur) about it, as in God's words: ﴿لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا﴾.

(وَالَّذِينَ) is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the omitted oath (qasam), and whose answer is: "We will surely guide them." By this and its like, the view of Abu al-Abbas Thaʿlab was refuted; he prohibited the clause of the oath and the thing sworn to from being the predicate of the subject. Its parallel is: ﴿وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ لَنُبَوِّئَنَّهُمْ﴾ ("And those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely settle them...").

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 29, verses 56–69 (part 1 of 2):**

[p. 157] ﴿O My servants who believe, indeed My earth is vast, so worship Me alone.﴾ ﴿Every soul will taste death; then to Us you will be returned.﴾ ﴿As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely settle them in lofty chambers in Paradise, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. How excellent is the reward of the workers!﴾ ﴿Those who are patient and upon their Lord rely.﴾ ﴿And how many a creature does not carry its provision; Allah provides for it, and for you. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon?" they would surely say, "Allah." Then how are they deluded?﴾ ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing of everything.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who sends down water from the sky and thereby gives life to the earth after its death?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Praise be to Allah." But most of them do not reason.﴾ ﴿And this worldly life is nothing but amusement and play. Indeed, the Last Abode is the true life, if only they knew.﴾ ﴿So when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them safely to land, at once they associate others with Him.﴾ ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them and enjoy themselves; but they will soon know.﴾ ﴿Do they not see that We made a sanctuary secure, while people are being snatched away from around them? Then do they believe in falsehood and deny the favor of Allah?﴾ ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies the truth when it comes to him? Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾ ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths. And indeed, Allah is with the good-doers.﴾

Most of the exegetes (mufassirun, the scholars of tafsir, or Qur'anic exegesis) held that His saying: "O My servants..." up to the end of the verse, was revealed concerning those who were residing in Makkah. They were commanded to emigrate from it to Madinah. That is: distance yourselves from the people of polytheism, and seek out the people of faith. Abu al-Aliyah said: "Travel in search of His allies." Ibn Jubayr, Ata', Mujahid and Malik ibn Anas said: "The land in which injustice and evil are committed, this verse applies to it, and emigration from it to a land of truth becomes obligatory." Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: "Indeed My earth is vast" is a promise of the abundance of provision throughout the whole earth. It was also said: "The earth of Paradise is vast; I shall give it to you." Mujahid said: "Travel to fight His enemies."

As for "so worship Me alone" (fa-iyyaya fa-'budun), it is from the construction of ishtighal (the construction in which the verb is preoccupied with a pronoun referring to the object, so the object is fronted). That is: "So worship Me alone, so worship Me." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the meaning of the fa' in 'fa-'budun', and the fronting of the object?" I (al-Zamakhshari) answer: the fa' is the response to an elided conditional clause, because the meaning is: "If My earth is vast, then if you do not make worship sincere in one land, make it sincere in another." Then the condition was elided, and the fronting of the object was given in its place, along with the fronting conveying the meaning of exclusivity and sincerity. End of quote. This answer requires reflection.

When the Exalted informed of the vastness of His earth, and this was an indication of emigration, and He commanded the worship of Him, one might suppose that whoever leaves his land in which he grew up, for the sake of those who inhabit it from the people of disbelief, to the abode of Islam, will not find things going for him there as they went for him in his own land, and that may perhaps lead to his destruction. So He informed that every soul has a term that it will reach, and it will die wherever it is, and that the return of the gathered to their parts will be on the Day of Resurrection.

Ali read "turja'un" (you will be returned) in the active voice (with the verb built to the subject); the majority read it in the passive voice, with the second-person "ta'" (you). It is narrated from Asim that he read it with the third-person "ya'" (they). Abu Haywah read "dha'iqatu" with tanwin, and "al-mawti" in the accusative. He also read "la-nubawwi'annahum" (we will settle them) from al-mabā'ah (the dwelling). Ali, Abdullah, al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, Zayd ibn Ali, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it from al-thawa' (to dwell); and "bawwa'" (to settle) is transitive to two objects. Allah the Exalted said: "He settles the believers at their stations for battle" (Al 'Imran 3:121). It has also come transitive with the preposition "li-" (for). He the Exalted said: "And when We settled for Ibrahim the place of the House" (Al-Hajj 22:26). The meaning is: He will make for them a place of dwelling, that is, a place of return to which they retreat. "Ghurafan" means lofty chambers. As for "thawa," its meaning is "to stay," and it is an intransitive verb. The hamzah of transitivity (af'ala) was added to it, so it became transitive to one object. It has been read with shaddah as "'addā" with doubling, so "ghurafan" is in the accusative, either by dropping the preposition (in chambers), and then the usage was widened and it was elided; or by the verb being understood to include the meaning of settling, so it is transitive to two objects; or it is like a place-adverb specific to the vague, through which the verb reaches it. It is narrated from Ibn Amir: "ghurufan" with a dammah on the ra'. Ibn Wathhab read "fa-ni'ma" with a fa'; the majority read it without fa'. "Those who are patient" means: patient over leaving their homelands, emigration, and all hardships, from carrying out the commands and avoiding the prohibitions.

"And upon their Lord they rely" — these two are the total of all good: patience, and entrusting affairs to Allah the Exalted.

[p. 158] When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded those who had embraced Islam in Makkah to emigrate, they feared poverty and said: "This is a strangeness in lands where we have no home, no property, and no one to feed us." So He gave them an example from the most common animals that feed themselves without storing, and that do not worry about their sustenance, and do not carry their provision. "Carry" here means: do not transport, and do not look toward storing. This was said by Mujahid, Abu Mijlaz and Ali ibn al-Aqmar. Storing (al-idikhar) has come in a hadith: "How will you be when you remain among the dregs of the people, who store up the provision of a year, due to weakness of certainty?" It was said: it is also possible that it comes from the sense of "hamalah" (surety/guarantee), which does not undertake responsibility for itself and does not worry. Al-Hasan said: "(does not carry its provision)" means does not store; it only rises in the morning and Allah provides for it. Ibn Abbas said: "None store except the human, the ant, the mouse and the magpie." It was said: the nightingale hoards in its lap, and it is said the magpie has hiding places, except that it forgets them. The negation of its carrying of its provision is either due to its weakness and inability to do so, or because it was created without intellect, so it does not plan for what it might store for the future. That is: He provides for it despite its weakness. "And you" means: despite your ability to earn, and your cleverness in obtaining a livelihood, and despite that, your provider is Allah. "He is the All-Hearing" of your saying, "We fear poverty," "the All-Knowing" of what your hearts conceal.

Then the Exalted followed this with their acknowledgment that the originator of the world and the subjector of the two luminaries is Allah. He followed that with the extending and restricting of provision, and said: "Allah extends provision to whom He wills" that He extends it for, "and restricts it" for whom He wills to restrict it. The pronoun in "lahu" (for him) apparently refers back to "whom He wills," so that one individual is extended provision at one time and restricted at another time. It is also possible that the pronoun refers back to him in wording, while the intended meaning is another person whom He wills. This becomes similar to His saying: "And none is granted a long life, nor is his life shortened, except that it is in a Book" (Fatir 35:11), that is, from the life of another person who is granted a long life. And the saying of people: "I have a dirham and half of it," meaning: and half of another dirham. So the one who is given extended provision is other than the one whose provision is restricted. Alqamah al-Himsi read "wa-yuqaddiru" with a dammah on the ya', a fathah on the qaf and a shaddah on the dal. "All-Knowing" means He knows what sets right the servants and what corrupts them.

When He informed that they acknowledge that the Creator of the world, the subjector of the two luminaries, and the giver of life to the earth after its death is Allah, that acknowledgment obligated them that the provider of the servants is Allah, who is the one who guarantees it. He commanded His Messenger to praise Him the Exalted; because in their acknowledgment is the affirmation of Allah's oneness in creation, and the negation of partners from Him in that, and this was a proof against them, since they attributed that to Allah and yet worshipped idols.

﴿But most of them do not reason﴾: since they acknowledge the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life, yet worship other than Him.

﴿And this worldly life﴾: the pointing with "this" is a display of contempt for the world and a belittling of its matter. And how could it not be so? For it does not weigh the wing of a gnat with Allah. That is: in the speed of its passing away from its people, and their death from it, it is nothing but like children playing for an hour and then dispersing. "Al-hayawan" and "al-hayah" (life) have the same meaning, and according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh it is the verbal noun of "hayiya" (to live). The meaning: indeed it is the abode of life, that is, the enduring one that does not cease. Mujahid said: "There is no death in it." It was also said: "al-hayawan" means "the living," and it is as if the verbal noun was applied to the living thing. The Last Abode was described as "life" for emphasis by attributing life to it. The appearance of the waw in "al-hayawan" and in "Hayway" (a proper name of a man) is used as evidence by those who hold that the waw in such a structure is changed to ya' because of the kasrah before it, like "shaqiya" (he was miserable) from "al-shiqwah." As for those who hold that the final radical of the word is ya', they claim that the appearance of the waw in "hayawan" and "hayawa" is a substitute for a ya', as an anomaly. The response of "law" (if) is elided, that is: "if they had known, they would not have preferred the abode of perishing over it." The verbal noun of "hayiya" came in the pattern fa'alan because it indicates movement and agitation, like "ghalayan" (boiling), "nazawan" (leaping), "lahayan" (panting/desire), "jawalan" (roaming), and "tawafan" (circling). And "al-hayy" (the living) is one of much agitation and movement, so this pattern carries the sense of abundant movement.

When the Exalted mentioned that they acknowledge Allah when asked: "Who created the world?" and "Who sends down water from the sky?", He also mentioned another state in which they return to Allah, and acknowledge that He is the one who does what He wills. That occurs when they board the sea, the waves surge and the winds change. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: to what is His saying '"So when they board ships"' connected?" I answer: to an elided element indicated by what He described them with, and explained their situation in terms of what they were described with, of polytheism and obstinacy.

﴿So when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [p. 159] being in the form of those who make religion sincere to Allah from among the believers, since they mention none but Allah and call upon no other with Allah. In "sincere" there is a kind of mockery. "And at once they associate others" is the response to "lamma" (when), meaning: their association with Allah surprised their natural disposition; that is, it did not delay from it even for a moment. The apparent reading of "li-yakfuru" (so that they may deny) is that the lam is the lam of purpose ("kay"), and "wa-li-yatamatta'u" (and that they may enjoy themselves) is coordinated with it in the reading of the one who vocalized the lam with a kasrah, and they are: the two Arabs (Abu 'Amr and Ibn Amir), Nafi' and Asim. The meaning: they returned to their polytheism. "So that they may deny" means: what drives them to polytheism is their denial of what Allah the Exalted has given them, and their pleasure in what they were given of the passing goods of this world. This is unlike the believers, for when they are saved from such hardship, that becomes a cause of gratitude to Allah the Exalted and increased obedience to Him. It was also said: the lam in "li-yakfuru" and "wa-li-yatamatta'u" is the lam of command. This is supported by the reading of the one who made the lam of "wa-li-yatamatta'u" sukun (without vowel), and they are: Ibn Kathir, al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. This command is by way of threat, like His saying: "Do what you will" (Fussilat 41:40).

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "How is it permissible for God, exalted is He, to command disbelief, and to tell the disobedient to do as they wish, when He forbids that and threatens punishment for it?" I say: this is a figurative usage (majaz) for abandonment (khidhlan) and leaving them alone (takhliyah), and that command is a displeasing one, to a certain end. End of quote. Takhliyah (leaving someone to themselves) and khidhlan (divine abandonment) are terms of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist theological school).

Ibn Mas'ud recited ﴿فَتَمَتَّعُوا فَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ [al-Nahl: 55] with the ta' in both places, meaning: it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves, for you will come to know." The same reading appears in the codex of Ubayy (Ubayy ibn Ka'b's mushaf, a copy of the Qur'an). Abu al-Aliyah recited فَيَتَمَتَّعُوا with the ya' and in the passive voice. Whoever reads وَلْيَتَمَتَّعُوا with a sukun on the lam, and takes the lam in لِيَكْفُرُوا as the lam of purpose (lam kay), then the waw is coordinating one clause with another clause, not coordinating one verb with another verb.

Ibn Atiyyah reported from Ibn Mas'ud: لَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ, with the lam.

Then God reminded them of His blessings, in that He settled them in a town where they felt secure, where no one raided them or plundered them, despite their being few in number and dwelling in a place with no crops. These are among the greatest blessings they disbelieved, and it is a blessing that none can bestow except God, exalted is He.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read يُؤْمِنُونَ and يَكْفُرُونَ with the ya' in both. Al-Sulami and al-Hasan read them with the ta' of address in both.
